All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
22:03:02 UTC
07:03:02 KST

Nvidia interim CEO and long-time CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.
For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.
Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’s company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.
Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.
Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.
An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, the Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.
So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO and any talks to bring him back.
China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.
But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’s company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.
Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed was located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.
So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.
China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.
The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.
Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.
Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours' (techcrunch.com) 2
			
		 	
				The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports:  Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. [...] After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool's developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains "widely accessible" for use in cyberattacks.
It's not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration -- including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:47:19 UTC
06:47:19 KST

Spamhaus Sender Guidelines
Requirements and recommendations to help email senders follow best practices and strengthen trust and safety on the internet.
Starting in November 2026, we are gradually rolling out a requirement for every sending IP to have a valid HELO, a reverse DNS (PTR) record, and a matching A record. Use the HELO checker below to see whether the DNS meets our best practices, and follow the guidelines to avoid being listed.
Minimum requirements
Guidance for senders, mail admins, and postmasters on meeting Spamhaus's sending requirements. All senders must meet these minimum email sending requirements to avoid being listed.
- Use confirmed opt-in (COI) for all subscribers Each recipient should confirm their address by clicking a link in a confirmation email. If no confirmation is received, do not send email to that address. Purchased, rented and harvested lists are the most common source of spam trap hits, and hitting traps is one of the fastest routes to a listing. See section
- Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. See section
- Use a HELO/EHLO hostname that resolves to the sending IP The hostname the server announces in the HELO/EHLO command must resolve to the IP it is connecting from, and must stay consistent across connections from that IP. Placeholder values, hosting-provider defaults, and hostnames that vary between connections are treated as signals of misconfiguration or compromise and can result in a listing. See section
- Meet the IPv6 allocation and reverse DNS minimum If sending over IPv6, the sending address must fall within an allocation of /64 or larger (a /64 is the standard block size we recommend assigning), and that space must have valid reverse DNS. IPv6 ranges without reverse DNS or with allocations smaller than /64 are often misused by spammers. See section
- Authenticate mail with SPF, DKIM and DMARC Publish SPF and DMARC records for every sending domain, sign every outbound message with a signature, and align the DKIM sending domain with the domain in the message's RFC 5322 From address. Authentication is one of the signals that shapes reputation, so gaps here make a listing more likely when other signals are weak. See section
Operating an Email Server Provider (ESP) or other shared sending infrastructure? See the ESPs and Large Senders guidelines
1. Infrastructure and DNS
All sending infrastructure must have the following DNS and mailserver configuration. Failure to do so can result in IPs being listed on the Email Spam IPs (CSS) or compromised IPs (XBL) zones.
Do
- Ensure the sending IP address has a valid reverse DNS (rDNS) entry resolving to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for the sending IP address. Spamhaus will treat emails originating from IP addresses without rDNS as suspicious and this will be reflected in the IP's reputation, and receivers using Spamhaus data may subject it to additional filtering.
- Ensure the rDNS hostname resolves to the connecting IP address via a corresponding forward DNS (A/AAAA) record.
- Abusive actors often rely on the reputation of upstream DNS records to hide their identity. Instead, configure a branded reverse DNS to use the sender's own domain, to improve trust signals for the IP address.
Don't
- Do not use generic or auto-generated rDNS entries for dedicated IPs that point to the hosting provider (e.g., static-203-0-113-25.hosting.example.net, 203.113.0.25.broadband.example.net, vps-25.dedicated.hosting.example.com etc). These can negatively impact reputation.
- Do not use random dictionary words in the rDNS and make it identifiable to the sending infrastructure.
How to check
Use the Spamhaus DNS checker tool to check your rDNS configuration.
Do
- Ensure the hostname used in the HELO/EHLO command resolves to the sending IP address.
- Maintain a consistent HELO value that resolves to the sending IP address. Multiple HELO values resolving to different IP addresses may indicate residential proxy and/or malware behaviour.
- Where possible, ensure the HELO/EHLO hostname is consistent with the rDNS hostname.
- Host a webpage on the domain of the HELO, that explains what the domain is for, or that redirects to the main brand domain.
Don't
- Do not use placeholder values such as localhost or generic hostnames that point to the hosting company/ISP as the HELO value.
- Do not resolve HELO hostname to infrastructure that is not used for sending — this behaviour is associated with spoofing and misconfiguration.
- Do not use generic or auto-generated names provided by the hosting provider, use the sender's own domain where possible.
- Do not impersonate the HELO value of well-known mailbox providers like Gmail or Hotmail.
How to check
Enter an IP address into the Spamhaus DNS Checker at the top of this page, to check its HELO value. An email can also be sent to helocheck@abuseat.org to check the HELO being used.
Do
- IPv6 customer allocations must be at least /64 and must have valid reverse DNS. The /64 minimum is consistent with IPv6 subnet architecture and RFC 6177's guidance that email senders should be able to obtain at least a /64. This is further discussed in M3AAWG best practices for IPv6 allocation.
- Add routes for all IP space owned by the sender to reduce vulnerability to BGP hijacking, which can allow hackers to send email that appears to originate from the IP space.
How to check
Run dig -x <an IPv6 address in the allocation> to confirm reverse DNS is present. To confirm the space is actually routed, look the address up at bgp.he.net.
Do
Don't
- Do not allow freemail addresses such as gmail.com or hotmail.com as the 'Envelope FROM.'
- Do not use the NULL envelope sender <> for anything other than indirect out-of-band delivery reports, DSNs and MDNs.
- Do not send bounce messages after accepting unwanted mail. Reject it during the SMTP transaction instead. Bounces sent to forged senders are known as backscatter, which is indirect spam and can severely harm reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <envelope sender domain> and confirm an SPF record is returned and includes the sending IPs.
Do
- Audit DNS regularly and remove records for services, hosts and IP space that are no longer used, including CNAMEs, NS delegations, A records and SPF include: entries for former providers.
Don't
- Do not leave records pointing to decommissioned hosts or former providers. Dangling records can be claimed by others and used to send mail that appears to come from the domain.
- Do not use wildcard DNS records.
This article explains domain, hostname terminology and domain alignment in email. Also, use aboutmy.email to check for email configuration setup.
How to check
Run dig against the subdomains and look for CNAMEs that resolve to a provider that no longer serves the domain.
2. Authentication
Authentication is how receiving mail servers verify that emails are authorized to send from the domain. Without SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, the domain is exposed to spoofing and phishing, and emails are more likely to be rejected or flagged by Spamhaus.
Do
- Publish an SPF TXT record in the domain's DNS zone file that specifies exactly which IPs and hosts are authorized to send email on the domain's behalf.
- Ensure the sending IP is explicitly included in the SPF record. Email sent from IPs not included in SPF will not pass SPF checks.
- Make sure both the HELO domain and the envelope From domain have a valid SPF record. Publish SPF records on this domain (which might be the infrastructure domain) and not the visible header From domain.
- Keep the SPF record within the 10 DNS lookup limit (this includes all nested include: statements). Exceeding the limit returns a PermError, which is not a pass, so SPF cannot authenticate mail or satisfy DMARC alignment.
- Keep the SPF record as narrow as possible. Only include the sending infrastructure actually in use.
Don't
- Do not use overly permissive qualifiers like +all or broad include: ranges that authorise IP space not under the sender's control.
- Do not leave include: statements for providers no longer used for sending. Audit the SPF and remove outdated vendors. Check for typos.
- Avoid using SPF macros unless needed. They are expanded per message at evaluation time, which is costly and makes failures more likely.
- Do not use a or mx mechanisms where ip4: or ip6: would work. Each one costs a DNS lookup against the limit of 10, while ip4: and ip6: cost none.
How to check
Run dig TXT <domain>, then count the mechanisms that trigger a DNS lookup — include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect — and confirm the total is 10 or fewer.
Do
- Ensure every outbound message carries a valid DKIM signature, using a minimum 1024-bit key length while 2048-bit is recommended.
- Ensure that the d= domain on the DKIM signature matches the domain on the header From.
- Rotate DKIM keys at least annually, or immediately if a key is suspected to be compromised.
- Use a different d= domain for different mailstreams (for example, separate subdomains for transactional and marketing email), so that each mailstream builds its own reputation.
How to check
Run dig TXT <selector>._domainkey.<domain> (the selector is set in the ESP's DKIM setup page) and confirm a DKIM key, starting v=DKIM1, is returned.
Do
- Publish a DMARC record with a policy defined for the sending domain.
- Ensure the header From domain aligns with the DKIM signing domain (d=) so that DMARC alignment passes.
- Set up a DMARC aggregate report address (rua=) from day one as this will help audit email sent from the domain.
Don't
- Do not remain at p=none permanently. Starting with p=none is acceptable, but we recommend having an enforcement policy.
How to check
Run dig TXT _dmarc.<domain> and confirm a DMARC record, starting v=DMARC1, is returned.
3. Permission and List Hygiene
Send email only to people who want to receive it. Once the technical infrastructure is in place, the next step is building a legitimate list of email addresses from people who have provided explicit permission to receive the email. Lack of permission is one of the most common reasons for being listed by Spamhaus.
Do
- Ensure all bulk email is ONLY sent to recipients that have Confirmed Opt-in (COI). Send a confirmation email requiring recipients to explicitly opt-in to verify their email address. This will prevent unwanted signups, bot signups and typo email addresses. If no opt-in is received, do not send email to that address.
- Utilise available signals like bounce data, feedback loops, postmaster tools and engagement data to ensure the mailing list is up to date and email is sent to an engaged audience.
- Keep a timestamped record of when and how permission was obtained.
Don't
- Do not send emails to purchased, rented, or harvested lists, as these are the most common source of spam trap hits.
- Permission is NOT transferable. Do not grant or assume permission retroactively or transfer it between organisations or domains.
How to check
Look for high bounce rates, low engagement and unusual sign-up patterns in the mailing platform.
Do
- Refer to the guidelines from M3AAWG for managing spamtraps, and follow the best practices outlined in our resources.
- Implement a robust email sunset policy to help remove temporary email sign-ups and email addresses that no longer engage with email.
Don't
- Do not attempt to identify or suppress a spam trap address. Audit the acquisition process to identify which list segment or collection method introduced the problem address, and remove that source entirely.
Spamhaus spamtraps do not subscribe to email or engage with them.
According to M3AAWG spam trap best practices, mailboxes that remain inactive for more than 12 months can be repurposed as spamtraps.
4. Sending best practices
How email is sent matters as much as what is sent. Warming the IP and domain, maintaining a consistent volume, using trusted links and domains within emails, and providing clear, legitimate ways to opt-out of emails will help improve overall deliverability.
Do
- HELO domains which DO NOT have a sending history will be subjected to additional filtering. Please read our best practices around IP/Domain warm-up.
- Start sending slowly, and consistently for any IP address or domain that has not sent email in the past 90 days, before gradually increasing volume.
- Domains which have been registered in the past 24 hours will be part of Spamhaus Zero Reputation Domains (ZRD) list.
- Additionally, domains used for mailing within 30 days of registration will be treated suspiciously and we recommend following best practices for newly registered domains.
- Treat any change in IP or HELO hostname as a new asset if no prior sending history is available, and apply the same warm-up process as used for a new IP or domain.
- Begin with a few initial campaigns sent to the most engaged recipients to reduce the risk of hitting older invalid addresses. Maintaining a slow and consistent email volume will help build a strong sender reputation.
Don't
- Do not use warm-up services that generate artificial traffic or simulate opens, clicks and replies. Using an engagement inflation service will result in the IP or domain being listed.
- Infrastructure operated to inflate engagement or otherwise trick filters will be listed as a spam-enabling service.
- Do not send inconsistent email volumes or trigger a sudden spike in sending, as this could negatively impact reputation.
- Do not send to addresses which are old and unengaged while warming the IP or Domain.
- Do not send the entire daily volume in a single burst at the top of the hour. Spread it across the day as spikes in mail volume can look suspicious.
- Do not use more IPs than required to manage the mail volume as this can be perceived as snowshoe behaviour.
- Do not begin sending on new infrastructure without carrying the suppression list across. Addresses that previously bounced or unsubscribed will otherwise be mailed again, and old inactive addresses are where recycled spam traps sit.
How to check
Plot the daily send volume for the IP or domain against the warm-up schedule and confirm it is increasing gradually, not spiking.
Do
- Keep the overall bounce rate below 5%.
- Suppress hard bounces immediately.
- Investigate and remove repeated soft bounces after a defined threshold; this is typically 3–5 consecutive bounces.
Don't
- Avoid using email list validation as a source to clean spamtraps as it does not do so, and is not and never will be a replacement for permission.
Do
- Bulk commercial senders: Implement the List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click header enabling one-click unsubscribe directly from the inbox (RFC 8058).
- Include a clearly visible unsubscribe link in the body of every commercial email.
- Action unsubscribe requests within 2 days and add them to a suppression list.
Don't
- Do not hide or obfuscate unsubscribe links.
- Do not require recipients to authenticate to unsubscribe.
- Avoid use of one-click unsubscribe in the body of an email; instead, make sure the link leads to a confirmation page.
How to check
Send a test campaign to a test mailbox, open the message headers (e.g. Gmail's "Show original"), and confirm that List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post are both present. Also check that all links in the email work.
Do
- Use HTTPS for all links, and only use links generated by the sender's own system.
- Sign or validate tracking and redirect links so they cannot be altered to point elsewhere. This prevents malicious actors from abusing them as open redirects.
Don't
- Do not use free or unbranded URL shorteners in the content of an email. URLs and/or domains used in the content of an email will affect the overall reputation of the sending domain.
5. IP and Domain Reputation
The reputation of the IP and domain as seen by Spamhaus can be checked via our reputation checker.
Spamhaus looks at multiple signals before assigning a reputation score, and a strong negative signal can outweigh the absence of positive ones — so following all email best practices consistently is essential.
Factors that influence reputation include: the service provider, the IP neighbourhood, the infrastructure the IPs are associated with, the upstream networks that connect to internet backbones, and the IP or domain's history — when it was first seen, when it was last used, and how it was used.
Do
- Check the IP reputation and domain reputation regularly and do not wait for a delivery issue or listing to discover an issue.
- Associate the domain with network providers and registrars that maintain a good reputation. The reputation of the hosting provider or registrar can be checked on our reputation statistics page.
- Ensure newly registered domains are not used for at least 30 days from registration. The domain can be used for non-email purposes during this period, and establishing a web-presence prior to sending email will help improve the credibility of the domain.
- Refer to our recommendations for best practices when using newly registered domains.
Don't
- Do not use newly registered domains in SMTP as a FROM domain or a HELO domain unless the domain is properly warmed up. Similarly, using a newly registered domain in the content of the email can also look suspicious. The age of the domains used in the email can affect the overall sending reputation.
- Do not use cousin domains for additional mailstreams or geographies for the same brand. Use sub-domains.
- Do not hide WHOIS information for the root sending domain. The reputation of the upstream provider may be used for evaluating domain reputation. The reputation of the upstream provider can be checked in our Registrar reputation page.
How to check
Run the domain through the Reputation Checker to get more insights.
Note: We do not accept requests for explanations of the attributes shown here or requests to reset reputation.
6. ESPs & Large Senders
ESPs and shared infrastructure hosts are responsible for the email sent via their infrastructure. Hosting abusive senders will negatively impact the reputation of shared domains and infrastructure.

In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:41:57 UTC
06:41:57 KST

Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

OpenCode Browse

Browse
An MCP server and a Chromium extension that let your agents use your real browser, with your tabs, your logins and your extensions. They open tabs in the background, grouped out of your way, and read pages, click, type, take screenshots and record tabs. When it's your turn, for a login, a 2FA prompt or a payment, they hand the tab back to you and continue once you click Continue.
- Your real browserChrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Helium, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium.
- Out of your wayAgent tabs open in the background, in collapsed groups.
- HandoffsDo the login or 2FA step yourself, then click Continue.
- Lend a tabClick the toolbar button to hand an agent a tab you have open.
- Record and captureScreenshots, tab recordings and network traffic.
- Any MCP clientOpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Zed and many more.
- All your loginsAgents use the sites you're already signed into. No keys, no setup.
- Allowed sitesKeep an agent's tab on the sites you name.
Install the Chrome extension first. It walks you through the rest of the steps. To install the CLI directly (you should not need to do this), use any of these.

CNN, Zoom, Fox News Served Visitors a Crypto-Stealing Skimmer – OPTIMJACK (Nov 2026)
Attacker JavaScript injected into Optimizely bundles swaps visitor crypto addresses and skims cards on 10+ sites. Chain, payload, IOCs.
Summary
One poisoned tag layer, 15 household-name websites, millions of exposed visitors. Attacker JavaScript injected into Optimizely bundles is serving a crypto-clipper + card-skimmer to visitors of CNN, Zoom, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce, GitLab, American Eagle, Hootsuite and seven more — plus side vectors through a first-party bundle, a Jscrambler-protected script, and one malvertising impression. If your site loads Optimizely, assume your visitors are in the blast radius until you check the bundle.
Terms
Risk to a marketing and IT team
If your site loads Optimizely, your visitors are the targets: pasted wallet addresses get swapped before submission, card forms get skimmed, and page URLs plus cookies plus a screenshot leave with every hit. Your origin can be clean while your visitors are robbed — the compromise sits in the tag layer. Three-step check: (1) fetch your served Optimizely bundle and search it for 1688360; (2) alert on Content-Security-Policy script-src violations naming unknown hosts; (3) verify with a test wallet address on a staging page that what you paste is what gets submitted.

My Quest to push native Three.js quality match AAA Game Engines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:07:43 UTC
06:07:43 KST

Building the AAA Lighting Pipeline in Three.js
From the G-buffer to temporal upscaling, here is each stage of the lightmap, probe and screen-space reflection pipeline measured against Three.js: what games require of it, what Three.js has today, and the pull requests in review or still to write.
Ben Houston • • 34 min read
This post is the progress report: the recommended pipeline from Part 2, measured against Three.js one stage at a time.
It uses the lighting terms from Part 1: indirect diffuse and specular, source, coverage, SSR and SSGI. It adds five more:
- BRDF: the material's shading function: how a surface turns incoming light into the light you see.
- G-buffer: per-pixel images of the visible surface (depth, normal, roughness) that screen-space effects read.
- TRAA: temporal anti-aliasing; each frame is blended with the reprojected frames before it.
- TAAU: temporal anti-aliasing with upscaling; the same accumulation, but the scene is rendered below the output resolution and the history is kept at the output resolution.
- PMREM: an environment map pre-blurred for every roughness level, which is how Three.js lights from a cubemap.
The pipeline#
The pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.
The setup: three caches. Lightmaps take the most work, and the probe grid is a single bake. Solid steps are in Three.js today; tinted ones are in review.
Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:
One frame of the pipeline. Solid stages are in Three.js today, tinted ones are in review or partly there, and outlined ones are still to build. The output of TRAA, or of TAAU when upscaling, feeds the next frame's SSR and SSGI.
Where things stand#
Here is how each stage compares with what the games require. Each row is explained in its own section below:
The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF. Everything else is in Three.js, in review or drafted.
It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.
So far, though, these pieces have been proposed and reviewed one at a time, each on its own merits. Nobody has been asked to sign up to the whole. This series is my attempt to put them together into one coherent picture, so that each PR can be judged for where it fits as well as for what it does.
The pipeline, stage by stage#
The rest of this post walks through the frame one stage at a time. For each, it asks three questions: what do the games require, what does Three.js already have, and what is missing. The answers to the third question are where the work is.
The G-buffer#
What the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers all run in screen space before lighting, so they need a per-pixel description of the visible surface: a G-buffer. A deferred engine stores everything lighting will need, including base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. A forward renderer like Three.js has an advantage here: the beauty pass shades each material directly, so the G-buffer only needs what the screen-space passes read.
Base color, emissive and the material AO map are not on the list: the beauty pass reads them straight from the material.
What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today. Normals are packed into RGB8 with roughness in alpha, base color with metalness in a second RGBA8 target, and velocity in a third:
const scenePass = pass( scene, camera );
scenePass.setMRT( mrt( {
	output: output,
	diffuseColor: vec4( diffuseColor.rgb, materialMetalness ),
	normal: vec4( packNormalToRGB( normalView ).rgb, materialRoughness ),
	velocity: velocity
} ) );
So the mechanism exists. The gaps are the layout and the normal precision.
G-buffer structure and memory#
A layout that covers the table above, in three render targets plus depth:
Sixteen bytes per pixel is lean by AAA standards. Deferred engines commonly spend 20–28, because they also store base color, emissive and baked lighting.
The G-buffer is not the only screen-sized memory, though. The rest of the frame adds a half-float beauty target (8 B), TRAA history and output (16 B), the previous depth for reprojection (4 B), SSR's Hi-Z pyramid (about 5 B with its mips), the half-resolution SSR working set (6 B), the half-resolution SSGI working set, which holds the occlusion too, with the reprojected previous frame it reads (about 5.5 B together), and scene-resolution upsampled SSR and SSGI results (15 B together). That brings the planning budget to roughly 76 bytes per pixel with every effect on: about 157 MB at 1920×1080 and 626 MB at 4K. Part 2 links the calculator behind these numbers, with TAAU and lower-tier examples. These are estimates for the proposed cascade and simple filters, not measured allocations of the current addons. The upsampled targets are included in this inventory. Half-resolution effects still need a depth- and normal-aware upsample so reflections and occlusion do not bleed across object edges. I have drafted that filter as jointBilateralUpsample(); more on it under occlusion below.
Normal precision#
The one field Three.js stores too coarsely today is the normal. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of quantized directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.
AAA G-buffers solve this with octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. We have added packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal() to Three.js in PR #35480:
That is fifteen times more accurate with half floats, and over a hundred times with snorm, for the same four bytes. RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.
Reflections traced from RGB8 normals (left) show banding; octahedral RG16F normals (right) are smooth.
Angular error of the stored normal: RGB8 (left) and octahedral RG16F (right), at the same scale.
Global illumination#
What the games require. From the survey:
- Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move.
- A probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.
Lightmaps. The runtime side has been in Three.js for years: every standard material takes a lightMap, read from a second UV set. What was missing was everything needed to make one: an unwrapper, a baker, a solver worth using, and a way to store and ship the result. Those now add up to a complete baking pipeline that runs in the browser. It is a large enough subject that it has its own post, Part 4, Adding Robust Light Baking to Three.js.
Light probes. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example). It worked well; the limit was how long a capture took.
Sponza lit by LightProbeGrid.
Probe capture speed. Batching probe captures made LightProbeGrid four times faster, and later changes doubled that again: it now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, and supports multi-bounce light. Profiling showed the bake was limited by the CPU submitting render passes, not by the GPU, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera: a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%. The second doubling came from culling each draw against its own sub-camera.
Leaking probes. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. DDGI-style visibility weighting for LightProbeGrid works as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly per pixel, so the draft can instead use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four. On Sponza that adds about 10% to the render time, where eight probes add 30%.
Probe visibility weighting: the warm room and the blue room no longer light each other through the wall.
Ambient and specular occlusion#
What the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.
GTAO finds occlusion by searching the depth buffer for the horizon around each pixel. Horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same search and gathers the light it finds along the way, so one pass returns both. The pipeline therefore never runs the two side by side: with SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs on its own only when SSGI is off.
Which light occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. In this pipeline occlusion is not a step of either cascade. It is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext as it is today, and the sources that need it read it and darken their own answer:
- The lightmap, probe grid and environment apply AO to their indirect diffuse, combined with the material's AO map as min( materialAO, gtao ).
- The reflection probes and environment apply GTSO to their indirect specular.
- SSR and SSGI apply neither. A screen-space hit is something the ray actually found, so it is already correctly occluded.
- Behind SSGI, the diffuse sources skip AO. SSGI's coverage is the share of the hemisphere that something on screen blocks, which is the occlusion itself. The cascade already scales the lightmap or probe grid by 1 − coverage, so applying AO as well would darken them twice.
- Direct light is untouched, because it has shadows.
The cascades never see any of this; they combine colors by coverage and nothing else. The one rule a source must follow is that occlusion darkens its color, never its coverage. An occluded probe still answers the pixel, only darker; lowering its coverage instead would let the next source's unoccluded light leak into the corner.
Applying AO to lightmapped surfaces darkens them slightly twice, since the bake already includes static self-occlusion. We do it anyway, because dynamic objects still need to occlude static ones.
What Three.js has. GTAO is already there, and it already feeds the lighting rather than being multiplied over the final image. The AO example renders a prepass, runs GTAO on it, and hands the result to the beauty pass through a lighting context:
const aoPass = ao( prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera );
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext( aoPass.getTextureNode().sample( screenUV ).r );
This is exactly the pattern the rest of the pipeline needs, and it matters again below.
The gaps. There are three.
- Specular occlusion. Today GTAO outputs a single visibility value, and the physical lighting model turns it into specular occlusion with a heuristic based on the view angle and roughness. It does not know which directions are blocked, so metal keeps reflecting the sky inside folds. Bent normals and GTSO are up as a draft PR. The bent normal comes out of the same horizon search with no extra depth samples; the cost is an AO target that grows from one byte per pixel to four.
- Edge-aware upsampling. Half-resolution GTAO upsampled with a bilinear filter leaves dark outlines around objects, because occlusion from the surface behind bleeds across each silhouette. jointBilateralUpsample() upsamples using the full-resolution depth and normals as guides (Kopf et al. 2007), so the result stops at the edges. It is drafted and not yet submitted, with the AO example as its first user; half-resolution SSR needs the same filter.
- Bent normals from SSGINode. The draft adds the bent normal to GTAONode. SSGINode needs the same output, taken from the directions its search found open, so that specular occlusion does not need a second pass when SSGI is on.
With GTSO (left), folds and cavities stop reflecting the sky. With a scalar specular occlusion (right), they still glow.
Reflections: screen-space reflections#
What the games require. From DOOM, Frostbite and the others, SSR in a cascade has to:
- Trace efficiently over any distance, using a Hi-Z depth pyramid.
- Output coverage, so the probes can fill what it misses.
- Trace the previous frame's lit image, so its result can feed the current frame's lighting.
- Denoise spatially and temporally, so one ray per pixel is enough.
What Three.js had. In September, Three.js's SSR was built for a different job: adding reflections on top of a finished image, in a compact scene. It took few samples, so rough surfaces were noisy. It was composited over the image, so it did not go through the BRDF. And its rays stopped at a fixed distance, so reflections of anything far away were missing.
Much of that has changed since. SSRNode now importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, validates and refines its hits, and uses Houston Stratified Noise, also known as HHW (Hierarchical Hashed Weyl) noise, in place of a blue noise texture. Its result is reprojected and accumulated over time, and fed back so reflections show reflections.
What it does not yet do is fit into a cascade. Here is how the SSR example combines it with the scene:
const litColor = scenePassColor.rgb.add( denoisedReflections.rgb );
The beauty pass renders first, SSR traces that same image, and the reflections are added on top. Each requirement above is a gap from there.
Hi-Z tracing. SSRNode currently marches the depth buffer in up to 64 steps out to a maxDistance, with a thickness tolerance for deciding a hit. Long rays are expensive, and both values need tuning per scene. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the minimum depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and fine steps only near surfaces, so cost grows with the log of the ray's length. Every ray can then go as far as the screen allows, with no maximum distance to tune. Storing both the minimum and maximum depth in the pyramid also helps the thickness test: a single depth layer cannot tell whether a ray passed behind an object or into it, and the extra bound narrows that ambiguity. The technique is from Uludag's Hi-Z Screen-Space Cone-Traced Reflections in GPU Pro 5, building on the screen-space ray marching of McGuire and Mara. Frostbite (for smooth surfaces), AMD's FidelityFX SSSR and Killing Floor 2 all use it. A first prototype matches linear marching bit for bit across 48 GPU test cases, but it is not yet a net win: the traversal saves up to about 7%, and building the pyramid costs more than that. On a GTX 1050, one test scene fell from 199 to 159 fps and another from 126 to 97. The next step is a cheaper pyramid build, in a single compute dispatch as in AMD's SPD, measured together with the traversal.
Hi-Z ray marching: large steps across empty space, small steps near the surface.
Coverage. Today, a ray that misses samples an environment map itself, inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice: once in the beauty pass, and once in SSR's own fallback. In a cascade, SSR should instead output its reflection and its coverage, lowered near the screen edge, at grazing angles, behind thin geometry and on very rough surfaces, and leave the rest to the probes. We have prototyped this; it lands together with the BRDF integration below.
Tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.
Two rules keep this loop healthy. First, the image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping, bloom and other post-processing; otherwise reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. Second, the fed-back radiance must be clamped. Each frame's reflections become the next frame's input, so a single firefly or a slight energy gain in the denoiser compounds frame after frame instead of fading away.
Reflections only. With previous-frame feedback, reflections appear inside reflections.
Denoising. Rough reflections need more than one ray's worth of information per pixel, and Three.js does not yet have a spatio-temporal denoiser designed for SSR. Frostbite's is the model: reuse rays from neighbouring pixels, weighted by each pixel's own BRDF, then accumulate over time, reprojecting history by the reflected hit point's motion rather than the surface's, since reflections move differently from the surfaces that show them. zalo is working on this. His SVGF-based DenoiseNode has merged, but the SSR examples have gone back to the previous denoiser while it is reworked for reflections. The next attempt will be judged with a debug harness. One piece is already prototyped: demodulation, which divides the surface color out of the signal before filtering and multiplies it back afterwards, so the denoiser blurs lighting and not texture detail.
The same noisy signal and the same filter, without demodulation (left) and with it (right).
Screen-space global illumination#
SSGI is the diffuse counterpart of SSR. It adds the bounce light a bake cannot know about, it reuses almost everything SSR needs, and it replaces GTAO whenever it is on.
What the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of a cascade, as Part 1 describes. That means SSGI has to:
- Output coverage: the share of the hemisphere in which it found a surface on screen. The rest falls through to the lightmap or the probe grid.
- Trace the previous frame's lit image, so its result can feed the current frame's lighting, and so bounce light gains a bounce each frame.
- Accumulate over time, at half resolution, with the same edge-aware upsample as SSR.
What Three.js has. SSGINode already exists, built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. For each pixel it steps outward along a slice of the hemisphere, marks which sectors of that slice the depth buffer blocks, and collects the color of whatever blocks them. One search of 24 depth samples by default yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. That is why this pipeline budgets one temporal history for it and no separate spatial filter. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it:
const composite = vec4( scenePassColor.rgb.mul( ao ).add( scenePassDiffuse.rgb.mul( gi.rgb ) ), scenePassColor.a );
The gaps. The same as SSR's, and for the same reason.
- Coverage output. The sectors the search marks as blocked are the directions in which it found a surface, so coverage is 1 − ao, and the node already computes it. What is missing is handing the GI and that coverage to the cascade as a pair. Without that, SSGI can only be added on top of the baked bounce, which counts it twice, and cannot replace it.
- Previous-frame tracing. Reading the current frame's beauty pass forces SSGI to run after it, as a composite. The previous-frame tracing being added for SSR applies here with the same rules: linear HDR before tone mapping, and clamped. One thing differs. SSR reads the previous frame once per pixel, where its ray lands, and SSGI reads it at every sample that finds a surface, so reprojecting at each read is paid many times per pixel. A draft measures it on an Apple M3: reprojecting every sample by camera motion costs 14–22% of the frame rate, and by per-pixel velocity, which also follows moving objects, 32–44%. So the previous frame is instead reprojected once, by velocity, into a half-resolution buffer lined up with the current frame, and the search reads that directly. That runs at the same frame rate as tracing the current frame, with no visible artifacts in the test scenes.
- A diffuse source. Once it has both, SSGINode becomes the first entry in the diffuse list described below, with no change to the materials.
Reflections: local probes and the cascade#
What the games require. Three.js grew up rendering a single object floating in space, lit by one environment map, and for that it is superb. Indoors, one environment map is simply wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue, not the sky.
Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, solves this with local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected: the reflection ray is intersected with the room's box first, and the cubemap is sampled toward that hit point instead of along the raw ray. That one step removes most of a cubemap's parallax error, so the far wall's reflection stays put on the floor as you walk (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend, and the sky beyond them is just the outermost probe: one with an infinite box and no box projection.
What Three.js has. The ingredients are there. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it for roughness, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. But that is one probe per material, set by hand. There is no notion of a set of probes in a scene, of influence volumes, or of blending between them.
The gaps, and how we are filling them.
- A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
- Fast access to many probes. Binding one cubemap per probe does not scale. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, the texture class is in review.
- Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so it sees that room's bright, open view everywhere it is used. A dark corner or the inside of a cupboard then reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both, so it costs almost nothing. It does mean a reflection probe needs to see the diffuse result at the pixel, which the pluggable design allows for. It is still to do.
- Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is plenty for blurry room reflections, since SSR in front of it handles the sharp ones, and it takes a quarter of the memory. Prefiltering at 128² is still to do.
Two connected rooms, each reflecting its own walls, from three box-projected probes.
Indirect lighting in the BRDF#
What the games require. The cascades only work if the bounced light goes through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it exactly as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer, that means the beauty pass needs two inputs:
- Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage; then the lightmap on static meshes; on everything else, the probe grid, falling back by coverage to the environment map outside the grid's volume.
- Indirect specular: SSR, falling back by coverage to the box-projected probes, falling back to the environment map.
The sources that need occlusion apply it themselves, as described above.
Both then go through the usual split-sum approximation (Karis 2013) alongside the direct lights.
Engines differ in where this happens. Deferred engines like Unreal sample lightmaps while filling the G-buffer and composite reflections in a separate full-screen pass. Three.js renders forward, so the natural fit is to compute everything screen-space, SSR, SSGI and AO, before the beauty pass and let each material read it while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.
What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO already reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.
The gap. This is the biggest missing piece. There is no way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. What we want is the AO pattern, extended to both terms, with today's environment map as the unchanged default. The proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
TRAA and TAAU close the loop#
What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing is standard in every modern engine. Here it does double duty: its output is next frame's input to SSR, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections.
What Three.js has. A good TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history.
TRAA is in good shape, and no major gap stands in the way. Two refinements remain:
- Sharper history. History sampled with a bilinear filter blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp.
- Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping is what stops ghosting: it rejects history that no longer matches the current frame. But it also rejects good history. TRAA already tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories actually scored worse. A drafted change, not yet submitted, widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Measured with the TRAA harness, a static view gains 2.15 dB of PSNR against the supersampled reference and a still camera with moving objects gains 1.3 dB, while fast camera motion is unchanged to within 0.06 dB.
Upscaling with TAAU#
Every engine this series measures itself against renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077. It is the largest single performance lever in a modern frame, because every pass before the resolve gets cheaper at once.
What Three.js has. TAAUNode already does this, and the TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels. It follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The scene pass renders at a reduced resolution, set with setResolutionScale(). The node jitters the camera, reconstructs each output pixel from the 3×3 jittered input samples around it, and blends that with a history kept at the output resolution, using the same depth rejection and variance clipping as TRAA plus a lock that protects thin features:
scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );
const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );
How it fits. TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame, and nothing else in the frame changes shape:
- Everything before it runs at the render resolution. The G-buffer prepass, Hi-Z, SSR, SSGI and the beauty pass all take the same resolution scale. The node applies its jitter to the camera for the whole render pipeline, so the prepass and the beauty pass stay aligned.
- Its output is the image the next frame's SSR and SSGI read. That image is linear HDR at the output resolution, so reflections are traced at the render resolution but read colors that are sharper than the frame that traced them. The two rules from the SSR section still apply: read it before tone mapping, and clamp it.
- Bloom, tone mapping and the rest of post run after it, at the output resolution.
It also changes the memory budget above. With SSR and SSGI on, the 76-byte native-resolution TRAA budget has about 60 bytes in scene-resolution resources and 16 bytes of history and resolve. TAAU uses about 24 canvas-sized bytes instead, including its lock history, so its model is 60 × resolution scale² + 24 bytes per canvas pixel. At a scale of 0.5 that is about 39 bytes instead of 76: a 4K frame drops from about 626 MB to 322 MB, and shades a quarter of the pixels. The extra TAAU history means the memory reduction is smaller than the pixel reduction. Part 2 links the calculator, which includes a provisional traffic allowance for the upscaler.
TAAU and the joint bilateral upsample are not alternatives. They upscale different things. jointBilateralUpsample() is spatial and works within one frame: it takes a half-resolution intermediate buffer, AO or SSR or SSGI, up to the render resolution before the beauty pass reads it, guided by depth and normals. Those buffers are smooth and noisy, with no detail to recover, only edges to respect. TAAU is temporal: it takes the finished image from the render resolution to the output resolution, and recovers real sub-pixel detail from jittered frames. A frame can use both. With both at 0.5, though, SSR and SSGI run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so with TAAU on it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral step.
The gaps.
- Wiring it into the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline here has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and SSR's previous-frame read has to take TAAU's output. None of that has been tried together yet.
- Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Every temporal upscaler pairs with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale. Three.js does not apply one yet.
- The TRAA refinements. TAAU samples and clips its history the way TRAA does today, so Catmull-Rom history and the wider clip at rest apply to it as well, and the TRAA harness should measure it against the same supersampled reference.
- A cheaper lock. The lock is one value per pixel but is stored in a second half-float RGBA history target. A single 8-bit channel would save 7 bytes per output pixel.
Future work#
A few threads are worth pulling once the pipeline is complete.
- Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise gives SSR excellent sampling without downloading a texture, but it costs about 400 operations per sample, and every pixel pays that every frame. That is too much for something so basic. The promising trade is to shift some of the work into a small precomputed map: a few hundred kilobytes, generated at startup in 50 ms or less, that keeps HSN's properties while making each sample a lookup and a few adds.
- Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, as every game has. Three.js does not have it yet.
- A physically based sun and sky. The Three.js sky is built for artistic control, not physical light levels. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky that agree with each other and with the exposure: atmospheric scattering computed on the GPU, with the sun's color and intensity derived from the atmosphere in real units. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
- Reflection probes in glTF. KHR_lightmap carries lightmaps, but there is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load; a fuller version would also carry the prefiltered cubemaps, so nothing needs capturing at all.
- Directional lightmaps. The lightmaps here store a single irradiance value per texel, so normal maps cannot respond to baked light. Directional lightmaps restore that response for a few more bytes per texel: an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.
What is left#
The biggest gap is the last one a frame needs: a way to plug both cascades into the material's BRDF. It changes more of Three.js than any other stage here, so it has its own post.

Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:01:02 UTC
06:01:02 KST

As promised last month, Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”
“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple wanred in a new blog post aimed at app developers.
Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.
While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models.
To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.
Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making.
For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes is designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections.
To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders.
The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes.
Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche.
There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option.
The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making.
Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.”
Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park (www1.wdr.de) 27
			
		 	
				Slashdot readers djgl and Mirnotoriety shared a story about how a Microsoft Outlook outage contributed to a chlorine leak at Germany's Phantasialand theme park, injuring 15 guests, four of whom were hospitalized. German broadcasting institution WDR reports (translated to English):  We were all affected by this problem: On Friday, there was a disruption that crippled the US software company Microsoft, including its email program Outlook. Phantasialand was also affected. Due to the disruption, no emails were received, as the company informed WDR on Saturday. As a result, no one was aware that the sauna area's maintenance safety system had already issued an email alert. This was because the automatic dosing system had pumped too much chlorine into the pool.
Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Bruhl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday. Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15.  Cybersecurity architect and computer scientist Stephan Skrobisch said Microsoft is not responsible for the incident. "It's clearly the system's design that's the problem. They failed to implement an additional notification mechanism."
Slashdot reader davidwr agrees, writing in a comment: "Proper alarms would be a hardwired alarm that would be visible or audiable to someone who was on-site who could've gotten everyone out of the water. The blame for the injuries goes to the water park and/or whatever consultant told them it was okay not to have an on-site, hardwired alarm."

Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:48:08 UTC
05:48:08 KST

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

Caltech professor no longer grades homework's because everyone uses AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:47:53 UTC
05:47:53 KST

Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday.
Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large.
Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion.
"There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."
Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student.
And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all.
From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT.
In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions.
Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods.
The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record.
So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major, said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts.
"I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around.
"I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said.
If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least.
Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora.
But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs.
Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed."
"Syllabuses are changing," he said.
