First phase of embedded assessments at OpenAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:07:20 UTC
01:07:20 KST

Our first phase of embedded assessments
We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.
Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.
Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems(opens in a new window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.
In this pilot assessment, Apollo Research(opens in a new window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:
- Training did not incentivize subversion.
- Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.
- Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.
- Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.
For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.
Goodfire(opens in a new window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.
We intend to conduct two assessments with METR(opens in a new window), focused on model alignment and monitoring:
- Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.
- Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment(opens in a new window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.
Transluce(opens in a new window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.
OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.
We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.
Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.
Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.
Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.
Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.
Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.
Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.
Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.
These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.
We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.
In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

Serena Williams winds down her VC firm, launches new fund, targets $200M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:06:30 UTC
01:06:30 KST

Serena Williams and longtime business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures.
The firm is seeking to raise $200 million in capital to back AI-native companies that are “solving critical, underserved problems for individuals across the experience economy,” including in areas such as fintech and health and wellness, the fund said in a press release announcing its launch.
This fund is separate from Serena Ventures, which Williams founded in 2022. A rep for Starfire confirmed that Serena Ventures has recently cut its last check, though a team remains to support the existing portfolio. Serena Ventures backed more than 100 companies and raised over $100 million in capital. Ferreira worked as an advisor and general partner at Serena Ventures and has co-invested with Williams since 2015 when they backed MasterClass’ seed round.
This new firm, Starfire, is a continuation of that business partnership, with Williams saying in the press release that it was “designed to live beyond” them and that the goal remains to broaden “access to capital” and create “opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”

01:00:14 KST

Even in an era of inflation like the one we’re living through now, $100 can still buy a lot… if you know where to look. In fact, it’s enough to get something useful and well-made, but not so pricey that it’s likely to leave you with lingering guilt or lead to insurmountable debt.
The Verge’s guide to the best gifts under $100
A Benjamin can score you one really sweet gift or several memorable stocking stuffers.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
As reviewers, shoppers, and endless tinkerers ourselves, we’re well-versed in recommending stuff in this price tier. Below, you’ll find our favorite items at $100 or less that we think are fun, eccentric, and surprisingly handy. From open-style earbuds and gaming gear to handheld vacuums and e-readers, our picks should suit just about anyone on your shopping list, at a price most can get behind.
Anker’s 140W hub is a stellar gift for anyone short on plugs but loaded with gadgets. It turns a single AC outlet into two and provides four USB ports in total. That means you can charge two USB-C gadgets and two USB-A devices at once while still powering more demanding products.
BougeRV T1 Portable Telescopic Light
BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.
We’re big fans of Epilogue’s Operator Series, which lets you play retro game cartridges on a macOS or Windows machine with streamlined emulator software. Like the company’s Game Boy Operator, the Super Nintendo / Famicom version offers a simple way to play, save, and copy those old cartridges over a USB-C connection.
Blissbury Ear Pillow
If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
The first 3D Zelda game has been remade for the modern era. And if you fear it will diverge too much from the Nintendo 64 original, fear not: This carefully crafted remake delivers updated graphics and improved controls alongside the same stellar adventure we remember.
It seems melodramatic to say a good power drill can change your life, but anyone who does a lot of DIY projects knows it’s at least partially true. The Power Driver from Skil offers simplified driving, drilling, and screwdriving with up to 200 inch-pounds of torque and USB-C charging to tackle a range of jobs.
CMF Clip Pro earbuds
Open-style earbuds can compromise bass quality, but the convenience of an airy, clip-on option that keeps your ear canals open is hard to overstate. CMF’s Clip Pro leverage the Nothing offshoot’s talents for slick design in an affordable package, offering solid performance, fun features, and serious comfort.
Google Home Speaker
Google’s orb-shaped Home Speaker is impressive in terms of design and sound quality, especially for a speaker this compact. We’re less enthused about Gemini’s sluggish response time, but it offers intuitive conversational understanding, and the speaker’s ability to link with Matter and Thread devices adds real convenience.
For giftees with pets and / or children, there’s no such thing as having too many vacuums on hand. The cordless Ryobi One Plus perfectly bridges the gap between a robovac and stand-up models. With powerful suction and handy accessories, it’s just the ticket for quick cleanups, especially in the car, on stairs, and in between couch cushions.
We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks, a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.
The Switch 2 is a great device for gaming on the go, but its bulky dock is tough to pack. Genki’s pocket-sized brick is a brilliant alternative, with USB-C, USB-A, and HDMI 2.1 passthrough for displaying Switch 2 (and other handheld) games on your TV without Nintendo’s first-party behemoth.
Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.
Igloo KoolTunes Bluetooth speaker cooler
If you’re looking to spice up your barbecue or tailgate party, look no further than Igloo’s KoolTunes. The retro-inspired boombox cooler holds up to 26 cans and, for a twist, features a built-in Bluetooth speaker with up to 10 hours of battery life.
No, it’s not a AAA membership for 24-hour roadside service — your giftee’s parents probably already bought them that. An A24 membership is much more fun, since it includes movie tickets to every weird, wild, and existential A24 film that hits theaters, plus zines, merch perks, and more.
Apple AirTag (second gen)
You can give the gift of lost-then-found with a four-pack of Apple’s AirTags. With seamless, accurate tracking, they’re the perfect way for iPhone owners to locate everything from luggage to puppies. The latest models also have better tracking and louder sirens, boosting your chances of reuniting with your favorite things.
Camp Snap’s 110D is like catnip for vintage camera nerds. The digital point-and-shoot offers basic 8-megapixel resolution, a built-in flash, and filter compatibility, letting you capture both wide-angle and macro shots. Its photos likely won’t win you any awards, but its stylish, tactile design makes it a blast to give and get as a gift.
Oxo Cold Brew Coffee Maker
Cold brew is as expensive as it is delicious, but it doesn’t have to cost you a ton. Oxo’s excellent Cold Brew Coffee Maker provides a way around the cold brew tax, without the hassle. Its overnight brew method provides storable, low-acid results so your favorite giftee can get their chill fill straight from the fridge instead of the cafe.
Brick
For the phone-addicted person in your life, there’s Brick. The physical key lets users block up to 50 time-dissolving apps, from X to TikTok, while still letting them access essential software. It’s too bad that some of us need tech like this, but perhaps using it for a while will help you find the balance you need.
Mobile gaming is a big business, but not everyone likes playing on a touchscreen. Accessories like the Prio make it easier, and unlike competing options, Razer’s solution gets super small. The controller folds down to fit in your pocket and expands to seven inches for full-sized control and compatibility with a bunch of modern phones.
Portable electronics seem to be all about going foldable these days, and why shouldn’t keyboards get in on the fun? Keychron’s B11 Pro is a swell gift for anyone who likes to pack an on-the-go keyboard, with concave keys, an ergonomic layout, and versatile connectivity over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz.
If you have a budding filmmaker in your circle, give them this tunable smart light and watch them work. Unlike most color bulbs, the Accent B7c has a built-in battery that lets it run for up to 70 minutes when unscrewed, and it offers granular, flicker-free control for perfect scene lighting.
Reto’s Kodak-branded camera offers some neat tricks for $99. It uses 35mm film and glass elements in the lens, while adding modern extras like auto-wind, rewind, and an automatic flash. Its coolest features include a double-exposure setting that lets artistic shooters create stylish photos on glorious film, plus two focus points.
Packing light is essential for all travelers, but it’s particularly vital for those who trek long distances. This high-capacity Nitecore charger is a killer addition to any pack, with water resistance, fast charging, and a slim, lightweight design that can power your devices without weighing them down.
Xteink X4 Pro e-reader
If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.
Pokémon Pokopia
Pokopia brings Pokémon to life in a cozy worldbuilding game that borrows the best from predecessors like Minecraft and Animal Crossing. The twist? The slow-burning Switch 2 title eventually rolls into an expansive adventure that lets you customize as you go.
Built for jet setters, Anker’s 100W travel adapter features a durable design, a handy LCD display to track charge percentage, and compatibility in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does have four USB inputs for all your portables, including a trio of USB-C ports.
For those who enjoy clever devices that just work, we give you Nimble’s “breakable” SharePower Portable Charger. The magnetically joined power bank quickly snaps into a pair of 20W batteries, letting two people charge their phones, or works as a single 10,000mAh unit for larger top-offs.
For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.

I Just Hosted My First Friendsgiving — Here’s Everything I Made That People Loved
It’s that time of year again: hosting season. Between all the official holidays that are approaching and all the other ones that our friends and family have created to spend more time together, there are many reasons to start prepping a holiday menu now.

I know it’s customary to do a potluck-style Friendsgiving, but we had 11 guests traveling in for the weekend so we decided to divide the cost of groceries and all other prep duties. A few people were on the decorating committee, others were on drinks duty, and we even had someone in charge of bringing the vibes.

And if I can take all the empty plates and compliments to the chef as anything, it’s that this spread delivers a delicious (yet pretty easy) Friendsgiving meal. Just make sure to prep what you can ahead so you can spend more time sipping wine! After all, this day is about being together with friends.

Generative AI Usage in the Games Industry
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:59:48 GMT
00:59:48 KST

The following manifesto was written by members of the IWGB Game Workers' Branch in collaboration with members of Game Workers Unite Ireland of the Republic of Ireland, CSVI of Spain, and the FIOM-CGIL Milan Work Council
Introduction
Our Aims
We, a collective of video game unions and work councils from Europe, write this manifesto to raise awareness of the harms of generative AI (genAI) use within the video game development sector.
GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce. Left unchecked, this harm will continue to grow and impact more workers, more games, and more players, even more acutely.
Our goal is to bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce, as well as to set guidelines and standards for games industry workers, stakeholders, and regulators, suggesting actions which can be taken to reduce – and ideally eliminate – these dangers.
Scope
This manifesto discusses genAI in the context of the video game development sector. These uses include, but are not limited to:
- The creation of assets included in a released game which are experienced by players – for example: art, sound, code, and dialogue assets.
- The creation of materials which are used as part of the process of development but which players won’t experience when playing the released game – for example: early concept art, reference materials, pre-translations, etc.
By “genAI” we mean a specific type of AI used to generate text, pictures, videos, or music in response to limited inputs (usually just text “prompts”) using LLMs and other energy-intensive models. The wider harms of genAI won't be covered here, but they constitute additional extremely compelling reasons to resist the use of genAI. These include:
- Severe harm to the environment (Zewe, 2025)
- The destruction of communities (Nguyen, 2025)
- The exploitation of the Global South (F.Regilme, 2025)
This document won’t go into detail about how different genAI models work, nor discuss the comparative quality of their output.
The focus of this document is on games industry workers (us!), how we are and will be impacted, and how we can resist.
The Impact of GenAI
GenAI Creates Worse Working Conditions
- GenAI is both directly and indirectly replacing game industry workers.
- Many game workers are being forced to use genAI, either explicitly or implicitly.
- Working with genAI is less desirable, fulfilling, and educational than the same work without genAI.
- Over time, working with genAI leads to worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout.
- Using genAI removes a sense of ownership from workers.
- GenAI is causing a marked decline in junior positions within the industry, leading to a lack of new talent.
Proponents of generative AI claim that it is a tool of empowerment for workers. For that to be true, every worker would be free to choose if, when, and how to use it. We would also need to trust that every employer would use the promised productivity improvements to benefit their workers.
In practice, this is not what we are seeing.
In many workplaces today, workers are being forced to use genAI ‘tools’, sometimes in very specific ways (Plunkett, 2025). Some companies do not explicitly impose the usage of genAI, but set expectations which cannot be reached with or without its use. Allowing the choice of usage, while also creating expectations that the worker should be able to keep pace with automated procedures, is no choice at all (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025).
When workers do use genAI, they find work more onerous than before. Many of the tasks related to genAI work are more tedious and less fulfilling, since the work becomes less about exercising the skills workers have built and invested in, and instead pivots to a plethora of small, parallel tasks which amount to supervising genAI and bug-fixing its output.
Workers using genAI have reported ‘AI brain fry’ and reduced focus (Pearl et al., 2025). Although gains to productivity are possible, these tend to be short term. Employees often initially work faster, take on larger tasks, work overtime, and ignore breaks, due to working with genAI feeling 'more like chatting' (Rangantathan & Ye, 2026). However, once this novelty declines, so does productivity, with workers reporting cognitive fatigue, burnout, and inhibited decision making.
A recent study (Shaw & Nave, 2026) showed that participants who used genAI frequently adopted results that were systematically incorrect, especially under time pressure but also in the face of incentives and feedback. The researchers were able to prove that users of genAI habitually delegate their agency and offload decision making to an external party with relative ease. They call this process ‘cognitive surrender’ (Shaw & Nave, 2026).
The use of genAI also removes a sense of ownership from workers, who become alienated from the results of their labour: the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers’ stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them.
GenAI is disproportionately used for work which would traditionally be given to junior workers, and is hence directly reducing the amount of junior positions available within the industry. This is worsening an already existing problem for newcomers to the industry, who are finding it harder than ever to find work, but it is also a loss of potential fresh perspectives, and is staggeringly short-sighted when it comes to the industry’s sustainable future.
GenAI has a profound negative impact on workers by reducing the availability and appeal of work. Games are best made by people, and people do their best when they are healthy and connected to their work, refining their skills and accumulating real experience.
GenAI Harms Relations Between Workers and Employers
- GenAI is sold to employers as an alternative to workers.
- GenAI often increases pressure on workers when used by employers to set policy, timescales, etc.
- GenAI can be used by employers to abdicate responsibility.
GenAI’s promise to employers is to more fully automate processes, to enable them to be completed with fewer workers. This directly reduces the amount of jobs available for game workers. In some cases, workers have even been forced to train the models which then replaced them, leaving them unemployed.
GenAI interfaces are engineered to be human-like and eager-to-please, to prioritise keeping the user engaged, even if engagement comes at the cost of providing them with incorrect information. GenAI’s predisposition towards this sycophancy and lack of real-world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions (Cheng et al., 2026).
In addition, when employers engage with human-like genAI models which never tell them ‘no’, they become less receptive to criticism and pushback from other workers.
GenAI can also obfuscate and confuse employers’ accountability, in two main ways. Firstly, employers may shift their own accountability onto these platforms, blaming an error on the “tool”, rather than accepting responsibility themselves. Secondly, they may blame workers for issues which arise through the use of genAI – which the employers have mandated.
Any time genAI is used without exacting human verification, the possibility of error increases. Exacting human verification takes time, which negates the promise of genAI automation, and therefore many employers are choosing to skip this step, either directly or indirectly by imposing time constraints on workers which make detailed verification impossible. Workers are then blamed for failures in the genAI’s output.
Employers see genAI as a way of cutting labour costs, employing fewer workers than they would need to without it. GenAI companies ingratiate themselves with employers, by promising the impossible. Moreover, mistakes made by genAI are often blamed on the workers, rather than the employers mandating its use.
GenAI Appropriates the Work of Workers
- GenAI models are often trained on stolen third-party data, with employers failing to credit or compensate the original creators.
- Where genAI models are trained on internal data, employees/creators are likewise rarely credited or compensated.
GenAI models are mostly trained on stolen datasets, and, as stated by the owner of a genAI company, ‘impossible to create’ without stealing data (Milmo, 2024). Employers often feel entitled to automatically include their employees’ contribution into their internal dataset without consent and/or extra compensation.
This point does not require much explanation, but please do not let the relative smallness of this section undermine its importance: stealing the creations of others is wrong, creating very similar versions of those creations is wrong, and using those similar versions to generate wealth which the original creator does not share in is wrong.
GenAI does not create, it appropriates. Content output by genAI has its origins in the work of humans, who are rarely compensated for that output.
GenAI Perpetuates Discrimination
- Most genAI models are trained on datasets that carry an intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities.
- GenAI content averages out data used to train the AI, leading to a homogenisation of culture.
GenAI models are trained on vast swathes of historical data which is often unvetted and without context, as they aggregate large amounts of data and look for commonalities to generate a response without any direct connection to reality. The use of old data can reflect outdated opinions and values which we would be horrified at today, as well as generate middle of the road solutions.
The predominance and absence of certain types of people in historical data can also reinforce their predominance or absence in the output of genAI models today: for example, the predominance of white male doctors in historical medical literature may lead genAI models to assume that a referenced doctor is white, or to create a white male character when asked to create a doctor.
Within the games industry, this has two main types of effect: it can increase discrimination within workplaces, for example, when used in hiring practices, and it can reduce the range of representation within created media, leading to more homogenous characters and viewpoints in the games we create and play.
GenAI reproduces both historical and contemporary biases and can lead to both implicit and explicit discrimination, including but not limited to racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, etc.
GenAI Has Hidden Costs
- GenAI’s output is unreliable and often incorrect.
- GenAI providers obfuscate the cost of genAI, its inner workings, and its limitations.
- GenAI providers aim to silo and monopolise knowledge to sell it back to corporations.
GenAI providers obscure a significant portion of their associated costs (to the environment, mental health, etc.), which impacts the ability of workers to make an informed choice on whether and how to use them (Nguyen, 2025).
GenAI platforms also disincentivise education on their limitations. Average usage of genAI goes down with increased understanding of how genAI actually works behind the scenes (Tully et al., 2025, 20).
GenAI providers sell employers a seductive image of the future, where production can be fully automated. However, in actuality, genAI platforms are gatekeeping transferable skills (Shadmi & Merchant, 2025). Once a model is trained, the ‘owner’ (usually a large conglomerate) of the trained AI has a uniquely powerful position and complete ownership over skills that were previously owned and shared by workers.
This is bad for workers, but it is also bad for employers who outsource their knowledge and skills to third-party genAI providers, as once these companies have a monopoly on this previously institutional knowledge, their prices are unlikely to remain competitive.
GenAI providers aim to replace employers’ dependence on workers with dependence on their own models. Companies which buy into this promise while genAI usage is cheap may come to regret this when it is the only option and prices increase. Workers will regret this much sooner.
Recommendations
Given the present and future impact of genAI on the games industry, we make the following recommendations:
Recommendations for Workers
We understand that the industry is very unstable at present, and that can make it more difficult to speak out. Please do as much as you are comfortable with, and remember that we are stronger together.
- Avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible.
- Make your voices heard.
  - Distance yourself from genAI usage.
  - When genAI content is presented to you, question its use and express dissatisfaction.
  - Talk to your colleagues about the risks and harms of genAI.
  - Make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI.
  - Support other colleagues when they speak out about genAI.
- Do not burn yourself out because of artificially inflated expectations. Do not be a hero by trying to work at an unrealistic pace.
- Educate yourself on how to spot genAI content so that you can avoid accidentally using it in your own work.
- Seek out information on your company’s genAI services from impartial sources, and share it with your colleagues.
- Ask your local worker representatives to negotiate an agreement on genAI usage for your company. Discuss its contents with your colleagues.
  - This agreement could reinforce protections on refusing to use genAI.
  - You could ask to form a committee to evaluate/investigate violations on genAI usage.
- Organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat.
Recommendations for Employers:
- Listen to your workers.
  - Involve the workforce in development of policy regarding genAI.
  - Workers should be the ones who decide when, where, and how to use it.
- Listen to your customers.
- Avoid the use of generative AI entirely.
  - Ensure that no worker is required to use genAI.
  - Disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development and prototyping.
  - If it is absolutely impossible to avoid usage, label/declare usage precisely.
- The chain of accountability at work should be respected and managers should be held accountable for the output of their team.
- Inform workers about the negative outcomes of using genAI. Information should come from impartial sources, not companies trying to sell their genAI services.
- Schedule training for workers on how genAI actually works behind the scenes, its real limits and capabilities.
- Do not use your employees’ work as training data. If you do:
  - Only use data after explicit consent.
  - Ensure fair compensation for reuse of their labor.
  - Allow them to withdraw their work from such datasets.
Recommendations for Players:
- Support games made without genAI.
- Be vocal about disliking genAI in games – leave comments, make videos, ask for change.
- Educate yourself on how to spot genAI content so that you can avoid it.
Recommendations for Regulators:
The UTAW Tech Workers’ Inquiry have put together an incredible resource with suggestions for regulators which we wholeheartedly agree with:
https://techworkersinquiry.org/ai/
In addition to their points, we would also like to suggest that:
- It should be forbidden to submit a person’s work to any genAI dataset without explicit permission and consent, and most importantly without fair compensation for reuse of labour.
- Any acceptable submission must be for datasets that are transparent in how data is used, stored, and retained. Workers must be able to withdraw their content from such datasets at any time
Conclusion – GenAI Against Humanity
GenAI is worsening our working conditions. Our belief is that workers should be the ones who decide when, where and how to use it, as they are the ones who know how to do their jobs. No one likes being forced to do something that harms them, and a lot of workers are being forced to use genAI against their will.
We do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games;
it is not inevitable.
If genAI was just a useful tool, as advertised, it would make our lives easier and we would have more free time, but the opposite is happening. The owners of these tools are aware of this and that is why they push it: to normalise it, to spread its use, and to ensure it becomes indispensable before raising prices. They are the ones in power, not workers, not even CEOs in video game studios.
We firmly believe that video games are nothing without the humans who make them – they are a way for us to express ourselves, to share knowledge or a point of view with the world, to entertain all kinds of gamers. There is no intent in anything made by a genAI probabilistic engine. If no one put their skill, effort, soul, and time into making a game, why would anyone waste their time playing it?
In the current context, everything has to be data-driven: percentages, averages, time spent, productivity… But quality is subjective and cannot be measured, so companies disregard it. People want high-quality games, they want to spend their time playing a game whose developers poured everything into making it, because they are more enjoyable, as it happens with any other art form.
Years after the public release of genAI chatbots, their use has not been as widespread as their owners would like, but they have been deployed as an excuse for mass layoffs with the goal of pleasing shareholders. We should stop thinking about what is good for business, but instead think about what is good for society in general, for workers, for gamers. What good is it if a CEO earns millions every month if the working conditions at their studio are worsening, along with the video games they create?
No genAI will be able to replace the humanity in any work of art.
We are sick of shareholder value being the be-all and end-all of this industry.
We are sick of watching five giant conglomerates just shuffling money around in a giant scam to be the winner of this never-ending hype contest.
We are sick of seeing people fired or forced to quit just to maximise profits.
We are sick of being told to just accept that this is what is good for business.
GenAI is bad for workers and games. Workers, protect your interests. No games get made without our collective strength. Organise. Fight for your rights.
FAQ
- What happens if most of my colleagues want to use genAI in some capacity? In other words, if a developer really wants to use genAI as part of their process, can they use it?
- The short answer is yes. Obviously the other problems are still there, therefore you should decide as a collective if you want to use it, on the whole, given concerns around the environment, cost, ethics, law, honesty, the sanctity of art, etc. Our aim in this document is to educate people about the harms of genAI, so that both employees and employers are less inclined to use it.
- What if the quality of the output is good, or good enough?
- This doesn’t change the main focus of our manifesto. We want workers’ conditions to improve, and to organise against abuses and for better ownership.
- Why are you talking about AI and not layoffs, RTO mandates, workplace toxicity, etc.?
- While the issues caused by genAI are coming from the same place as these other adjacent crises, the genAI situation is developing rapidly and has practical knock-ons to every aspect of our industry. We’re still working on the other issues plaguing our industry, with old and new methods, and we encourage everyone to join us in that fight.
- How do I know if I should get compensation for an AI-generated output? Is there even a way to find out if a specific data entry was important for a generated output? Or to remove a data entry from a set?
- There are examples of research going in this direction like “WAGLE: Strategic Weight Attribution for Effective and Modular Unlearning in Large Language Models” (J Jia, J Liu, Y Zhang, P Ram, N Baracaldo, S Liu, 2024) and “Losing is for Cherishing: Data Valuation Based on Machine Unlearning and Shapley Value” (Ma, Le ; Yang, Shirao ; Wang, Zihao ; Wang, Yinggui ; Wang, Lei ; Wei, Tao ; Zhang, Kejun, 2025), but the specific implementation is not important.
- Why are you against the future?
- We are not. We simply believe that workers have the right to shape their future. Being exploited and overworked is not a future we are willing to accept. Time will prove genAI ‘tools’ and their usefulness, let us not be trampled in the meantime. The future is not yet written.

Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:52:19 UTC
00:52:19 KST

Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book. The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says.
The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.
The feature follows last month’s launch of a handful of AI tools that let users engage more with the story, interact with characters, or catch up with the help of recaps. These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions. That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.
Audible’s new feature takes a cue from how Amazon is already using AI to help people shop: On the Amazon storefront, AI can summarize buyers’ product reviews so shoppers can get a quick sense of what people had to say, as well as the pros and cons of a particular item. In Audible’s case, it’s pulling information about what people liked about the book from publicly available reviews.
But such a feature could limit users’ exposure to negative reviews if the AI only pulls information from those that offer positive remarks. (Further testing will be needed to see if this is the case, of course.)
Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.
The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.
The company’s other recent AI features, Recaps and the interactive “Ask a Question” tool, are also now expanding to more U.S. titles, and will become more broadly available in December. These features will only be available to customers who have purchased a title or who have access to the book as part of their Audible membership, the company said.
“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author. Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

Psychic: Like fzf but learns from your actions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:33:34 UTC
00:33:34 KST

psychic: like fzf but learns from your actions
psychic is a fast file browser with ML-powered ranking
Most days I’m in the terminal cd’ing into directories and opening files in my editor. In any given week it’s mostly the same files and dirs because I’m working on the same projects. I was annoyed I had to remember where files live, and tired of tab-completing the same few paths. My computer should already know which file I want to open!
So I made psychic, a fast terminal-based file browser. It tracks the directories you go to and remembers which files you open. It trains a lightweight ML model on your data and ranks results using that model. It prioritizes interactivity and speed above all else: results update as you type and the UI renders in under 16ms.
Everything about how it works flows from a key design decision: it has to be fast enough to update within one frame after a keypress. I’d rather do 10 fast searches in the space of a couple seconds, than 1 smart search that takes many seconds to complete.
I use psychic every time I’m on my computer. It’s become the main way I move around the filesystem. Some numbers: Since I started using it in October 2025,
- I’ve opened it 1450 times. On average, I typed 1.6 characters before I had what I wanted.
- 29% of the time I typed nothing! psychic knew what I wanted, top result. All I did was open and hit enter.
- Median time from opening psychic to getting where I wanted to go was 2 seconds. 41% of searches happened within 1s, 69% within 3s.
- 80% of the time, I picked the top result. 96% of picks were in the top 3.
- The paths I selected were about 50 characters away, on average. So I’m typing 3% of that to get there.
(These are from the built-in psychic stats command, which you can run on your own history!)
It’s on homebrew: brew install kshitijl/tap/psychic.
On the left are search results. On the right is a preview of the file or directory currently selected. You type a query in the bottom and the results are filtered and ranked, changing with every letter. If you hit Enter on a file, it opens your terminal editor in the same window and waits in the background. If it’s a directory, it restarts the search from inside there. It remembers every file and dir you open, and a shell integration records every dir you cd into from outside psychic. All of those are included in every search.
It’s like fzf and zoxide had a baby, plus a small ML model that learns your patterns and favorites. It’s doing ad optimization on your own data, to help you navigate your computer faster.
How it works
All your searches and clicks get written to a sqlite db on your computer. psychic trains a LightGBM model on that data. The model learns to predict which files you’ll open, based on your search query. psychic uses the model to rank search results. After every keypress, psychic reruns the model and reranks all results.
For more details, see the README in the repo.
Some key design decisions
The model I use is LightGBM, an implementation of gradient-boosted trees. It’s tiny and fast and trains in seconds. It can learn rules that depend on threshold values. For example, it can learn a rule like “Files above 1 MB are only opened if they’ve been modified in the last 24 hours”, like log files. LightGBM also has the excellent LambdaRank objective, which is specialized for exactly this kind of ranking task.
The latency budget ruled out any model that’s not local: a network call could easily be over 10 ms or worse. It also ruled out LLMs or any kind of transformer model. Linear and logistic regression were too simple and performed much worse than LightGBM.
The model is re-trained from scratch every time you open psychic. This means it always reflects your current usage patterns. Training happens in the background and writes the model to disk when it’s done. We don’t switch to using the new model while you’re looking at results, because it’s jarring when apps do that. Instead, we wait for when you’re not looking at the screen, like when you’re opening a file in an editor or when you click on a directory. Then we switch to the new model. I’m proud of this careful little dance.
When a user has just started using psychic, there aren’t enough clicks to train on. We use a simple model that rewards recent clicks, recent modification time and a fuzzy match between the query and filename. The final score is a weighted sum of the simple model and ML model. With few clicks, the simple model dominates. As more clicks accumulate, the ML model’s score gets higher weight, until it’s basically 1.
How to be psychic
I use a carefully chosen set of features to try to predict which file you’ll open. Some features are simple: how recently you last clicked it within psychic, its modification time, whether the filename starts with the query, a fuzzy text match score between the query and the filename. Here’s a debug pane that shows the features and some performance stats:
One feature is “number of recent clicks on files that are in the same directory as this one”. This feature helps the model boost files that are in currently active projects.
The feature “clicks for this query” helps the model associate specific queries with specific files, without having to literally remember filenames and query texts. This way, while the model doesn’t directly see filenames, it can still remember associations.
An episode is defined as everything that happens from opening psychic (or from the last click) to clicking on an item. So a single episode has a bunch of queries, including hitting backspace and trying new queries. The feature “engagements in episode with query” counts the number of times you clicked on a file at any point in an episode that had the current query. So if you always type “es” and end up clicking on “bayesian-estimate.md”, then the model can see that association. Next time you type “es”, the model will put that file at the top of the list.
Computer go fast
I watch perf closely and spent a lot of effort on a good benchmarking setup, plus perf logging. Every commit has performance benchmarks. If you use psychic and get bad performance, that’s a bug! Let me know and I’ll fix it.
My tech choices were driven by performance. Probably the most important choices were Rust and LightGBM.
Syscalls are expensive but of course this whole program is syscalls. I tried to minimize syscalls. No filesystem syscalls in the main render loop; I carefully made sure that we ask for file metadata at the time we walk the filesystem and then carry that around everywhere else.

Today I’m talking with Mikie Sherrill, who’s been New Jersey governor for just a little under a year, and you’ll hear her say her election was a preview of the huge Democratic victories in these recent midterms because she ran on the dual themes of affordability and accountability.
Why NJ’s governor thinks Republicans are trapped in an X bubble
Gov. Mikie Sherrill on AI, Elon Musk, and the future of privacy.
So I wanted to ask the governor exactly how corruption became such an animating issue for voters, in an era of tech billionaires who own platforms like X and TikTok and who also now control huge swaths of local media and even national broadcast media like CBS News.
You’ll hear us get into the new era of influencer politics, which plays out as social video and takes its cues from rising stars like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and how I think influence on platforms like Elon Musk’s X is starting to backfire in big ways for conservatives.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
But the real story this election cycle might be the states. With President Donald Trump concentrating power in the executive branch, governors like Sherrill are starting to exercise their own power in ways that haven’t been tested in a long time.
This runs right into tech policy and anti-AI backlash, as states around the country try to address topics like child safety and Big Tech overreach in lieu of any form of meaningful federal regulation. That’s how politicians like Sherrill have found themselves at the forefront of the data center fight, online privacy, and age verification — all topics you’ll hear us dive into here.
We also dig into the Meta settlement, why Sherrill expects more Big Tech litigation, and what happens to privacy in the Flock and AI era. She had a lot of questions about the last one, and honestly, so do I. It’s a conversation I think we’re all going to be having for a while.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Governor Mikie Sherrill, you’re the governor of New Jersey. Welcome to Decoder.
Well, thanks so much for having me. I really appreciate it.
I’m excited to talk to you. It’s after the midterms; there’s a huge blue wave, and you’re a Democrat.
I noticed.
Yeah. I noticed that you were saying, “New Jersey is like the bellwether,” and you “paved the way...” This is your big quote. Tell me about that, and tell me how you’re feeling about the midterms.
I’ll answer the easy question first. I feel great about the midterms. I feel absolutely fantastic about the midterms. And yeah, I was thinking about it because New Jersey has those off-year elections. So, there are very few statewide races — really only two in that cycle: New Jersey and Virginia. Right after Trump won, we started our campaign. And by right after, I mean, he won in November of 2024, and we started our campaign in November of 2024. What’s so interesting about New Jersey is that, even for a governor of this state, it’s still so retail. I don’t think a lot of other big states do as much retail, meaning I’m getting in front of thousands and thousands of people, sometimes per day, at small business stops, at diners, in their community... We have so many municipalities. I am able to go to gatherings of people up and down my state.
And that means that we always have a real pulse on what’s going on very quickly. After 2024, we had to get the vibe because it was different; people were furious. They wanted movement, they wanted change, and then suddenly you have Elon Musk with a chainsaw. People are scared, they don’t like what’s happening, and they want a leader who’s going to address it. And I think what we did in that time, because we heard from everyone, is really centered on what the race was about, and it was about affordability and accountability.
I know now that seems obvious... Yeah, it’s about affordability, and everyone knows that. I don’t think it was obvious in 2024 what it was all about. What was driving people? And in New Jersey, we were able to figure that out, and I think because the campaign was so incredibly successful, and we had such a huge win at the end of the day, that people then thought, oh yeah, that’s exactly the path. We’re all going to run on affordability and accountability, and that’s powerful in the Democratic Party. I think we’re at the center of our power when we’re fighting for working families, and that’s where we are right now, and I think it bodes really well for the future.
One of the really surprising aspects of this last election cycle was corruption leading the polls in several places. You don’t often see people on CNBC being like, “Our poll says corruption is the number one issue in America.” I think it was number two in The Guardian poll. I feel like I can connect corruption to all the tech CEOs being at the White House all the time, and to data centers. Is that a real connection, or is that just because I happen to live in the tech bubble?
So, as somebody who has worked with polling, good, bad, and everything in between, I would say, and not to sound like a broken record, we were talking about... And that corruption piece was part of the accountability, the affordability. And I was hearing about that anger at corruption on the trail, even from very small, modest businesses, tying it to Trump pocketing billions of dollars as their costs are going up. I think you’re exactly right. People are very upset at the tech billionaires, and when they’re hanging out at the White House, especially those flip-floppers. They’re all in on liberal values, and then they’re all in on Trump values. It’s just to make a buck. The reason corruption popped so much is people... It’s not just corruption; it’s the corruption that’s costing them money.
It’s Trump going into this Iranian war that he can’t explain and somehow making billions of dollars. It’s Trump trying to allow Russian diesel here, as everyone else is paying higher and higher gas prices, and everyone knows that Russia is funding Iran. And oh, by the way, the oligarchs are funding the wedding of Trump’s kid. Just so much corruption, and it’s tied, I think, specifically, to people’s ideas of their pocketbook and what’s making this go up. Everyone thinks it’s because Trump’s partly on the take here.
One of the things that I’ve been really thinking about is how people found out about the corruption, how they talked to each other about it, and why it became such an issue. And the reason I’m asking that way is, well, Elon Musk owns X, right? He bought a social media network. Larry Ellison and Oracle have some controlling stake in TikTok. Mark Zuckerberg owns Instagram. Skydance exists, and it owns CNN. The idea that the tech billionaires control the media, and have bought more and more of the media, was supposed to create even more of an epistemic bubble. We are going to tweet policy into reality is as much a part of Trump Two as anything, and people found out what they wanted to find out, and yet they had these conversations. I haven’t been able to figure out why; do you have a theory about that case?
There was a lot of corruption that we were trying to bring to the fore that was really hard to have people connect with. I think, for example, when we had Congress block some of the most high-end semiconductor chips so that we could win some of the technological battle against China, and Trump basically got paid off by the UAE, and then suddenly the floodgates were open. So, we had seen all of this cryptocurrency and stuff going into his pocketbooks. I suspect there’s a lot we don’t even know. But your point is really a good one because we were sort of saying he’s corrupt, and people sort of felt that he was corrupt, but the specifics of it were hard to bring out or get into the public consciousness. I tend to think that the interesting thing is... And look, I was very worried. I first ran in 2018, and I started to see the misinformation that people were getting online, and how people were getting algorithms driving them into more and more extreme places.
I was quite skeptical of some of this new media and what it might mean for people getting information. That is certainly one concern, but the flip side of that has become, as people have gotten used to some of that extremism and maybe started to filter it out a little bit, that there’s not much you can hide now, and I think that’s really good for democracy. So, for example, we had a problem here with our voter rolls. We discovered that the last administration had registered people who were not citizens, and they had not cleared them off the rolls. And so, we discovered this, and there were a lot of people saying, “Just put out a paragraph and just kind of duck and cover and hope it goes away. Sweep it under the rug a little bit.” And to me, that’s not accountability, that’s not what I ran on, and that’s not being a strong leader. Being a strong leader is saying, “Yeah, a problem happened, but I’ve got the solution to it, and I’m going to handle it.” And I think that breeds trust in government.
The reason that I maybe felt so strongly about this was that there’s no sweeping things under the rug in that way, and I think that’s really healthy. Meaning that if I had just put a little paragraph out, then the narrative would’ve gotten out anyway. I wouldn’t have been able to tell people exactly what happened, why it happened, and what we were doing about it; it would’ve been put out in whatever way somebody else wanted it out there. And so, I think what some people aren’t realizing is: you can’t hide much from the American people. The best thing you can do, and I think this is also my view of democracy and good government, is to be accountable to people. And to come forward strongly and say, this is what happened, this is why it happened, this is how I’m fixing it.
One of the things that I’m really curious about in that construction is how much of this cycle was dominated by politicians who had essentially learned the visual and social vernacular of influencers. And Zohran Mamdani here in New York City has obviously learned how to wield social media as well as any influencer. Abdul El-Sayed has learned that language. After the election, I think it was a House Oversight Committee that released what can only be described as an NBA hype reel with just the words “lawyer up” over and over again.
And there’s a part of me that’s like, this is incredibly effective. This is also a totally new brand of... Chuck Schumer should not do that. He doesn’t know how to do that. You need a new generation of politicians who speak this language, and sort of wield the algorithms against their owners in a very specific way. Do you think that’s permanent? Is that just a moment in time, or is influencer politics here to stay?
I think getting out on social media and being very present there feels very permanent to me. There certainly are people who do it incredibly well. But the interesting thing to me is that it’s not replicable because I think you have to be so authentic. And so, Zohran Mamdani is gifted; he’s like a social media prodigy. I think he does a great job. Don’t I wish, right? I think part of the reason I like what he does is that he comes across with a lot of humanity, a lot of empathy for people, reaching out to all different kinds of people, and it’s New York City, and it feels very authentic.
But I also like that empathy piece. I think some people take from the more bravado and maybe the Oversight Committee, this idea that social media has to be real… I mean, just that you have to be kind of an asshole, and you have to get out there, and that’s how you get attention, and you’re just... And I see some people trying to do that. Look, I was in the Navy, and sometimes I curse like a sailor. I do not like to do that online. I want to ask about New Jersey then, in that context. A year, not even a year into your first term, I think state governments are very opaque to people. So, I want to ask you the basic Decoder questions just to illuminate that a little bit. How is New Jersey structured? How have you structured your administration?
We have structured it differently than New Jersey has ever been structured. We are a large economy; we’d be the 22nd largest economy in the world if we were a country, and yet Trenton has not operated in that way. We added a chief operating officer. So, the top three people under me, my sort of lieutenants, if you will, are the chief of staff, and that’s a very traditional role. That’s sort of the person that works on the politics of the legislature and getting legislation passed... And I’m making these faces because I served in a legislature. Sometimes you have to muscle things through legislatures, even when you’re in them. You’ve got to get the coalitions; you’ve got to kind of arm-twist to get people there. In fact, the vote getter in a legislature is called the whip, to whip people into shape, to get them to vote on your bill.
That’s what the chief of staff does. She also works with the outside groups, and the grassroots groups, and the politics of it... Because if you are going to get people in your state to support legislation, you have to go communicate with them, and that’s politics, that’s getting in front of mayors and county commissioners, and talking about what this is going to do for their towns, and why it’s important. So, that’s the chief of staff.
Then you have the chief counsel. Now, the chief counsel sort of looks at the legislation and makes sure it’s constitutional. Are there any technical fixes that need to happen? Or are we going to get involved as a state in some of the different state legislation, like the Meta settlement and stuff? Are we going to take on some of these challenges? So, that’s sort of your chief counsel. And then we’ve added a third person, the chief operating officer.
The reason we added this person is that we just felt like the state wasn’t operating on... I come from the Navy, so on mission, meaning there were a lot of different cabinet departments, and you think of that as the federal level. So, you have the Department of Human Services, the Department of Health, the Department of Education, the Department of Transportation... I mean, what you would expect at the state level. And yet they all seem to be very siloed. They were experts operating in certain areas to do things, but if you’re going to do permitting reform, that’s going to touch on your Department of Community Affairs, your Department of Environmental Protection, your Department of Transportation. That is not a single sector; that crosses your different departments. So, your cabinet department. That is why we have the chief operating officer. She sort of brings everyone on mission, brings the cabinet together, and makes sure they’re all driving what we need to do.
Another thing that I think I have felt for a very long time, not just in New Jersey but across the board, is that the government just hasn’t been listening as well as it could, or serving people as well as it could. Running a good government hasn’t been appreciated for a very long time, and I wanted to make sure our government was delivering for people. So, when people were working on outdated systems like Cobalt, believe it or not... And yes, I’m not making that up. We were getting those systems up to date. When permits were too hard, and you had paper permits that everyone had to turn in across different departments, we were getting them online. When you have microfiche... Yes, microfiche. I’m old enough to have used it in the library; I’m sure a lot of people aren’t. Making sure we’re transferring that so that we’re getting the government to run well and then serve people better.
The other Decoder question I ask everybody is about decisions: how do you make decisions? What’s your framework?
I think it’s really critically important to just make decisions on a thing. And in politics, it’s often that if you’re just doing things for politics, not for policy or to deliver, it’s better not to make a decision. That’s kind of the dirty secret that has led to, I think, some government not serving people well. It’s often better to just stand back. I don’t know if you’ve seen that Homer Simpson one, where he goes into the tree? That’s what a lot of politicians seem to want to do, right? It’s just, “Whoa, that’s a tough one. That’s not popular, that’s not a good one; I’m going to let somebody else handle it.” And then when the decision is made, if it’s a good one, they’ll be like, “I supported that from the start.” So, I’ve raised my hand to be governor because it is my job to lead in tough things and to make tough decisions.
I center that work and making decisions on the people I serve. That is why, again, just being able to get in front of thousands of people helps me understand where people are so I can make decisions knowing how it’s going to impact people in my state, and then going back and checking in with people. I like a lot of information, but if you’re going to onboard a lot of information, it has to come to you very particularly because of the human brain. I have fantastic, fantastic people that work in Trenton. I think we have the most talent of any state government in the country, and so we have these feedback loops so I can make decisions. But part of the reason I’m able to do that, to get a lot of great information and to make these decisions, is because I trust the people who work for me. They’re that good, so I know when they’re giving me this information and their point of view, I can trust them and say, “Okay, that makes sense.” Because you’re sometimes doing things you don’t want to, and there are a lot of hard decisions you have to make.
You have to trust the people saying, “We’ve looked at every single path forward here, here, and here; we would pick here.” And you don’t feel like they’re leaving a lot out, or haven’t looked at it, or haven’t researched it well.

Maybe a little bit of both. I don’t think a lot of people know all the different kinds of data centers or what it might mean to their community. We have local control here in New Jersey, so towns make their own decisions. And in some communities, data centers probably don’t make sense. But then there are other communities that have big industrial parks and big warehouse areas, away from where people live, that would make sense. But we want to make sure they’re not harming the communities — that they’re not utilizing too much water or driving up power costs. So, yes, we put in pillars to hold those data centers accountable. And for example, one of the data centers in the South that had been built before I got into office was not really following our different permitting laws and stuff. We’ve given one of the largest fines to them in the country — over a million dollars in fines — to hold them accountable.
We continue to work with communities. We’ve said we’ll have their back if they’re negotiating community benefits agreements, because what we want to make sure is that if a community goes forward with a data center, that it benefits the community and doesn’t just send billions of dollars to Big Tech in Silicon Valley. And what does that look like? That looks like ensuring that, with a community benefits agreement, they’re investing in the town. Some of the money being made there gets into the town and helps people. That they’re employing people, use good union labor, and stuff like that. And we’re not super scalers; we’re not building some of what you see out in Texas, but people do want to have more insight into it.
The reason I say a little bit of both is because I don’t think data centers have shown a model where communities are confident that if they build in their community, they are not going to be harmed. And unless and until they do that, I think you’re going to see, and some of our local governments have passed them, you’re going to see more and more moratoriums until people are better informed about what is coming into their community, and how they can be assured that they are going to experience the upside.
I would say, I think what’s been missing in this conversation and many others in AI and technology is that the government has not been at the table. So, you have companies that are built to make money, maybe create jobs, but make money. You have innovators, and they are built to innovate and create new things. You have a government that is supposed to be there to protect people, to protect them from the downside risks. To make sure that, as money is made, it is fair, that workers are paid a fair amount, that companies aren’t dumping pollution into the river. I mean, the government has traditionally been there to protect people when the government is running well from downside risks. The government is nowhere to be found in this space. And now you have sometimes trillion-dollar businesses, like Elon Musk, where government is not at the table, and then you have, in AI, businesses saying, “Look, we need regulation here,” and government’s still sort of like, “Whoa.”
It’s like nothing I’ve seen, and there’s this false narrative out there that I think was sort of started under Reagan, “Get government out of the way and everyone flourishes.” I think what you were seeing in this recent election, and even some of the ones before it, is a country crying out and saying, look, we need good, effective government, and we’re not feeling it. You’re not addressing our needs. We don’t feel like you’re making the change we want. It’s why I kept, as I was running, I said to people, “I’m going to address these energy costs. Energy costs were set to go up by another double digits this year, when people were already under huge price pressures. I’m curious about this within the framework of what the federal government can do and what the states can do. So, the states are a little bit the laboratories of democracy. And you’re right, I mean, good regulation at the federal level might be number one in the priority, in the good-to-bad list. And then, as you see decent federal government, or you can even see this Congress setting something up, so the regulatory scheme is obvious, that gives businesses some understanding of where this is headed so they can get engaged. I would also say a lot of what you’re seeing in the online space, a lot of it was the Kids Online Safety Act that the Senate passed. What, 91 people voted in favor of it in the Senate? It was very popular, but it was killed in the House when they dumped a bunch of money on Steve Scalise. So, I think what you’re seeing are these pieces of the Kids Online Safety Act, and a lot of what we’re doing, and people will start coalescing around it. New Jersey just set up the first research center in the nation, because there’s not a lot of good information for parents or teachers about what to do. And there’s all this, I would call it BS, around, oh, the social media companies, oh, we’ve given parental controls. It would be a full-time job if I wanted to keep up with the parental controls for my kids.
We do put them on; you’re constantly hearing, “Can I have more time? Can I have less?” Oh, we’re in a car ride; I’ll give you more. Oh, I forgot to take it off; now you’ve been online for eight hours. It’s not good. It’s really, really bad. This should not be dumped on parents when Big Tech has all the power here. And I sometimes hear concerns, “Well, why should we have to figure out who’s...” They know exactly who’s online, they know exactly how old you are, they can always figure it out when they want to, and they want to sell you something. But somehow, when we’re asking them, “Hey, let’s have age-appropriate design code, let’s not get compulsive or addictive behavior…” And we’re seeing that in children. I mean, the average teen spends 35 hours per week online. That’s not healthy.
That is not mentally healthy; that is not good for society, that’s not good for our kids. That’s a full-time job. They’re not connecting with other people.
