That just doesn’t track.
I’m glad you brought up this trade-off. So many of your peers who have shown up on the show have basically offered me the formulation: “We failed to regulate social media; we will not fail to regulate AI.” That is the dynamic I’ve heard from-
So, we’re just giving up on social media?
Well, I would say we got to social media regulation 10 years later. We didn’t do it through acts of Congress. We didn’t pass a federal privacy bill. These things don’t exist. We got there through major litigation, which your state has participated in, and a bunch of state-level laws that recapitulate parts of the Kids Online Safety Act. And whenever I hear this formulation, the thing that I think is, well, it’s way easier to regulate AI because they want to build huge buildings. If there’s one thing Americans can do, it’s stop you from building huge buildings. We are good at that; we’re great at that. Maybe that’s not the right tool, but boy, are we good at swinging that hammer.
Everything about social media is speech. Everything about social media affects the First Amendment in some big and meaningful way, and we’ve never figured out how to have that conversation directly. We tend to have conversations about Section 230. We find other things that you can knock around so you don’t have to talk about, well, ultimately we are restricting how teens can speak online. And we think that’s for their benefit, and we should make that argument, but it is a speech restriction.
We’re actually not going at it as a speech restriction specifically, partly because we’ve seen this in the courts. Now, do I think that young children should be blocked from seeing hardcore porn? And do I think we should be able to restrict that? Yes. However, given some of what we’ve seen in the court cases, we are going after addictive and compulsive behavior. So, all of the algorithms that are designed to create this addictive or compulsive behavior in children, that’s what we have written the laws to address. And I think that will be very strong and resilient, and that will help address some of the First Amendment concerns that the courts are having.
And that’s the 10 years of figuring it out. Across the country, we have landed on product liability and not content moderation. The product is designed to be harmful; we’re not even going to talk about the content because then you will run into the First Amendment. There are some, I think, complications with that.
If you want to do age verification, and you want to make sure that the kids aren’t using these services when they shouldn’t be — which is part of the Meta settlement — then you’ve got to check my age too. You have to invade my privacy in some way. And the technical solution to that does not solve how I would like to be anonymous online. I have to tell Meta or the government I’m of age, and I have to produce some documentation of that.
Are you concerned about that trade-off, that as we try to protect kids by making sure they’re kids, we’re going to infringe on the rights of adults to be anonymous online?
Do you really think you’re anonymous online? I guess I don’t believe that you’re anonymous online.
Sure.
So, we’re pretending. We have this pretense that you can be anonymous online, and that they don’t know your age or that... I mean, they are tracking everything about you at all times. You just, by virtue of being online, give up this privacy. I guess I don’t quite believe that you can be anonymous online. I think that it would be very hard for them not to know everything about you and your behavior, unless you’re... Gosh, you would have to be very curated in your online experience in a way most people aren’t. But to that extent, I do worry about privacy concerns with online content because the federal government has come after a lot of our data. For example, our voter rolls, which I’ve refused to turn over, and a lot of privacy data; I’ve also seen them weaponize different personal data that they hold, including in my election against me.
So, I do worry about all this. And I think some people would suggest that I’m acting like people did about TV back in the day. Everybody acted like TV was going to be the disintegration of society. I think that there is always some adjustment period with new technologies. I do think the addictive nature of these algorithms has created a huge societal problem for children and a huge mental health problem, and I think we have to keep iterating and finding ways to address that. If there are privacy concerns, then we’re going to have to keep figuring out how to best address those and keep people’s privacy data as safe as possible.
I actually don’t think that’s a problem for this space; I think the problem is much larger than that. How do you engage online and protect your privacy, and who gets to hold that privacy data? And that’s very unclear to me. I don’t think right now anybody’s privacy is assured online. In fact, I would say quite the opposite.
Yeah, and operating from that would lead you to one set of conclusions about the legislation. Saying we should fix privacy online might lead you in another direction. I’m not sure that the big platforms want to go in that direction, right? I’m not sure they want to fix the issue of privacy. I’ll come back to that.
One of the things that’s really striking here is that New Jersey is part of the big Meta settlement; I think the state’s going to get $525 million out of that settlement. The rest of the money is unlocked if TikTok and YouTube agree to the same terms as Meta. Mark Zuckerberg is very proud of this arrangement, but Neal Mohan, the CEO of YouTube, has said YouTube is not at all interested in this. Are you going to put pressure on YouTube to agree to the same terms as Meta, or are you going to have to litigate against them too?
I assume we’ll have to litigate. We’ve just not seen anybody move in this space willingly, or kind of raise their hand, and I think they’ve learned their lesson. I think when you’ve seen people in the social media space, and you saw Facebook years ago try to move in a way that maybe made better algorithms, they just immediately lost market share to other companies. This is why I say the federal government, or any government, and state governments are so important in protecting people from the downside risks. The reason Dario Amodei has put out all of these prescriptions for regulation, and yet hasn’t unilaterally adopted them, is likely because he feels that if he did, his market share would go down, nothing would change, and everybody else would just move into that vacuum.
And so, that’s why you need the government to regulate this. Otherwise, just being a good Samaritan, a good actor in this space, doesn’t change things, and it actually harms you individually as a company.
I’m really curious about this dynamic, and I’m going to pick on Mark Zuckerberg because I love picking on Mark Zuckerberg. So, he would tell you that there should be no AI regulation; he said it out loud, and the reason is that the market will prioritize safety. If you have an AI lab and you’re going to kill everyone, people aren’t going to buy your product. This is his argument. That there is a market for this.
I know. I know it’s his argument; I just don’t buy it.
But he does not think there’s a market for social media safety, for teen safety. His settlement requires the government to pressure his competitors to agree to the same terms. I’ve heard a lot of people say that there’s no argument for safety on social media, right? But you’re a parent, I’m a parent; if you sold me an Instagram that was better for kids, I would probably say you can use that one and not TikTok.
Why do you think that market hasn’t developed? Because everyone’s asking for the government to regulate, but it seems like “this is the social media platform that’s actually safe” is a marketable product.
But it hasn’t appeared, so I assume it’s not. I assume that the money is just eyes on screens, and the safer product is not producing that. There was Kids YouTube, and I had my kid on Kids YouTube, but they gravitate towards something else, right? And so, even if you had that Instagram that was kid-friendly, and you put your kid on it, your kid would get themselves off it pretty quickly. This is why I think it’s really — I just keep coming back to it — unfair to tell parents like, “Oh, well, if you’re a good parent, you’re going to put your kid on these... We’re going to get parental controls. And if you’re a good parent, you’ll do it.” Again, I can’t tell you how many hours my husband and I have spent trying to make sure parental controls are working for our kid.
And now, the schools are just giving out laptops like candy, and my kid just goes and gets on whatever she wants to get on at school. Imagine, right? Here I am locking down her phone, and then she goes to school and can get on everything. And I’m like, I thought-
As the governor of New Jersey, you can’t make a phone call to keep the laptop out of the school? It feels like that’s a call you can make that most parents can’t.
Well, I got cell phones out of school, which my kids aren’t thanking me for, but I just got a standing ovation from teachers at the teachers’ conference. But I do think that is why we have this social media research center: what is best for children, what would the appropriate use of screens and computers be, how do you hand them out to kids, and what do you use them for? Because I’ll just tell you, to me, the canary in the coal mine was about the 2017, 2018 timeframe, when I was first running for Congress. I was speaking to people in Silicon Valley, and they were really proud to tell me that they were sending all of their children to schools without any screens. And it’s funny because that was just so foreign to me in 2018. I remember sort of thinking, like, the Amish? What are you doing?
And this is at a time when in New Jersey, we’re really proud of the fact that we’re getting every kid an iPad, right? We’re going to make sure every kid can be trained on and utilize a computer. And I think we’ve seen that those were the people developing algorithms, and those were the people that understood the brain science, how dangerous it was going to be, and making sure their kids were kept away from it. Now, we need to catch up here, but we need the data that they had, which is why we’re having this research center, so we can best understand what we can do to protect our kids.
It feels like one of the ways you would defend the sort of inevitable First Amendment lawsuit about teens and social media use is by having a bunch of data that overcomes strict scrutiny, right? You can do a proper balance of harms analysis. Is that where you’re headed? Because no one else has really tried to do that.
Yeah, that’s exactly... We have several reasons we’re doing this. We’re partly doing it to give teachers and parents good advice. When should your kid get a smartphone? I don’t know anyone who really feels like they totally know that.
My answer is never, just to be clear. My eight-year-old daughter is very upset with me because my answer is never.
I feel like that’s a great answer. Part of it is also to understand the data, because every time these social media companies have started studies, they’ve stopped them because the data is so bad. And so, that hamstrings us in lawsuits. We brought these lawsuits, and that Meta settlement was great, but we’ve lost a lot at the court level because we just don’t have the data we need. So, yes, you’re exactly right. Gathering the data and studying it so we can actually have what we need to prosecute these cases better and get better results is exactly what... That is one of the key reasons we’re doing this.
Do you think that Meta case was settled too early or for too little? I’m asking because there was a similar case in New Mexico that didn’t settle, and they won a lot more at trial. Do you think we caved too early on the Meta case?
I just think we need to keep bringing more cases. I don’t think the Meta settlement should be seen as the end of it. I think we should keep moving in this space to get better rules around it, especially given, as you’ve said, that the federal... I mean, this is another way to get kind of federal regulation to-
Right. It’s a lot of states.
And eventually the Supreme Court, to have that sort of federal standard in a way, if the government’s not going to act.
Just operationally, who makes the call and says, “We’re going to settle”? Is that a conference call? Do you have to press two to agree? How does that work?
Generally, there is a lead state in this space that kind of leads the other states in some of the litigation, and we are working closely. Our attorney general’s office works closely with the other states, and so there’s a state that is sort of the convening authority, bringing everyone together. They work together to determine, yes, this is how we’re going to move forward; this is when we think is the time to settle; we think we should pursue this; we think we should drop the case; they’ve agreed to do X, Y, and Z. So, generally, there’s a lead state that convenes everyone, and then they kind of come around to the agreement together.
This was a real dynamic in the first two years of the Trump administration. A bunch of Democratic state attorneys general said, “We’re going to do stuff because the federal government is doing nothing.” Do you think that dynamic will stay now that there’s a much more Democratic Congress?
Yeah, there’s still so much out there with HR1, with FEMA relief, with CMS... I mean, there are just tons out there still. We are still in court, litigating. We have been attacked quite a bit by the Trump administration on things like mass detention facilities and the Gateway Tunnel Project. So, we were in court very quickly there. I don’t think that will... I mean, if Trump just decides to suddenly stop, sure, but I don’t think that will be the case, unfortunately.
By the way, I’m very proud of myself for not doing the full hour on the Gateway Tunnel. I feel like there’s a great 10-episode podcast series on the twists and the turns of the Gateway Tunnel.
Oh my goodness, I am here for you. Tell me when you are ready to do that one.
It’s for another time. I want to end by talking about privacy. It has come up. It has been woven through this conversation. The notion that we don’t have any left is all over the tech industry, for a lot of reasons. And I actually think one of the things that is happening in tech and culture right now is a redefinition of privacy in very specific ways.
I’m wearing an Apple Watch right now; it has the Beta software on it, and it just makes summaries of every conversation that I have. It’s going to make one of this conversation, I’m sure. And Apple’s point of view on this is, well, it’s not a direct transcription; it is just a summary. It doesn’t identify speakers. We haven’t invaded anyone’s privacy.
There are any number of tech AI products that listen to you all day long and tell you how you feel. There’s one called the Amazon Bee that’s just come out, that you wear, and it literally listens all day long. Flock cameras exist, and Flock cameras are like a truck driven through the law that says you don’t have an expectation of privacy in public. It’s a big swirl where it’s, we’re going to take even more privacy away from you. Meta Glasses exist, and you’re like, people don’t like them, they call them pervert glasses, and Mark Zuckerberg’s entire answer is, “Well, phones don’t have a light,” and that is meant to end all conversation about the practical implications of Meta Glasses.
How do you feel about this? There are Flock cameras in New Jersey; people really don’t like feeling surveilled, and at the same time, the tech industry is rushing forward to collect even more data to feed even more AI in more and more intrusive ways. Where should we land?
I think about this all the time, and I wish I had a really great answer for you. I find it incredibly scary to think that every detail will be surveilled and that... What was it? Gattaca or Galactica? With a piece of hair that you dropped, they could do your genetic code, and then they would determine if you were in the right place because you were determined at birth to have to be in certain places or something.
That’s Gattaca.
Yeah, yeah.
The tech industry loves learning the wrong lesson from movies like this. It’s their favorite.
Oh no. But I think it’s this horrible impending sense that we are going to be so... So much is going to be known about us, that it’s going to take away our ability to thrive and live our lives. For example, you almost fear a world where, somehow, from a strand of hair, they can determine when you’re going to die and of what, and so you have to do X because you’re going to be dead by the time you’re 70. You know what I’m saying? It’s just very scary, all of the data and information, and I think what’s most scary to me is: I don’t know where it’s going and who has access to it.
I was speaking to a gentleman who was telling me about AI, and he said, “I had to give up tons of privacy, but it’s a godsend; it sorts everything out for me, it does my calendar, it reminds me to call people, it keeps my to-do list, it listens...” He said, “It is so awesome, but I had to give up a lot of privacy.” And I guess my concern wouldn’t be that if I had some system that could do that, my concern is where all this is being held, and who’s going to do something with it? When are they going to come after me because they’re like, I heard you did X, Y, and Z, or I heard you-
But this is the backlash to Flock. You’re describing in very specific ways how people feel about Flock cameras. Flock cameras are deployed by law enforcement agencies. You could change those laws today. Do you think you’re feeling the push there? Because the push there is going to connect to, okay, the FBI can subpoena my AI chat history. It’s all the same in some way.
Yeah, in some ways. I think Flock cameras are something that the communities really wanted. A couple of years ago, we had a huge outbreak in car thefts, and then everybody was having their cars stolen quite frequently. Then people were told, “Okay, lock your cars; don’t leave your key fobs in your cars.” So they stopped doing that, and they started having these break-ins in their homes, and they were very dangerous. Intruders would be in their homes while they were sleeping and stuff.
The community was very upset with law enforcement because law enforcement wasn’t ending this problem. And so, they argued for license plate readers, and law enforcement used those to track these cars and the car theft problem. Not to completely end it, but to do a lot of work there, and it seemed to have a big impact. In New Jersey, there are a lot of regulations around how long information could be kept. The attorney general audits it to make sure people aren’t using it inappropriately, et cetera, but you could still see a world where people are like, “Not good enough, I’m just going to lock down my house, and I want you to remove that camera from my street.” And those are choices that communities are making right now.
I get the tension. I get the desire to not have somebody in my home, or stealing my car, and if somebody’s going down my street and steals a car, that somebody can be caught, and that’s not threatening other people, et cetera. But I also don’t like my privacy being invaded. I don’t want everyone tracking what’s going on. Sure, you understand that they’re audited and there are all these rules, but we know some nefarious actor could break the rules. So, it is this tension, and it’s that constant thing. We could have a society where absolutely no one breaks the law. I’m sure with technology now we could monitor the hell out of everyone, and I think they do in places like Qatar.
Qatar would have you put a little app on your phone for FIFA, because we were studying all this when I was in Congress, and I was told by them, “Don’t put that app on your phone...” I didn’t go to FIFA there, but I was there to talk about one of our bases. And they said, “Don’t put that app on your phone because that’s just surveillance.” They were telling me that you can’t use your phone in your car, and if you pick up your phone, you just get a ticket because there’s that level of surveillance. Then they pointed out all the cameras to me.
That is not the surveillance state I would want to live in. So, it’s going on, and there is that tension: how much is too much? Who’s getting access to the data? That was already a problem. And now it’s not a who; it’s a what. What’s AI going to do with this data?
Right. If you link all the license plate readers together with an AI system, you can track anyone anywhere. We have supercharged the surveillance capability. That’s the thing that I’m just keyed on here at the end of this conversation because it is laced through everything else.
Everybody has had a camera on their cell phone for over a decade now, but taking all that video, putting it together through an AI system to synthesize some new reality was not a capability we had before. We didn’t have cameras on glasses, and now we have them. And again, Mark Zuckerberg’s argument is, “Phones don’t have a light,” but that means something different to people when you’re passively recording them from your glasses.
And I’m just wondering, that balance of privacy, for so long, has landed at: you don’t have an expectation of privacy in public. That is the state of the law. But you add a bunch of cameras and AI to that system, and I think people are pushing back against that law. Culturally, that expectation is changing. I should have some privacy in public.
Right. I was just thinking, though, what’s so interesting to me is, as you were talking about phones on cameras, how that has completely changed the dynamic in our understanding of police behavior, especially against certain communities of color. And I will just tell you the difference in seeing the phone videos of what was going on in communities, when police for years had been saying, “Oh, they pulled a gun,” or, “They had drugs,” or this... And the people recording it could show exactly what happened and what went down, and that was so critically important to civil rights, to criminal justice reform, and making a huge impact.
And again, that is what that tension is. What are you giving up? And you’re exactly right, the fear now is the supercharging. So, it’s not just one person’s phone. It’s like uploading all these videos, and then suddenly you have everyone being traced everywhere.
The term is sousveillance, not surveillance. We’re all going to surveil each other and put it all on Facebook, and then AI can search Facebook and find us all. This exists today. What I’m getting at, very specifically, is the idea that you have no expectation of privacy in public might be changing culturally faster than it’s changing politically or legislatively.
I’m curious if you see that balance changing state by state or at the federal level. This is the dynamic we’re in. We’re going to have little laboratories of democracy. It feels like Flock cameras are one little tick against “I have no expectation of privacy.” Actually, I want these gone. I don’t even want a license plate reader in my neighborhood because I want to feel that much less surveilled.
And you could see a world where, as we understand how AI is impacting all of these abilities, we start to create certain spaces where you do have this expectation of privacy, and say, “Look, you cannot have cameras in public parks, or you can’t have cameras in blah, blah, blah.” It’s a really difficult balance, I think. When I think about it as a woman, just about certain areas... We’re just dealing with some of the college campuses and how to keep people safe there. And as I think about removing cameras from public spaces, I also think about the concerns we have about some of the attacks on women on college campuses. Again, I just keep getting to those tension points, and I think these are just things that we have to come together as a society and say that we’re willing to accept this amount of risk, or we’re not, or we’re going to have a cop on the beat to protect people, and we’re not going to have cameras, or we are in certain dark alleys.
And that is the fear for me, though, is what you keep narrowing in on. It’s almost a little bit less about some of that, because all of that felt a little settled. It felt a little like, okay, we’re going to have some cameras out on some of these college campuses, and keep people safe. But adding that AI element takes it to a whole new, scarier level. And that’s why I think you’re saying we’re going to have to reopen these conversations.
Well, you made a face when I said my Apple Watch was recording, or summarizing —
I know, I can’t even have an Apple Watch because I can’t be looking at it every five minutes. So, I don’t do that-
Do you think that Siri feature in the Apple Watch is appropriate, where it makes summaries of all your conversations?
Again, where’s it going? Where are all these summaries going, and who’s looking at them, and why, and what are they doing with it? And are they uploading it into something? Is it anonymous? Is it not? Can they track it back to you? Who can hack into it? I mean, these are all the questions I have when I think about that. And that’s why I’m not wearing an Apple Watch.
Fair enough. Apple has a lot of technical answers to your questions. I’m curious if they will ever come up with the social answers. I have one more question for you. It is a total wild card, but I’m dying to ask you.
Oh. These are the ones that always get me. Okay, go.
New Jersey is in the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which, if enough states sign on, the presidency will be determined by the National Popular Vote winner. There are now enough new Democratic states with Democratic legislatures and Democratic governors that you could get it over the finish line. Are you going to push for that?
I’m really excited about that. I hate the Electoral College. I’ve got to tell you, I love this idea. And I was seeing some of the same reporting that you were maybe looking into. So, this is something on my mind. One day I was going to take on the Electoral College. Today might be the day, so I got to get hot on this one and see where everybody’s at because I’d love to see a popular vote.
Yeah. I’m rooting for it only because it would be a historic thing to happen in our lifetimes. But it does seem, from all of the headlines I saw after the election, I was like, oh, that is the most unlikely outcome.
You really cannot be in the most densely populated state in the nation and not want to get rid of the Electoral College. That just doesn’t make any sense. I mean, if you just care about your vote and the power of your vote.
Yeah. I think it’s a bunch of Midwest... I’m from the Midwest. There’s a bunch of Midwestern states that could sign on to it; we’ll do our best. If that happens, we’ll have you back. Actually, we should have you back to talk about privacy and all the things to come. Thank you so much, Governor Sherrill. This was great.
I really appreciate it. Thanks for having me.

From Pipe Cleaners to Clay, Baskets Break Craft Traditions in ‘Interwoven’

Unknown Publisher

From Pipe Cleaners to Clay, Baskets Break Craft Traditions in ‘Interwoven’
Conjure an image of a basket in your mind. Is it made of straw, or perhaps sweetgrass or willow? Does it have a handle? Was it made by hand, and what could it hold? At Mindy Solomon Gallery, a forthcoming exhibition titled Interwoven: Basketry As Expanded Practice challenges our perception of both object and craft.
Curated by Dee Clements, the exhibition considers the way basketmaking techniques are far from limited to the splinted white ash trug we might carry out to the garden or the simple vessel that holds recipes in the kitchen. This vibrant survey “breaks craft tradition,” a statement says, positioning the practice as an art form. The show asks “what happens when basketry is understood not as a fixed category of craft, but as an open-ended artistic language?”
The artists in Interwoven use a range of materials, from ceramic and steel to cotton and paper. Salvador Dominguez’s vibrant pipe cleaner vessels are complemented by wall works like Eric Gushee’s intricately interlaced wire sculptures and Miguel Arzabe’s woven, deconstructed paintings.
Viewers will find further explorations by artists like Dienke Dekker and José Santiago Pérez, who work with unexpected materials like paper and emergency blankets, respectively. And Colossal readers might also recognize work by Xanthe Somers and Sonia Barrett, among the nearly two dozen participating artists.
Interwoven opens on November 29 and continues through January 9 in Miami. See more on the gallery’s Instagram.

Move Over, Peanut Butter: This New Limited-Edition Holiday Spread Is So Good, I Ate It 7 Mornings in a Row
If you know me, then you know that I’m a nut butter fanatic. I typically have two to three jars in my pantry at any given moment — minimum. One brand that will always have a permanent spot is Big Spoon Roasters. 
Its premium nut butters are truly out of this world, and the company continues to create unique flavors that you won’t find anywhere else. Its latest limited-edition batch is no exception. This time eggnog gets the nut butter treatment, and let me tell you — it’s pretty incredible. 
Big Spoon Roasters’ Eggnog Cashew & Pecan Butter Tastes Just Like an Iconic Holiday Drink
Big Spoon’s latest nut butter is made in collaboration with beloved spice company Spicewalla (the brand behind favorites like Jugaad It!, which makes everything taste better). Over a shared love for making delicious food products that bring people together and a commitment to sourcing high-quality ingredients, the two collabed for a match made in heaven — blending the warming flavors of eggnog into a delicious spread. (Fun fact: Both companies are based in North Carolina.)
Big Spoon Roasters’ Eggnog Cashew & Pecan Butter is made with pan-roasted Fair Labor cashews, organic Texas pecans, organic Vermont maple syrup, Spicewalla’s freshly ground nutmeg, vanilla, and Jacobsen sea salt. It’s also gluten-, palm oil-, refined sugar-, and soy-free; vegan; and non-GMO. The limited batch launched on October 1 and is available through December while supplies last. You can purchase a 13-ounce jar for $18.99, or as part of Big Spoon’s Holiday Nut Butter Trio Gift Set for $61.99 (including other delicious seasonal flavors: Gingerbread Crunch and Sugar Plum).
My Honest Review of Big Spoon Roasters’ Eggnog Cashew & Pecan Butter
Okay, I must admit that I’m actually not the biggest fan of eggnog — so I was curious to see how I’d like this nut butter. But once again, Big Spoon has knocked it out of the park. What I’ve come to realize in trying so many different Big Spoon varieties is the ratios always replicate whatever flavor profile they’re going for. This nut butter perfectly encapsulates the flavor of eggnog — minus that super-rich, heavy creaminess, which is what I don’t really like.
Here, Spicewalla’s nutmeg takes center stage and is punchy. In fact, it is the first thing I tasted. The nut butter is sweet, thanks to the maple syrup, but not overly so, and the vanilla is prominent as well. The cashews and pecans are neutral enough to provide the perfect backdrop for the nutmeg to shine. Just like all other Big Spoon nut butters, the texture is spot-on: SUPER thick, with a tad of grit, and tiny nut pieces — the perfect blend of creamy and chunky.
I went through this jar shockingly fast, and every time I dipped in it felt like a treat. I put it on toast and yogurt bowls with stewed apples, and, of course, ate it straight out of the jar. I also think it would be great to use for holiday baking (try it sandwiched in between shortbread cookies!).
Buy: Big Spoon Roasters Eggnog Cashew & Pecan Butter, $18.99 for 13 ounces

Robert Pattinson Is Officially James Bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:27:19 UTC
00:27:19 KST

It’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson.
The “Batman” and “Odyssey” star has officially been cast as the next James Bond, ending months of rabid speculation about which young actor Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve would hand the keys to the Aston Martin.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Added Villeneuve, who recently directed Pattinson in the upcoming “Dune: Part Three”: “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Amy Pascal, who has produced the “Spider-Man” franchise and several 007 films, and David Heyman, behind the “Harry Potter” series, are producing the new Bond film, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Steven Knight is writing the screenplay.
Pattinson picks up the 007 mantle after Daniel Craig’s five-movie run as the womanizing super spy, which began in 2006 with “Casino Royale.” Craig’s final turn was in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” which ends with Bond sacrificing himself to save the world from a secret global terrorist organization. “No Time to Die” was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
Predictions about who would be the next James Bond had taken over media and the industry in the last month, and a shortlist of British actors took turns as the presumed favorite. Jacob Elordi was pegged for the role in the earliest days of swirling rumors, but reports since surfaced that the “Euphoria” star didn’t even screen test for the part. Jack Lowden seemed like another safe bet. In early September, his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman claimed Bond was already picked and cheekily added that his “fingers are crossed” for Lowden. However, Lowden’s run at the character was largely overshadowed by Callum Turner, who seemed like a sure pick until news of Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult’s auditions was revealed. At that point, it became anyone’s guess who would come out on top until Pattinson was ultimately chosen. Other actors in the mix included Josh O’Connor, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.
It’s not hard to see from Amazon MGM’s perspective why Pattinson was the obvious choice. He is, almost unquestionably, 2026’s most in-demand movie star and has the box office record to show for it. With help from Zendaya, Pattinson drove A24’s “The Drama,” an intimate yet squirmy original dramedy, to $134 million worldwide from a budget of $28 million. “Primetime,” in which Pattinson starred as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, likewise hit big with $61 million globally against a slim $18 million budget. Pattinson also starred as the sniveling Antinous in “The Odyssey,” which did $1.8 billion, and is set to star in “Dune: Part Three” in December, which is sure to pull in the big bucks. (It’s very possible Pattinson earned the part after impressing Villeneuve on Arrakis).
Pattinson also has the big IP experience needed to lead a franchise like James Bond. In 2022, Pattinson debuted as the titular Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman.” He is set to revisit Gotham for the sequel in 2028. Those doubting Pattinson would land 007 often pointed to his obligations to Bruce Wayne as a reason why he could never take on Bond. However, after several production delays with “The Batman Part II,” it seems Pattinson is ready for a new longterm relationship with another familiar big-screen icon.
“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” said producers Pascal and Heyman. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

====================================================================================================

Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:24:09 UTC
00:24:09 KST

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.
But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.
“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.
Already, competitors have started to move in.
Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.
Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.
Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.
Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.
And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.
Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.
In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.
China Challenge
While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.
Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.
Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.
Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.
Trend Spotting
Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.
Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.
Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.
But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.
But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.
Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.
Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.
Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.
“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

ChatGPT Wallet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:17:56 UTC
00:17:56 KST

Introducing ChatGPT Wallet
Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.
We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents. It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. Built in partnership with American Express, Chase, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available through dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents.
1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.
To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.
ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Users add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.
Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.
After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.
We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.
Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.
Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.
Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a Commerce Partner Playbook(opens in a new window) with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:
- Help customers find accurate product information. Claim your business in ChatGPT and, once verified, update your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.
- Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website. Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.
- Work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases. Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.
- Give agents more ways to work with your business. Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools.
ChatGPT Wallet begins rolling out today in dots, enabling users to have their dot complete purchases on their behalf. It will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards. We’ll work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to learn from early use and expand availability, helping more customers and businesses benefit from agentic commerce.

New James Bond Announced and the Name's Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:13:47 UTC
00:13:47 KST

Robert Pattinson has been announced as the successor to Daniel Craig, becoming the seventh actor to play the role in an official Bond movie.
The news was revealed on the official James Bond social media accounts account on Monday. All earlier content was abruptly wiped from 007 on X and Instagram just before 3pm GMT and a repeating message typed out: “Identity confirmed.”
The film studio then released a first photo of the actor in Bond’s trademark tuxedo with a press release confirming the news and saying Pattinson’s casting will “usher in a new era for one of cinema’s most celebrated characters”.
In a statement Pattinson said: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime … To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”
The announcement came after a drawn-out casting process, in which Pattinson was understood to be on a five-strong shortlist, which included Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. On Friday suggestions emerged that Pattinson had been offered more favourable contract terms than his rivals, fuelling rumours that he was the strong favourite for the role.
Craig’s final film as Bond was No Time to Die, released in 2021 after being delayed due to the Covid pandemic. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying before a title card promised: “James Bond will return”.
Craig made five Bond films in total, starting with Casino Royale in 2006. During his tenure the franchise became a box-office record-breaker, with 2012’s Skyfall alone taking $1.1bn globally.
Pattinson, 40, is due to appear in the next Bond film, the 26th in the franchise (although two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983, take the total to 28). The as yet untitled project will the first to be shot since Amazon-MGM Studios purchased the rights to the series for more than $1bn in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.
Harry Potter producer David Heyman and Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal will oversee the franchise, while the Dune trilogy’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.
Pattinson has demonstrated his versatility across a wide variety of roles, earning a reputation as an actor with broad enough appeal to support major blockbuster films while retaining artistic credibility with offbeat and unlikely choices. He first came to notice in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and achieved superstardom opposite Kristen Stewart as vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight film series. He appeared in films directed by David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, Maps to the Stars), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse) and Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and returned to franchise film-making with The Batman in 2022.
The first actor to play Bond on the big screen was Edinburgh-born Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No. So successful was the film that Connery returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many to be some of the franchise’s finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice. Bond creator Ian Fleming’s preference for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian model George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).
Roger Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, which include The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker and Octopussy. The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a six-year gap preceded Irish actor Pierce Brosnan’s debut in 1995 in GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig’s tenure began.
The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.
Catherine Shoard will be in the comments from 5.30pm today to answer readers’ questions about the casting.

====================================================================================================

US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:02:34 UTC
00:02:34 KST

The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.
“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”
The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.
Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.
The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.
“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

Google Maps can now build trip itineraries with real-time details about each stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:48:13 UTC
23:48:13 KST

Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.
The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.
Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.
For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.
When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.
Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.
The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.
Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”
The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

Apple TV is getting video podcasts you can watch for free
A new video podcasts section for Apple TV won’t go behind the subscription paywall.
The expansion follows other streaming services’ push into podcasts. Netflix announced it was adding video podcasts to its platform last year, and debuted its first original video podcast series in January. Hulu and Disney Plus also offer podcasts, including a mix of companion podcasts for their shows and licensed podcasts like We’re Here to Help, hosted by Jake Johnson and Gareth Reynolds. Spotify has had support for video podcasts for several years now, and last year expanded them to its tvOS app. YouTube’s TV app has long been an option for watching podcasts, as well.
Besides bringing its video podcasts to more screens, Apple is also planning to add more video podcasts to its regular Podcasts app, according to the Times. Apple added support for switching between audio and video podcasts in its iOS Podcasts app earlier this year, and added video podcasts on the tvOS Podcasts app in September.

America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:43:48 UTC
23:43:48 KST

Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.
America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.
America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.
A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.
For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta.
“It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”
“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”
— Amanda Khera
She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft.
Her flight landed safely. But she deplaned into a terminal frozen in place. More than 600 flights out of Atlanta, including their connection to Norfolk, had been canceled. And no one knew when they would be able to take off because every flight across the United States had been grounded.
On Friday, November 13, the nation’s air traffic control system began to fail. Around 3:15PM ET, pilots and air traffic controllers in the Midwest started reporting difficulty communicating with each other over the radio.
“We’re 11,000 [feet] over Grand Rapids airport, about nine miles to the west,” said the pilot of Allegiant Flight 547, his transmission already becoming garbled. “Unable to get… contact… approach on any [frequency].”
Four minutes later, controllers at Quad Cities Airport in Moline, Illinois, reported similar issues across the region.
“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated,” said one. “It sounds like Chicago Approach is going ATC zero, so it might be worse than we initially thought. We thought it was just here.”
With communication outages spreading around the country, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” From that moment on, no airplanes were allowed to take off in US airspace.
The sudden halt surprised both pilots and controllers.
“Just a heads up, we went in a national ground stop,” said a controller in Seattle.
“Are you saying national as in Reagan National,” asked one United pilot, “or national in the whole country?”
“Across all en route facilities, they’re having communication issues.”
Like so many of the safety incidents that have plagued the air traffic control system over the last few years, this latest failure began with a fragile and outdated piece of FAA infrastructure. In this case, according to the agency, the faulty system was the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI.
Built by defense giant L3Harris in the early 2000s, FTI is the data backbone of the entire air traffic control system. It links more than 4,400 aviation facilities and carries the voice and radar data controllers rely on to keep planes separated, bridging the gap between the FAA’s legacy phone-based transmission systems and modern Internet Protocol-based ones.
FTI is scheduled to be replaced in 2028. Until then, L3Harris must make incremental upgrades to keep FTI operational.
“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated.”
— Air traffic controller
One of these upgrades accidentally brought down the entire system, according to The Wall Street Journal. Early in the day, L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once activated, however, the router began to flood the network with hundreds of connection attempts every second.
This may have added enough extra load to the system to degrade the whole network’s performance, according to I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University.
Hou explained that telecom networks break pieces of information — radio transmissions or radar coordinates, for example — into data packets small enough to be transmitted over the network and reassembled at the other end.
“When the network is degraded, it may start to lose a small portion of packets,” Hou says. “Since you need all packets to reassemble the data feed, just dropping one out of 10 packets may cause your feed to completely stop.”
Most modern communications apps are built to compensate for packet loss. FaceTime, for example, will blur the video or switch to audio-only to preserve the connection.
Air traffic control doesn’t have that luxury.
“Many NAS [National Air Space] applications … require a highly reliable synchronization source with exceptional stability,” according to FAA technical documentation, which warns that instability may cause widespread failure of critical systems.
FAA technicians believe the El Dorado router’s repeated connection attempts created enough instability within the FTI to cut off radio and radar feeds to 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and several Terminal Radar Approach Controls.
“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on,” Hou says.
“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on.”
— I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University
L3Harris’s contractors isolated the malfunctioning router and another one at a nearby radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Once those two routers were taken offline, the network began to stabilize once again.
Four and a half hours later, at 8:15PM ET, the FAA lifted the ground stop. It was the nation’s longest since 9/11, spurring airlines to cancel more than 13,000 flights and delay more than 25,000 more through the weekend, according to FlightAware. And more than 1.5 million passengers were stranded.
Faulty technology created the crisis. The FAA’s hamfisted attempts to reassure the public that everything was okay made the situation worse.
For six hours after the ground stop began, the FAA did not provide any public updates except for a terse, 31-word press release and a single X post. Finally, at 11:30PM ET, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to explain the day’s events.
Instead of providing clarity, however, they issued confusing and sometimes even contradictory statements. Mullin opened the conference with a joke (“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”) before confidently declaring that “there is no cyberattack.” Instead, he appeared to blame the outage on the FAA’s modernization project.
“As Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and technology was just overwhelming the older system,” said Mullin.
Mullin’s remark appeared to surprise Duffy, who looked at the ground and shook his head. Mullin later walked the statement back after a reporter’s follow-up question, admitting that “there’s nothing completely certain right now.”
Duffy offered more details but did not exactly give a straight answer. “Our switches and routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” he said. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.”
“I don’t want to rule out nefarious activity,” he later added.
“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin concluded. “We are built to handle crisis like this.”
A follow-up press conference on Saturday afternoon was equally bizarre. It started with piercing audio feedback produced by a faulty microphone, which interrupted Duffy right after he introduced Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer.
After a four-minute delay, Duffy continued with the briefing. He floated the potential that contractor “incompetence” had caused the outage. And he demanded that Congress allocate billions more dollars to the FAA so it could complete its modernization efforts — calling its existing $12.5 billion modernization budget a “partial payment.”
The conferences only flamed online rumors that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or a rogue AI tied to the September rollout of the FAA’s new SMART system. (So far, no evidence has emerged for either.)
The problem was compounded by an administration already struggling to command public trust. When cabinet officials offered shifting, improvised explanations from the podium, millions of anxious travelers — and even prominent allies — simply refused to take the government at its word.
“Until proven otherwise, not some presser by our government, I firmly believe this was a DDOS attack,” former National Security Adviser Mike Flynn wrote on X. “This is what was being described by two smart cabinet officials who clearly did not understand the technical nature of what happened.”
Khera and her family didn’t know about the political gamesmanship behind the outage — and frankly, they didn’t care. She just wanted to get out of Atlanta on something other than an airplane.
After a night in one of the last available hotel rooms in Atlanta, she and her family rented a car and drove the nine hours back to Virginia Beach. They made it home late Saturday night.
Because of the FAA’s mishaps, they don’t plan to fly again anytime soon.
“We’ve had enough of planes,” she said. “It will take a couple months and more explanations from the FAA to make sure something like this or worse doesn’t happen again.”
Correction, November 16th: L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, not a wireless one. This story has been updated to reflect that fact.

A 512 KiB binary message teaching chess without a shared language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:38:54 UTC
23:38:54 KST

Golden Board
Or Why and How to Teach Chess to Aliens.
Intro
Golden Board is a binary message designed to teach chess to an unknown recipient without a shared language, culture, or prior knowledge of the game. It begins by teaching the format needed to read its own contents.
The full project code and documentation are available on GitHub.
This guide follows that process: recover numbers from the bits, use them to reconstruct pictures and interactions, then learn how those pictures describe chess. One complete game connects the layers, from its physical bits to its final displayed position.
Feedback is always welcome.
Before we dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things about the project.
What does it look like?
              In a nutshell, Golden Board is a sequence of 4,194,304 bits, or 512 KiB of ones and zeros.
              That number suggests arranging them into a 2,048 × 2,048 square.
            
What’s inside?
              The first 64 rows contain 32 drawings, each 64 × 64 cells.
              Together they form the bootstrap: it teaches how to read the rest of
              the message. It's chess-agnostic and can be used to decode other structured messages.
            
The payload below contains visual chess lessons, exercises with feedback, complete games, and the information needed to find, check and display them.
Where did the idea come from?
I took inspiration from messages intended for unknown intelligences, such as the Voyager Golden Record, Lincos, and others.
But instead of sharing scientific knowledge or works of art, Golden Board teaches chess.
Why chess?
Two reasons.
First, a small set of rules opens up an enormous world of possibilities, ideas and beauty.
Second, a game can share more than knowledge: it offers a glimpse of the human mind.
How did I test it?
I ran trials using LLMs as stand-ins for unknown recipients, testing decoding and understanding with raw bits, decoded content, and varying levels of assistance.
Correctly recovering the bytes and understanding the lessons are separate tests. These models already know chess, so correct chess answers alone cannot establish that the message taught them. The trials helped identify ambiguities and improve the design; they do not establish that an unknown intelligence would understand it. Read the trial account.
How did I choose the games?
No set of 64 games is complete.
              I chose games for their chess: brilliant attacks, surprising sacrifices, clever defenses, quiet strategy, and beautiful endings. The PGN anthology contains 64 games, while the binary message omits names, dates, and events.
            
What is it all for?
There is a special joy in sharing something you love.
What could we share with a civilization that knows nothing about us? They might already know our science or lack the context for our art, but chess can be taught from scratch, revealing centuries of human imagination, mistakes, and brilliance.
              Most likely, no one will ever receive this message. But even a small chance that someone might discover a position with a move like
              Bf5 makes the whole thing worth trying.
            
Can you build on it?
Yes. The chess-agnostic bootstrap, binary format and Python tools offer a starting point for teaching other subjects without a shared language or culture. Developers can adapt the system; researchers can use the trials to investigate what works, what fails and why. Source code and documentation.
How to read this guide
            In the source drawings, each cell shows a bit: black represents 1 and white
            represents 0. Decoded pictures are reconstructed from the stored data,
            rather than cropped from the source square.
          
Colors, fine gray guides, and labels are added here to make the pictures easier to read. They are not part of the original message.
The intended recipient can infer these arrangements without visual aids, using bounding boxes, fixed sequence lengths, and other previously learned patterns.
The frame below provides an example; its contents are explained later. The blue area covers a data row and its small marks underneath. The orange area picks out the small number to its left. The green area covers a whole boxed list. The gray guides make individual bit positions easier to count.
Hover over a colored phrase to keep only its matching highlights. Hover over the picture to hide all visual aids.
Reading numbers and pictures
The recipient begins with a clean sequence of bits or a sampled square, and is assumed to be able to count, recognize patterns and write simple programs. Obtaining those cells from a signal or physical object is a separate problem.
The first task is to recover pictures and interactions from the bits. The recipient can then use those displays to learn chess. The bootstrap establishes the reading rules through worked examples; the recipient supplies a program that follows those rules. The message carries data for that program to interpret, not executable code.
The bootstrap is the narrow strip at the top of the view below. The payload area beneath it includes the unused space at the end.
Headers show order and related groups
              Before looking inside each drawing, use its header to locate it in the strip. Each frame repeats
              the same corner mark. Its top row pairs a count of filled cells with a binary numeral to give its global number,
              1–32. A second pair two rows below counts steps within a
              related group. That local count restarts for each group; standalone frames leave its row empty.
            
              Compare these four headers. Frame 6 is sixth overall and second in its related group. Frame 3 stands alone:
            
                Frame 1: global 1 (00000001), group step
                1 (00000001).
              
                Frame 2: global 2 (00000010), group step
                2 (00000010).
              
Frame 3: global 3 (00000011), no local counter.
                Frame 6: global 6 (00000110), group step
                2 (00000010).
