Thanksgiving Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Roasting a whole turkey can be intimidating, but it really doesn’t have to be! That’s why I’ve put together this thoroughly tested (and tested, and tested again!) step-by-step guide to getting juicy, flavorful meat and beautifully golden, crispy skin without the guesswork. I’ll walk you through everything from safely thawing and prepping your Thanksgiving Turkey (including an optional dry brine) to roasting and carving, with plenty of helpful tips along the way. I’ve even included a printable Thanksgiving Day timetable you can stick on your fridge, so you can spend less time worrying about the turkey and more time enjoying the holiday!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
A Method You Can Count On
There is NO WAY I’d publish a recipe this important without making sure you have everything you need to get it right on the big day. I’ve worked through all the little details, from the seasoning to the roasting method, so you can feel confident making a turkey your whole family will love. Grandma likes dark meat? This method yields the juiciest, most flavorful thighs and drumsticks. Auntie Linda only eats white meat? The breast stays tender and juicy thanks to the garlicky herb butter tucked under the skin. And if your brothers and Dad love crispy skin, I can help you there! The optional dry brine and thin coating of seasoned oil give this roasted turkey a beautifully golden, crispy finish that the whole family will beg for.
But if there’s one thing I’ve learned through all my testing, it’s just how important a good meat thermometer is. The size of your turkey and even the pan you roast it in can affect the cooking time, so I always recommend checking the internal temperature rather than relying on the clock alone. Be sure to read my top tips and comprehensive FAQ section, too. I’ve covered everything you might need (including rescuing a turkey that’s still frozen on Thanksgiving morning!)
Recipe Success Tips
There’s a lot riding on this one bird, so naturally, there’s a lot of tips and guidance I need to cover, too. I recommend reading through this whole guide once (if not twice!) before getting started, including these tips and the FAQ section at the end.
- Season under AND over the skin. I tuck a garlicky herb compound butter (made from butter, garlic, dried herbs, and paprika) under the skin to keep the breast meat juicy and flavorful, then brush a micro-thin sheen of seasoned oil over the outside for beautifully crispy skin. Gently massage the butter through the skin to distribute it evenly, and dab the oil over the buttered areas, so you don’t accidentally move the butter out of place.
- Dry brine if you have the time. You don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference! Unlike a wet brine that waterlogs the skin, a dry brine uses salt to chemically restructure the meat proteins so they trap and hold onto their own natural juices while roasting. Plus, letting it sit uncovered in the fridge pulls surface moisture away, which is the absolute secret to getting that addictively crispy skin. Short on time? Just skip Steps 4 and 5 in my recipe below. The compound butter will still give your turkey plenty of flavor (promise!)
- Use a meat thermometer. Roasting times vary depending on your turkey’s size and the pan you use, so I’ve included weight-based guidelines in the recipe card below to help you plan ahead. I highly recommend an electronic probe thermometer so you can monitor the temperature without opening the oven.
- DON’T baste your turkey! Every time you open the oven door to baste, you let out heat, extending the cooking time. Pouring pan juices over the skin also adds moisture, which ruins all the effort you put into getting that skin bone-dry and shatteringly crisp. Trust the compound butter under the skin to do its job. If the breast or drumsticks start getting too dark before the turkey reaches temperature, tent them loosely with aluminum foil so they can finish cooking without overbrowning.
- Pull the turkey at 157-160°F and let carryover heat finish the cooking. Avoid touching bone with your thermometer, as this can skew the reading. As the turkey rests, the internal temperature continues rising, bringing it to a safe 165°F. Before carving, I always double-check three places with an instant-read thermometer: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F before serving. If not, let it rest a little longer and check again.
- Save those pan juices, too! Don’t throw away the flavorful juices and drippings left in your roasting pan, either. Save them to make a delicious homemade turkey gravy.
- Short on time? Break down your turkey first. Cutting your turkey into individual pieces before roasting can help it cook much faster than leaving it whole. If you’re pressed for time on Thanksgiving Day, check out Melissa’s video on breaking down a whole chicken (also below!) for a helpful demonstration. You can use the same basic technique for turkey, but remember that cooking times will vary depending on the size of the pieces.
Budget-Saving Tips for Feeding a Smaller Crowd
A whole turkey is actually one of the most economical ways to feed your family this Thanksgiving. I recently spotted frozen whole turkeys at Walmart for just $0.84 per pound, which is an incredible deal. If you have the time and freezer space, all that extra meat can be put to good use in soups, sandwiches, casseroles, and more over the following days (I’ve shared some leftover ideas below!).
However, if you’re only feeding a few people, don’t want a fridge full of leftovers, or simply want to skip roasting a whole bird, you can still enjoy those same delicious holiday flavors with our roasted turkey breast or swap to turkey drumsticks instead.
You can use the exact same aromatics, butter-under-the-skin technique, and dry-spice profile as my whole turkey recipe below, just adapted for dark meat turkey drumsticks!
Check out our baked chicken drumsticks recipe for the full step-by-step technique, then make these easy adjustments for turkey:
- Spices and fats: Keep the ingredients identical! Use the same compound butter tucked under the skin and the seasoning oil blend (canola oil, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and ground mustard) brushed over the exterior.
- Temperature and time: Because turkey drumsticks are significantly larger than chicken legs, roast them at 350°F for roughly 1 hour-1 hour 15 minutes, flipping them halfway through.
- Target temperature: Use your digital thermometer and pull them when the thickest part hits 165°F (or ideally 175°F so all that collagen in the dark meat melts into tender, succulent meat).
How many turkey legs do I need?
- 1 turkey leg per adult (or 1 leg per big eater).
- 1 turkey leg per 2 young children (or smaller appetites).
What to Serve with Roasted Turkey
Roasted turkey might be the main event, but it’s nothing without all the classic Thanksgiving fixings. Creamy mashed potatoes and plenty of turkey gravy are a must, especially for serving alongside the leaner white meat. Cranberry sauce (or my cranberry relish for something a little fresher) helps balance all those rich flavors, while sausage stuffing brings plenty of herbs and comforting holiday flavor to the plate. I’d also add a side of green beans, for something easy and colorful, and a classic sweet potato casserole for a little sweetness. Of course, there’s always room for more family favorites!
To make Thanksgiving Day easier, I like to make the cranberry sauce ahead of time and get any sides (like stuffing and sweet potato casserole) prepped in advance. The green beans and gravy can be made while the turkey rests. For more affordable holiday dishes and help planning your menu, check out my recent holiday guide.
Got Leftovers?
Once you’ve removed the meat from the bones, refrigerate any leftovers in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours. It’ll keep in the fridge for 3-4 days, or you can freeze it in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat leftovers in the microwave, skillet, or oven until they reach 165°F.
However, leftover turkey is also delicious cold! My family loves a good turkey sandwich with leftover cranberry sauce and stuffing, or you can tuck it between toasted bread with a little mayo and whatever salad ingredients you’ve got on hand. It’s also perfect for making meals over the next few days. Use it to make a turkey pot pie, swap it for shredded chicken in your favorite recipes, or make a big pot of turkey noodle soup (recipe coming soon!).
how to make Thanksgiving Turkey step-by-step photos
Gather your turkey ingredients: This recipe is designed for a 12-14 lb whole turkey. Mine weighed 13.72 lbs. If you’re planning to dry brine your turkey, you’ll also need 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Allow 3-4 days for your turkey to thaw in the refrigerator. Keep it unopened on a rimmed tray to catch any drips. If you’re dry brining, count back from the day you plan to brine.
Gather your compound butter ingredients: You’ll need 2 sticks (1 cup) unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic (pressed or finely minced, about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Make sure your butter is softened to room temperature so it’s easy to combine with the seasonings and spread underneath the turkey skin.
Gather your seasoning oil ingredients: You’ll need 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. This mixture goes on the outside of the turkey to help create the best crispy skin.
Unwrap, trim, and pat dry: Once your turkey is completely thawed, remove the neck and giblets from the cavities. Use kitchen shears to trim away any excess neck skin and tail fat, then pour out any pooled juices. Pat the turkey thoroughly dry inside and out with clean paper towels. Place it breast-side up on a wire rack set inside a large rimmed baking sheet or roasting pan.
This is what the neck and giblets bag looks like. You can throw them away, or save them for stock (see the ‘Don’t Waste a Thing!’ section below).
Tuck the wings underneath: Fold the turkey’s wings back behind its body so the tips are tucked underneath. This helps protect them from burning while the turkey roasts.
Gently loosen the skin: Carefully slide your fingers underneath the skin covering the breasts and thighs, separating it from the meat to create pockets. Work slowly so you don’t tear the skin. This creates space for the optional dry brine and the compound butter we’ll add later.
Dry underneath the skin, too: Gently lift the loosened breast skin and use clean paper towels to dab away any moisture between the skin and the meat. The drier you can get the skin, the better it’ll crisp up in the oven.
(OPTIONAL) Apply the dry brine: Measure out 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Rub ½ tsp inside the cavity, ½ tsp directly onto the breast meat underneath the skin, and distribute the remaining salt evenly over the exterior skin. Make sure the salt is spread across the turkey rather than concentrated in one area. If you’re skipping the dry brine, go straight to making the compound butter.
Refrigerate uncovered for 12-24 hours (optional): Pull the skin back over the breast meat and return the turkey to the refrigerator on its wire rack, uncovered. Overnight is ideal! The photo above is my turkey after dry brining for 24 hours. Notice how much drier the skin looks after resting in the fridge? That’s exactly what we’re after. The salt helps season the meat while the uncovered refrigeration draws moisture away from the surface, giving you extra-crispy skin once roasted.
Make the compound butter: In a bowl, combine 2 sticks (1 cup) softened unsalted butter, 4 pressed or finely minced garlic cloves (about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Mash everything together with a fork until mostly smooth, and the herbs and seasonings are distributed throughout the butter.
Mix the seasoning oil: In a small cup or bowl, stir together 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. Stir until the spices are evenly mixed into the oil to create a thin, speckled seasoning paste.
Add the butter underneath the breast skin: Take your turkey out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before roasting to take the chill off. Divide the compound butter into two equal portions, one for each side of the turkey. Gently push the softened butter deep underneath the loosened breast skin, directly onto the meat, working some of each portion toward the thighs.
Work the butter underneath the thigh skin: Continue distributing the compound butter into the pockets underneath the thigh skin on both sides. This helps season the dark meat as well as the breast, so you’re not keeping all that delicious garlicky, herbaceous flavor in one area.
Massage the butter into place. With clean, dry hands (or you can wear gloves, if preferred), gently massage the turkey from the outside, pressing through the skin to distribute the butter underneath. Aim for an even coating across the breast and thigh meat without tearing the skin.
Brush with the seasoning oil: Using a pastry brush, apply a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil mixture all over the turkey’s exterior, including the drumsticks and wings. Dab gently over the buttered areas rather than brushing aggressively so you don’t displace the butter underneath the skin. You want a thin, even coating, not a thick layer of oil.
Insert your thermometer and roast: Preheat your oven to 350°F. Insert an electronic probe thermometer into the thickest part of the breast facing the oven door, keeping the probe away from the bone. Positioning it this way keeps the cable close to the door and the temperature display conveniently on your countertop. Roast the unstuffed turkey at 350°F for roughly 2-2½ hours on a baking sheet with a wire rack, or 2½-3 hours in a high-sided roasting pan.
Remove the turkey when the thickest part of the breast reads 157-160°F. The temperature will continue rising during the resting period. I highly recommend using a probe thermometer rather than relying on cooking time alone!
Save those pan juices for gravy: Once roasted, don’t throw away all those flavorful juices left in the roasting pan. Carefully collect them after removing the turkey from the oven and save them for homemade gravy. Follow our turkey gravy recipe to turn those drippings into a rich, savory gravy to serve alongside your Thanksgiving dinner.
Rest and check the temperature: Let your turkey rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes before carving. During this time, carryover heat continues cooking the turkey and the juices settle back into the meat. Before serving, use an instant-read thermometer to double-check three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F, without the thermometer touching bone. Once your turkey has reached a safe temperature and finished resting, it’s ready to serve…
Now Carve Your Roasted Turkey
- Remove the drumsticks. Bend each drumstick away from the body and gently separate it, one at a time. (Photos 1 and 2)
- Separate the thighs. Pop the hip joints, then carefully use a knife to separate both thighs from the body. (Photos 3 and 4)
- Remove the wings. Pull away both wings, using a knife to separate them at the joints. You can also cut them into drumettes if you prefer. (Photos 5 and 6)
- Carve the first breast. Find the breastbone and make your first cut about 1 cm to one side. Follow the curve of the ribs as you gently pull the breast away. (Photos 7 and 8)
- Repeat on the other side. Cut along the other side of the breastbone, then follow the rib cage and cut underneath where the wing was attached to free the second breast. (Photos 9, 10, and 11)
- Arrange the turkey for serving. Set both breasts on a platter with the drumsticks, thighs, and wings. Slice the breast meat just before serving. Enjoy! (Photo 12 and photo below)
Don’t Waste a Thing!
I use a whole turkey for this recipe and remove the neck and giblets before roasting. You can discard them if you like, or put them to work while the turkey’s in the oven:
- Use the giblets for gravy: Unwrap the giblets and put the neck, heart, and gizzard in a saucepan with 1 chopped onion, 1 carrot, and 1 celery rib. Add enough water to cover and simmer for 45 mins-1 hour. Leave out the liver for a milder broth. Strain and use the broth in place of the chicken broth to make your turkey gravy.
- Save the carcass for stock: For a deeper roasted flavor, lightly oil the bones and roast them on a rimmed baking sheet at 450°F for about 30 mins, until well browned. Check them early if they’re already quite dark. Chill the roasted bones, then pack them in a freezer bag and freeze for later (up to 3 months). If you skip the optional extra roast, refrigerate or freeze the bones within 2 hours of cooking. Thaw frozen bones in the fridge when you’re ready to make stock.
- Make the stock on the stove or in a slow cooker: Add the turkey carcass, 1 large onion, 2 carrots, 3 celery ribs, and 1-2 bay leaves if you have them to a soup pot or crockpot. Roughly chop the vegetables and add enough water to just cover everything. Simmer gently on the stove for 2-3 hours, or cook on High for at least 6 hours using the method in our slow cooker chicken broth guide. Strain the stock and use it for soups or gravy.
Roasted Turkey FAQ’s
If a question comes up halfway through prep, you can jump straight to the answer here:
My Turkey is still frozen! Help!
Don’t panic! Do the cold-water emergency thaw. Keep the turkey in its original leak-proof wrapper and submerge it breast-side down in a clean sink or tub filled completely with cold tap water. Swap the water out every 30 minutes so it stays safe and ice-cold. It takes about 30 minutes per pound, so a 12-14 lb bird will take 6 to 7 hours to thaw completely. If it’s just icy inside the cavity, run cold tap water through the center to break up internal ice chunks, then dab every inch bone-dry before seasoning!
(And hey, if you’re realizing this the night before Thanksgiving, set your alarm. For a 4:00 PM dinner, you’ll need to kick off that cold-water bath by 4:00 or 5:00 AM sharp to give it those 6-7 hours!)
My turkey is starting to look too dark on top; what can I do?
Tent it loosely with a sheet of aluminum foil! If the top of the breast or the tips of the drumsticks are getting deeply browned before the center reaches temp, shield them with a piece of foil folded into a light dome over the bird. This deflects direct heat while allowing the oven’s ambient heat to finish cooking the inside.
Should I trust the pop-up turkey button to tell me when it’s done?
No! Toss it out and use an instant-read meat thermometer! Those little plastic pop-up timers are notoriously unreliable. They operate on a meltable metal alloy set to trip at around 180°F, meaning by the time it pops, your breast meat is already overcooked, dry, and chalky. Instead, insert a digital thermometer into the thickest part of the breast (without touching bone) and pull the bird at 157°F-160°F. Carryover heat will bring it up to a safe 165°F while resting.
Standard USDA roasting charts recommend 3-3 ¾ hours at 325°F for an unstuffed 12-14 lb turkey in a traditional high-sided roasting pan. They outline why you should never roast a turkey at a temperature below 325°F here. (Hello, Danger Zone!)
At 350°F (as I use in this recipe), standard estimates are 2-2 ½ hours for a sheet pan with a wire rack, or 2 ½–3 hours if using a high-sided roasting pan. If you are cooking your bird in a roasting pan with high sides, start checking your bird at the 2½ hour mark. I can’t stress enough how much of a difference having an electronic probe thermometer inserted into the breast meat while the turkey is in the oven will help ensure your bird comes out PERFECT.
Why 2-2 ½ hours worked for us
- Baking Sheet with Wire Rack: Cooking on a flat baking sheet with a wire rack allows hot air to circulate freely around the entire bird, cooking it significantly faster than a traditional high-walled roasting pan that traps steam and shields the sides.
- Dry Brining & Air-Chilling: Drying out the skin and outer layer of meat speeds up heat transfer and skin crisping.
- Targeting 157°F-160°F: Pulling the bird at 157°F-160°F (rather than waiting for 165°F in the oven) reduces total oven time by 15-25 minutes, relying on carryover cooking during the rest. This results in a super juicy, perfectly cooked turkey.
Do I have to brine my turkey?
No, you don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference. Just leave out Steps 4 and 5 if you decide not to. Skipping the brine won’t ruin your dinner, especially since you’re using our rich compound butter under the skin. But taking the time to salt the bird beforehand seasons the meat all the way to the bone and gives you that extra layer of flavor and moisture.
Wet Brine vs. Dry Brine: What’s the Difference?
- Dry Brine: Gives you concentrated, deep turkey flavor, incredibly juicy meat, and shatteringly crisp, golden skin because the fridge air dehydrates the surface. It’s low-effort and takes up minimal fridge space.
- Wet Brine: Plumps the meat up with extra water weight which does help it cook up juicy, but leaves the skin wet, rubbery, and soggy (making it really hard to get a good crisp). It also requires a giant bucket, gallons of water, ice, and a massive chunk of your refrigerator shelf.
Why rest before carving?
Because carving too soon empties all that hard-earned moisture onto your cutting board. During roasting, heat pushes juices into the center of the meat. Letting the bird rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb those juices so every slice stays amazingly juicy. Plus, carryover heat gently finishes cooking the center to a safe 165°F without drying out the outer layers.
Storage & Reheating
If you haven’t already, remove the leftover turkey from the bones (see the above carving guidance), slice or chop it into smaller pieces, and refrigerate it in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours of cooking (or 1 hour if it’s above 90°F). Keep the turkey at 40°F or below and use it within 3-4 days. Store any leftover gravy and sides separately.
Reheating
I’d warm only what you plan to serve. Add a splash of broth or water to keep the turkey from drying out, especially the lean breast meat. For several servings, cover the turkey with foil and warm it in a 325°F oven. For a few slices, use a covered skillet over medium heat or a microwave-safe dish with a vented cover. If you microwave it, turn the pieces partway through and let them stand briefly before checking the temperature in a few spots.
Whichever method you use, reheat the turkey to 165°F throughout. The skin will soften in the fridge and stay soft when reheated covered. If you want to crisp it back up, give the reheated pieces a quick sear skin-side down in a lightly oiled skillet.
Freezing
Freeze sliced or shredded roast turkey in meal-sized portions for up to 3 months for best texture. Press the air out of freezer bags, label them with the date, and freeze them flat so they thaw more evenly in the fridge. The meat can lose a little moisture as it thaws, so the breast may be slightly drier after reheating, and the skin will lose its crunch. A splash of broth helps when reheating, or you can use the thawed meat in soup or pot pie.
Thanksgiving Eve to Thanksgiving Day Schedule (For a 4:00 PM Dinner)
Here’s a play-by-play schedule to help you get your bird ready for the big day with minimal stress. Download it here, print it out, and stick it on your fridge so you know what to do and when.
Monday
Make sure your bird goes into the fridge by Sunday or Monday morning so it is 100% thawed by Wednesday morning!
If you are planning to do a 12-24 hour dry brine, make sure it’s fully thawed on Wednesday. (Still frozen the night before Thanksgiving? Refer to our emergency cold-water thaw guide above and make sure you start by 4:00 AM! Set your alarm!).
Wednesday (The Day Before Thanksgiving – Morning/Early Afternoon):
- Prep: Unwrap the turkey, remove the neck and giblets, trim any excess neck skin, and pat every single inch dry with clean paper towels.
- Dry Brine & Refrigerate (optional): Apply your kosher salt (a little inside, a little under the breast skin, and all over the exterior, see recipe for amounts). Place the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed sheet pan and put it uncovered on the bottom shelf of the fridge overnight. If you’re skipping the dry brine, leave the turkey wrapped in the fridge and do the prep on Thursday.
Thursday (Thanksgiving Day): 10:45 AM (5.25 Hours Before 4pm Dinner):
Take the turkey out of the fridge and let it sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes to take off the chill. (Not to exceed 2 hours at room temperature! Perishable raw poultry should never sit in the temperature “Danger Zone”, 40°F to 140°F, for more than 2 total hours, as surface bacteria can multiply rapidly.)
Mix your room-temperature compound butter and your exterior seasoning oils. Set aside.
11:15 AM (4.75 Hours Before Dinner):
Preheat your oven to 350°F. Slide the compound butter under the skin of the breasts and thighs. Brush a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil over the outside.
11:45 AM (4.25 Hours Before Dinner):
Place the turkey on a rack in your roasting pan or sheet pan and slide it into the oven.
2:15 PM (1.75 Hours Before Dinner – Check Temp):
Check the internal temperature with your probe thermometer or digital instant-read. For a 13-14 lb bird, it should be getting close! Crucial rule: Pull the bird the moment the thickest part of the breast hits 157°F-160°F (the thighs will be around 175°F). If the top is getting too dark before the temp is reached, loosely tent a piece of foil over the breast (but not tightly touching the breast or the skin may tear when you remove the foil!)
2:45 PM (Target Pull Time):
Transfer the turkey from the oven to your cutting board once the breast hits 157°F-160°F.
2:45 PM – 3:30 PM (The Rest):
Let it rest uncovered on the counter for 30-45 minutes so the juices settle and the internal temperature rises safely to 165°F.
3:30 PM – 4:00 PM (Final Check & Carving): Use your instant-read thermometer to double-check that all three key spots (breast, thigh, and wing) have reached at least 165°F.
4:00 PM: Carve and serve your perfectly juicy, crispy-skinned turkey!
More Ways to Use Leftover Turkey
- If I’m feeding a crowd again the next day, I’d make a tray of Turkey Sliders with cranberry sauce, melty Swiss, and buttery Hawaiian rolls.
- Give leftovers a completely different flavor with our three-bean Turkey Chili. Sauté the vegetables first, then stir in shredded roast turkey near the end of simmering in place of the ground turkey and heat it through to 165°F.
- When there’s a little bit of everything left, tuck the turkey, stuffing, and mashed potatoes into crescent dough for a golden Holiday Leftovers Wreath.
- For a quick lunch for one, crisp up a Thanksgiving Leftovers Tortilla Wrap filled with turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and melty brie.
Other Thanksgiving Favorites
SOURCES (USDA Food Safety):
- USDA Refrigerator Thawing Guidelines: You can read the official instructions on the USDA FSIS Turkey Basics: Safe Thawing Page, which outlines the requirement of roughly 24 hours of defrost time for every 4 to 5 pounds of turkey (requiring 3 to 4 full days for a 12–16 lb bird) kept unopened on a tray to prevent cross-contamination.
- USDA: Let’s Talk Turkey: You can see the three ways to safely thaw frozen turkey.
- USDA Safe Handling & Tray Protocols: Check out USDA FSIS — Your Safe Thanksgiving Guide, which confirms keeping raw poultry sealed in its original wrapper and using a rimmed dish or container to catch leaking juices during refrigerator defrosting.
- The USDA “Danger Zone” Rule (40°F–140°F): You can read the official guidelines on the USDA FSIS “Danger Zone” Page, which explains how bacteria grow rapidly between 40°F and 140°F and why perishable foods (like raw poultry) can sit out at room temperature for up to two hours during prep.
- The USDA 2-Hour Rule: For specific Q&A details, check the USDA AskFSIS 2-Hour Rule Entry, which confirms the strict 2-hour limit for leaving perishable foods out of refrigeration before cooking or serving.

Soldier files whistleblower complaint over Iran strike that killed 6 U.S. troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:17:53 UTC
23:17:53 KST

One of the US Army soldiers that survived an Iranian strike that hit a makeshift operations center in Kuwait and killed six has submitted a whistleblower complaint alleging that the Pentagon did not listen to concerns about the lack of proper protection for troops, according to a copy of the disclosure obtained by CNN.
The complaint, submitted last week to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS, comes as Democrats are poised to launch wide-ranging investigations into the Trump administration and its handling of the Iran war when they take control of Congress in January.
CNN has reached out to the congressional committees and the Pentagon for comment.
Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom outlined why he submitted the report in an exclusive interview with CBS’ Norah O’Donnell on “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, describing the March 1 attack as a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.”
“We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn,” he said. He added that some people described the operations center as a “trailer park.”
The six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in the strike at Kuwait’s Shuaiba port were the first US service members killed in the US’ war with Iran. Dozens, including Ramsbottom, were wounded.
While senior Pentagon officials said at the time that the building was fortified, a source familiar with the site previously told CNN it was only surrounded by concrete barriers that would provide protection from car bombs but had nothing to shield it from drones or missiles. CNN also previously reported that the attack came quickly and with no warning or sirens to alert troops to evacuate or get into a bunker, according to a source familiar with the situation.
Ramsbottom said he brought up the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors in various meetings and was told: “We don’t have to worry about protection.” Military leaders later said that they were going to try to get a counter-drone system sent to the site, but “it never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested,” he said.
The installation did not have a physician or a fixed aid station when the drone strike happened, according to the whistleblower report. There was only one ambulance at the site.
Ramsbottom has made similar claims in interviews with multiple outlets since the attack. In an interview with CNN affiliate KOAA news in April, he recalled that while the facility had protections for “legacy threats” like mortar fire or car bombs, it wasn’t prepared for modern drone warfare.
“It was well-fortified for that type of thinking from pre-Russian invasion of Ukraine. It was a pretty well fortified base. But it wasn’t well prepared for the type of fight that we’re getting into,” he told the news station.
At a press conference after the attack in March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the US has “incredible air defenders,” but acknowledged that “one” projectile had made it through in the attack.
“Every once in a while you might have one — unfortunately, we call it a squirter — that makes its way through. And in that particular case, it happened to hit a tactical operation center that was, that was fortified, but it — these are powerful weapons,” he said.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and is the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has asked Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing to answer questions and provide “all force protection assessments” about the facility at the Shuaiba port.

The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:15:31 UTC
23:15:31 KST

The Active Directory Era Is Finally Over
“Life was simpler on Active Directory, at least I could manage every identity”.
I made that quote up, but there is nostalgia for a golden age of corporate IT that’s never coming back: Many enterprises still (try to) track identities in Active Directory (AD), a service that’s old enough to drink and crumbles at the scale of modern cloud computing.
It held up because the architecture is simple enough: Active Directory is an LDAP directory to store identities and a Kerberos implementation to let them authenticate, wrapped in decent UX and with continued updates.
AD accomplished the goal of identity management: A way to know all identities, who vouched for them, and where they’re valid. It answered three questions in a unified catalog:
- What identities exist? With the directory, which records every user and machine
- What vouched for the identity? With a domain controller that approves authentication based on admin credentials
- Where is the identity valid? With AD domain architecture that reflects the company’s infrastructure
Security policies are moot if you can't answer any one of them. I spent many hours keeping our Active Directory catalog accurate so it could answer these questions, because everything downstream depended on it: issuing certificates automatically with Certificate Services, applying settings at scale with Group Policies, and more.
There were always some compromises: databases with local users, Linux servers requiring workarounds (Thank you SSSD!), but most users and machines in my network had an identity in Active Directory, and I knew which didn’t.
But unifying every identity in Active Directory (or any one directory) is nearly impossible with modern cloud architecture. There’s an AD ecosystem of security products, password rotations, and sync plugins that modernizes it, but nothing can undo architecture choices from a bygone era.
Active Directory is the new mainframe: great for its time, but you’d never choose to start from scratch. Replacing it is impossible because it’s so entrenched.
Active Directory can accurately reflect human identities with a few integrations and plugins, but machine identities are nearly impossible.
Maybe that’s controversial. You can come to me with torches, pitchforks, and architectural diagrams about Kubernetes pod identity attestation in AD, but Active Directory is still a piece of infrastructure built for a bygone era.
Visibility and attestation: Unified machine identity is nearly impossible in Active Directory
Most organizations are creating grave security risks because they don’t understand modern machine identity. I once spoke to someone at a conference who told me they had recently discovered a publicly exposed Lambda function. Bad enough, but that function’s policy was iam:* meaning it could take any IAM action, including crowning any attacker the organization’s superadmin. Oh, and by the way, this was a defense organization.
If an organization with high security requirements makes these blunders, you don’t want to know what happens at other organizations. This problem isn’t specific to AD, but it is a symptom of organizations not figuring out how to correctly attest machine identity in modern software development.
To understand why no organization can account for all of its machine identities in AD, we need to understand how a machine enters a domain. A domain is an administrative boundary that shares security rules. In practice, this is usually an organization.
When a new machine joins your domain, three main events happen:
- An object is created inside the directory (often called a machine account)
- DNS is updated, certificates are issued (assuming you have AD Certificate Services autoenrollment)
- Kerberos tickets are issued so the machine can assert its identity
When that machine logs in, it authenticates to a Domain Controller (the server running Active Directory for the domain), which trusts it because the machine is in its directory. But the machine had to enter the directory first.
When Active Directory was built, that meant a human manually added it. “Machines” were physical servers that got delivered to the office, installed in the server dungeon room, and registered by a human admin.
Human approval doesn’t scale to developers creating and deprecating testing databases, Kubernetes clusters, and CI runners at will. Contemporary AD implementations deal with this by deferring authority. An admin token (sometimes hardcoded…) automatically joins new identities.
Using human credentials to join new machines is a workaround that negates the point: Admin approval implies a human can tell you about each trusted device.
No admin can know every EC2 instance, PostgreSQL database, or CI runner in the organization. This is also because when AD was built, machine identities were long-lived devices, not ephemeral cloud resources.
Active Directory was built for human approval of long-lived infrastructure, but now often auto-approves short-lived cloud resources.
Even if you built all of the complex automations to reflect every testing database and Kubernetes pod in AD with automated admin approval, it’s security theater. The unified directory would exist on paper, but lack authority.
Modern cloud infrastructure automatically asserts machine identity:
- In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster.
- In Azure, you can configure a machine identity in Entra ID and let Azure’s Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) automatically issue OAuth tokens when machines request them.
These two examples have modern assumptions baked in: machines need to self-serve their identities when they’re spun up. They also assume a narrow scope.
Scope: how identity perimeters have changed
The unified directory of identity management aimed to encompass every device, user, and piece of infrastructure. Authenticating to the Domain Controller would be enough to get access to everything a user/machine needs and nothing they don’t.
This is the identity perimeter: where an identity is valid. In the Active Directory era, the perimeter was as large as possible. The more complete the perimeter, the more authoritative the directory. As an example, SQL Server accepts Windows authentication (i.e. an AD identity) or SQL authentication (username and password). Active Directory admins choose Windows auth to keep the perimeter large.
Anything outside of the directory would be a “shadow identity”: a valid identity that grants access to corporate infrastructure, but isn’t accounted for in identity management (unless you consider the post-it note on my monitor identity management).
A separate username-password set creates a separate perimeter. This used to be a problem, but is now the norm. Each API key, database string, or auth token creates a separate perimeter because they’re a credential that represents an identity for just one service. As an example, GitHub automation requires personal access tokens or GitHub private keys and doesn’t work with any directory identity.
But just to make it harder, zero-trust architecture makes machines constantly authenticate to each other, which skyrockets the count of credentials and creates hundreds of perimeters.
In theory, a small perimeter shrinks the blast radius of any breach: A compromised Notion session token should only give Notion access. In practice, an attacker may find additional credentials in Notion, which lets them expand their access. Oh, and the physical security layer of firewalls and physical perimeters is gone in the cloud era, so a leaked credential works from any attacker’s laptop.
This should concern admins more than it does: many teams keep troves of sensitive plaintext credentials in .env files or hardcode them in configuration files. The response is often lackluster:
- Use SSO where it’s available for human users
- Teach the team how to securely handle plaintext machine credentials
A solution like Active Directory is nearly useless for solving these issues.
The new paradigm
Organizations can tame the complexity of machine identity in the cloud, but not as simply as one massive Active Directory list. Instead, we see two main vectors to fix this:
The first is identity federation, where one platform trusts another platform’s approval to authenticate a workload. All three major clouds support this.
Using OpenID Connect (OIDC), AWS can sign a token for an EC2 instance to access PostgreSQL in Azure. Entra federated credentials natively support this use case and would trust the EC2 workload.
This works for many use cases. If you’re exclusively on AWS and run Terraform from GitHub Actions, OIDC federation straight into IAM does the job: You get visibility, know why you trust it, and know its scope. But it’s laborious to implement each relationship, which means it relies on IAM administrators who can barely keep up with group membership requests. Moreover, if said pipeline is breached by, say, a supply chain attack (which are common nowadays), the whole perimeter is breached.
Even if your admins are bored, no cloud has native bridges between every possible tool, so federation stops as soon as any service only accepts an API key. Organizations shouldn’t accept unruly, long-standing plaintext credentials outside of security purview.
That’s why organizations adopt a brokering approach. Here, credentials live in a secrets manager like Infisical (which securely stores and then delivers secrets to workloads at runtime). This creates a meta-perimeter for all of those micro-perimeters. Infisical (or another tool) acts like a broker: Machines authenticate to it, they broker access to the credential store, and inject the credentials the identity can read into its runtime.
These two patterns can bring order to the Wild West of machine identity in the cloud era. They check the boxes Active Directory once did:
- What identities exist? You have an overview of who authenticates and what they do
- What vouched for the identity? You know where workloads originate and why they’re trusted without relying on a human to approve everything
- Where is the identity valid? Keys, tokens, and strings have a natural perimeter.
This is especially important as organizations increasingly adopt AI agents, which often need their own identities, separate security policies, and even separate security tooling. Getting machine identity right is more important than ever. If you can’t keep track of testing databases and a Stripe API key, you don’t want autonomous software that can create its own databases and send that API key to strangers online.

Using human credentials to join new machines is a workaround that negates the point: Admin approval implies a human can tell you about each trusted device.
No admin can know every EC2 instance, PostgreSQL database, or CI runner in the organization. This is also because when AD was built, machine identities were long-lived devices, not ephemeral cloud resources.
Active Directory was built for human approval of long-lived infrastructure, but now often auto-approves short-lived cloud resources.
Even if you built all of the complex automations to reflect every testing database and Kubernetes pod in AD with automated admin approval, it’s security theater. The unified directory would exist on paper, but lack authority.
Modern cloud infrastructure automatically asserts machine identity:
- In Kubernetes, each pod gets a service account token, which allows it to assert its identity within the cluster.
- In Azure, you can configure a machine identity in Entra ID and let Azure’s Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) automatically issue OAuth tokens when machines request them.
These two examples have modern assumptions baked in: machines need to self-serve their identities when they’re spun up. They also assume a narrow scope.
Scope: how identity perimeters have changed
The unified directory of identity management aimed to encompass every device, user, and piece of infrastructure. Authenticating to the Domain Controller would be enough to get access to everything a user/machine needs and nothing they don’t.
This is the identity perimeter: where an identity is valid. In the Active Directory era, the perimeter was as large as possible. The more complete the perimeter, the more authoritative the directory. As an example, SQL Server accepts Windows authentication (i.e. an AD identity) or SQL authentication (username and password). Active Directory admins choose Windows auth to keep the perimeter large.
Anything outside of the directory would be a “shadow identity”: a valid identity that grants access to corporate infrastructure, but isn’t accounted for in identity management (unless you consider the post-it note on my monitor identity management).
A separate username-password set creates a separate perimeter. This used to be a problem, but is now the norm. Each API key, database string, or auth token creates a separate perimeter because they’re a credential that represents an identity for just one service. As an example, GitHub automation requires personal access tokens or GitHub private keys and doesn’t work with any directory identity.
But just to make it harder, zero-trust architecture makes machines constantly authenticate to each other, which skyrockets the count of credentials and creates hundreds of perimeters.
In theory, a small perimeter shrinks the blast radius of any breach: A compromised Notion session token should only give Notion access. In practice, an attacker may find additional credentials in Notion, which lets them expand their access. Oh, and the physical security layer of firewalls and physical perimeters is gone in the cloud era, so a leaked credential works from any attacker’s laptop.
This should concern admins more than it does: many teams keep troves of sensitive plaintext credentials in .env files or hardcode them in configuration files. The response is often lackluster:
- Use SSO where it’s available for human users
- Teach the team how to securely handle plaintext machine credentials
A solution like Active Directory is nearly useless for solving these issues.
The new paradigm
Organizations can tame the complexity of machine identity in the cloud, but not as simply as one massive Active Directory list. Instead, we see two main vectors to fix this:
The first is identity federation, where one platform trusts another platform’s approval to authenticate a workload. All three major clouds support this.
Using OpenID Connect (OIDC), AWS can sign a token for an EC2 instance to access PostgreSQL in Azure. Entra federated credentials natively support this use case and would trust the EC2 workload.
This works for many use cases. If you’re exclusively on AWS and run Terraform from GitHub Actions, OIDC federation straight into IAM does the job: You get visibility, know why you trust it, and know its scope. But it’s laborious to implement each relationship, which means it relies on IAM administrators who can barely keep up with group membership requests. Moreover, if said pipeline is breached by, say, a supply chain attack (which are common nowadays), the whole perimeter is breached.
Even if your admins are bored, no cloud has native bridges between every possible tool, so federation stops as soon as any service only accepts an API key. Organizations shouldn’t accept unruly, long-standing plaintext credentials outside of security purview.
That’s why organizations adopt a brokering approach. Here, credentials live in a secrets manager like Infisical (which securely stores and then delivers secrets to workloads at runtime). This creates a meta-perimeter for all of those micro-perimeters. Infisical (or another tool) acts like a broker: Machines authenticate to it, they broker access to the credential store, and inject the credentials the identity can read into its runtime.
These two patterns can bring order to the Wild West of machine identity in the cloud era. They check the boxes Active Directory once did:
- What identities exist? You have an overview of who authenticates and what they do
- What vouched for the identity? You know where workloads originate and why they’re trusted without relying on a human to approve everything
- Where is the identity valid? Keys, tokens, and strings have a natural perimeter.
This is especially important as organizations increasingly adopt AI agents, which often need their own identities, separate security policies, and even separate security tooling. Getting machine identity right is more important than ever. If you can’t keep track of testing databases and a Stripe API key, you don’t want autonomous software that can create its own databases and send that API key to strangers online.

Our Most Saved Sweet Potato Recipe Is A Thanksgiving Hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Our Most Saved Sweet Potato Recipe Is So Much Better Than the Thanksgiving Casserole
Sweet potatoes have been a staple in my household ever since I was little. My dad is from the South, so every Thanksgiving, Christmas, or other special occasion, there were always sweet potatoes (or candied yams) on the table — soft and covered in brown sugar, maple syrup, and butter.
I love sweet potatoes in any form — be it fries, simply baked, roasted, or mixed in a sweet potato pie. So when I saw Rachel, our culinary producer, whip up this melting sweet potato recipe, I was intrigued and knew I had to try this new method STAT. Let’s just say I wasn’t disappointed, and you won’t be either. 
Get the recipe: Melting Sweet Potatoes
What Makes Melting Sweet Potatoes So Good
The recipe is ready from start to finish in about 45 minutes, and the oven does most of the work. To start, coat sweet potatoes in a mixture of melted butter, olive oil, salt, pepper, and fresh rosemary. Then bake in the oven until they get nice and golden brown on each side. To get that melt-in-your-mouth texture (hence the name), vegetable or chicken broth is poured over the sweet potatoes, along with a few cloves of garlic, and cooked until all the liquid has been absorbed.
The texture of the sweet potato is unmatched. It’s SUPER soft, slices like butter, and literally melts in your mouth. The roasting technique really allows its natural, almost candy-like sweetness to come out, while the garlic, rosemary, and broth add moisture and depth of flavor. The sweet potatoes also get beautiful caramelization on the outside while the skin becomes crispy. They’re so delicious and would make a stunning side to whatever dish you pair it with.
How to Make Melting Sweet Potatoes
- Cut the sweet potatoes. Slice the sweet potatoes into 1-inch thick rounds, then toss in a mixture of melted butter, olive oil, salt, pepper, and fresh rosemary leaves. Arrange the potatoes onto a rimmed baking sheet or 9×13 baking pan.
- Roast the sweet potatoes. Bake the sweet potatoes in a preheated 500°F oven until they’re lightly browned on one side for 15 minutes, then flip each round and bake for another 15 minutes.
- Add the broth. Remove the pan from the oven and pour in vegetable or chicken broth and a few smashed garlic cloves. Return to the oven and bake once more for 15 minutes until the sweet potatoes are tender and the broth is absorbed. Remove from the oven and enjoy!
If You’re Making Melting Sweet Potatoes, a Few Tips
- Keep a close eye on the oven. Since the sweet potatoes bake at 500°F, a very high temperature, it’s easy for them to burn quickly. Every oven is different, so check them periodically while cooking. You may want to rotate the pan in the oven as well if there’s a hot spot.
- Swap the herbs. If rosemary’s not your thing, add whatever other fresh herbs suit your fancy. Thyme or fresh sage would be lovely.
Get the recipe: Melting Sweet Potatoes

Show HN: Coral – Open-source gateway where agents write their own tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:14:51 UTC
23:14:51 KST

Execution rails for agents.
Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs, and save the ones that work as custom tools to reuse. Coral checks every call against your policy before it adds credentials and forwards the call.
Quickstart · Download · Demo video
In this example, an agent posts unreviewed pull requests to Slack for the first time. The agent searches for the GitHub and Slack tools and writes code that calls them. It cannot post to Slack without approval, so the user approves the post. The agent then saves its code as a custom tool. The next day, the agent runs the same task by calling that custom tool.
Control what agents can do. Most MCP gateways decide only which tools an
agent can see. That is all or nothing: if an agent can call update_record, it
can update any record in any way the tool allows. A custom tool is code, so it
can hold a rule that Allow and Block cannot. For example, closeStaleTicket
changes one field, and only on tickets with no activity for 30 days. You set
Allow, Ask, or Block on the custom tool like any other tool. Coral still checks
every provider call inside it against your policy.
Less duplicated agent work. Agents start every task from scratch. They re-read tool schemas, retry failed calls, and spend tokens rewriting code for steps they got right yesterday. With Coral, agents save the code that worked as custom tools, and call them again in one step. Workspace owners can share those tools with the whole team.
Thousands of developers at more than 450 companies use Coral for safer, more efficient agent work. They use it in customer support, SecOps, business intelligence, SRE, and more.
- Install Coral. 
  - To use Coral yourself, download the desktop app from the download page. It runs on macOS (Apple silicon), Windows (x64), and Linux (x86_64).
  - To use Coral with your team, run a shared server with Docker Compose or Kubernetes. You need an OIDC identity provider, a reverse proxy for TLS, and SQLite or Postgres.
- Add a provider. A provider is one service your agents can use, such as GitHub or Linear. Pick one from the catalog, or bring your own OpenAPI document or MCP server. By default, tools that read data run right away and everything else needs your approval. See Add a provider.
- Connect your agent. Copy your workspace's MCP URL from the Coral UI and add it to your MCP client: claude mcp add --scope user --transport http coral <your-mcp-url> # Claude Code codex mcp add coral --url <your-mcp-url> # Codex For Cursor, VS Code, OpenCode, and other clients, see Connect an MCP client.
- Ask a question. Ask your agent something that uses that provider, such as "What are my open pull requests?"
We started Coral while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry and undocumented relationships between internal and external systems. It needed broad permissions and a lot of tokens, and it started from scratch the next time.
We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent saves the steps that worked as a custom tool. Next time, it finds that tool in the same search as provider tools such as Datadog and Slack. Coral started with SRE. Teams now use it for agent work across the organization:
- SRE. The agent investigates alerts. Custom tools let it roll back only the services you name.
- Customer support. The agent issues refunds, and escalates to a person in the cases you define.
- Business intelligence. Custom tools aggregate warehouse, CRM, and billing data, and pass only the metrics to the agent.
- SecOps. The agent uses custom tools to isolate devices within approved groups.
What you get:
- Precise control. Set Allow, Ask, or Block for each provider tool and each custom tool. An approval shows the exact call and its arguments, so Security approves one refund lookup, not the whole payments API. See Roles & Permissions.
- Shared tools. You can set each provider to use the caller's own account, so teammates share tools without sharing API tokens. Read how Slackbot uses this.
- Cheaper models, same accuracy. With custom tools, a smaller model performs like a bigger one. For many tasks, this means Opus 5.5 accuracy at Haiku 5.5 cost.
- Faster, leaner agents. Across 34 tasks on GitHub, Linear, and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools cut tokens by 37%, cost by 31%, and time by 29%. See every task.
- Ahead of other MCP gateways. In blind benchmarks of 100 enterprise tasks, agents were more accurate and cheaper with Coral than with other MCP gateways. See the benchmarks.
- Training data you own. Each run leaves a structured trace of the goal, the tools used, and the outcome. The trace works well for post-training your own model.
How Coral fits your stack:
- Runs on your infrastructure. Coral is written in Rust. It runs as a desktop app on your laptop or as a shared server in your own cloud, with zero data egress.
- Open source. Coral is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, with no limits on users, agents, or volume. Everything in this README outside Coral Enterprise is in the open-source edition.
- Any agent, any system. Coral works with any AI app or agent that supports MCP. You can connect anything with an MCP server or OpenAPI document, including more than 5,000 databases and SaaS tools.
Agents write programs. Coral builds on code mode, and adds custom tools, policy controls, and managed identities. To use tools, an agent writes a short TypeScript program. One program can call several tools, filter the results, and return only what the task needs. Less raw data passes through the model's context.
Coral runs them on rails. Each program runs in a fresh V8 isolate with no network access, no credentials, and no imports. Coral checks every tool call against your workspace policy, then adds the credentials and forwards the call to the provider. A policy can also require a person to approve the call. Coral attributes every run to the person or agent that started it.
graph LR
    Agent["Your agent"] -->|"exec: run a program"| MCP["Coral MCP server"]
    You["You"] -->|"providers, policy, approvals"| UI["Coral UI"]
    subgraph Coral["Coral (your laptop or server)"]
        MCP --> Run["Program runs in a V8 isolate"]
        Run <--> FN["Custom tools (private and shared)"]
        UI --> Gate["Policy check and credentials"]
        Run --> Gate
        Gate -.->|"approval request"| UI
    end
    Gate --> GH["GitHub"]
    Gate --> SL["Slack"]
    Gate --> Own["Your OpenAPI or MCP service"]
    The agent sends Coral programs through the exec tool. A program calls
coral.search to find the tools the agent can use and read their
TypeScript signatures. Then the agent sends a program that does the work.
This one finds open pull requests that have no reviewer and posts them to
Slack:
const { data: pulls } = await coral.providers.github.pulls.list({
    owner: "withcoral",
    repo: "coral",
    state: "open",
});
const unreviewed = pulls.filter((pull) => pull.requested_reviewers.length === 0);
await coral.providers.slack.chat.postMessage({
    channel: "#engineering",
    text: unreviewed.map((pull) => `#${pull.number} ${pull.title}`).join("\n"),
});
return unreviewed.map((pull) => pull.number);
If posting to Slack needs approval, the run pauses there until you approve it. Only the pull request numbers go back to the agent, not the full GitHub response. The run happens on the Coral server, so it continues even if the agent disconnects.
What works becomes a custom tool. When a program succeeds, the agent saves
it as a private tool. Next time, the agent calls it in one step as
coral.private.<name>({ ... }). Agents find custom tools in the same search
as provider tools, and reuse or edit them instead of starting over. A
workspace owner can publish a private tool as a shared tool under
coral.shared, so everyone in the workspace can call it.
To learn about providers, accounts, policy, and workspaces, read Concepts.
To run Coral for a team, see Run a shared server.
Coral Enterprise is coming soon under its own license. It adds organization-wide governance and support: SSO with SAML, SCIM provisioning, advanced RBAC, an immutable audit log, and support SLAs. See Coral Enterprise or book a demo.
To run Coral from a checkout, follow the
development guide. To contribute, read
CONTRIBUTING.md. The
release notes list what changed
in each version.
Ask questions, share ideas, and show what you built in our Slack community or on GitHub issues.
Do not report security issues in public issues or pull requests. See
SECURITY.md.
Coral is ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified. Each program runs in its own V8 isolate, and Coral logs every approval.
Coral is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE.
The ee/ directory holds Enterprise Edition code under its own license,
ee/LICENSE. A plain cargo build at the repository root
builds only code under the Apache License 2.0. NOTICE states
which license covers which files.
Coral v1 replaces the SQL interface with TypeScript programs. It starts from fresh state and does not convert what 0.x stored. If Coral finds 0.x state, it tells you at startup. See Upgrade from Coral 0.x.

Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you

Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days.
Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you
The AI-powered Ask Maps feature can suggest stops for your next trip, while providing real-time details about each location.
As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop.
You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip.
In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”
Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start.
