Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.
But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.
Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.
“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.
Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.
If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.
Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.
Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.
Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.
Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.
Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.
High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said.
Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.
“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”
That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.
“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”

====================================================================================================

Show HN: CheeseDB – agent memory where deleting a source deletes what it taught
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
13:54:50 UTC
22:54:50 KST

A database engine purpose-built for AI memory. Native Go · Provenance-aware · Revocable · Embedded
Every memory knows its sources. Ask it anything in plain English. Recall a bad source, and everything learned from it goes too.
An embedded, append-only, hash-chained memory database for AI agents, written in Go with the standard library only. Use it from Go, from the cheesedb command, or from Claude Code, Cursor and other MCP apps.
Website: cheesedb.dev
Status: preview. cheesedb is in active development. It has not yet had an independent security review, and the API and on-disk format may change before v1.0, so it is not yet recommended for production data. See Limits and the changelog.
An agent's memory is built from sources it cannot fully trust: user messages, web pages, documents, tool results. Sooner or later one of them turns out to be:
- wrong: a tool returned bad data;
- malicious: a web page planted instructions or false facts (prompt injection, memory poisoning);
- private: a user asks for their data to be deleted.
Deleting that source is not enough. Everything the agent learned from it stays in memory, and the agent keeps acting on it. A plain memory store cannot tell which memories came from where, so it cannot remove them. The demo shows this with a real LLM: after the bad source is deleted from a plain memory list, the model still gives the same wrong answer.
- Every memory records its sources. A memory is stored with the sources (or other memories) it was learned from. The engine refuses a memory without one.
- Recall removes exactly what depended on a source. One call removes the source and every memory built on it, however deep the chain goes. Memories that are still backed by another, independent source survive (Fair); or remove everything the source ever touched (Strict).
- Ask it in plain English. With an embedding model of your choice, cheesedb finds memories by meaning (search), answers questions from them (ask), and forgets what you describe after you confirm (forget). A recalled memory is never found again. Without a model, everything else works the same.
- Erase really erases. Recall(..., Erase) removes the text from the files on disk before it returns. cheesedb find searches the raw bytes to prove it.
- The history cannot be edited silently. Every record is chained by hash to the one before. Damage or edits are detected on every open, and erasing text keeps the chain verifiable.
- Agents are isolated by design. Each agent is reached only through its own token. No method takes another agent's name, so a prompt-injected tool holding one agent's handle has no way to reach another.
- Embedded and dependency-free. A Go library and a folder on disk: no server, no external dependencies.
You can model sources and memories in SQL, or as a graph in Neo4j. We did both, to compare: the same data on all four engines, with the same durability (every write flushed to the physical disk before it is acknowledged).
Benchmarks with 1M memories per agent, median of 3 runs, on an Apple M1 Max (macOS, internal SSD), SQLite 3.53, PostgreSQL 17 and Neo4j Community 2026.10. Full results, method and caveats: BENCHMARKS.md; the raw output of the run: bench/results/v0.3.0.
¹ A new connection to a server that is already running; booting the Neo4j server took 6.5 to 8.2 s in an earlier run. PostgreSQL and Neo4j ran over TCP on localhost, which adds a round trip to each statement. We wrote the Neo4j model and queries ourselves, and an expert may do better.
- Recall is where it wins. cheesedb keeps the dependency graph in memory and removes 10,000 memories with one write: about 13x faster than Neo4j, 45x faster than SQLite and 370x faster than PostgreSQL. The SQL versions run several statements for each affected memory. A graph database fits the job better, and Neo4j is the closest competitor, but it is still slower.
- The rules live in the engine, not in your code. No memory without a source, no memory built on a recalled source, recalls are permanent, agents cannot see each other. With SQL or a graph database you write and test these yourself.
- Erasure is built in. In a general database, a deleted row's bytes can stay in the files (free pages, the write-ahead log) until a vacuum or checkpoint. cheesedb's Erase rewrites the file without them before it returns.
- Writes are about even, because the disk flush dominates for every engine.
- You need SQL-style queries, filters or keyword search. cheesedb finds by id or by meaning. Keep other queries in your database, store only memory ids there, and check each result against cheesedb.
- Startup time matters with very long histories. cheesedb replays its log when it opens an agent: about 0.7 s at 1M memories. SQLite opens instantly. Snapshots are planned.
- An agent's memory does not fit in RAM. cheesedb keeps about 205 bytes per memory in memory, plus about 0.8 KB per searchable memory (768 values, one byte each).
- You need production guarantees today. cheesedb is a preview; see Limits.
go get github.com/govinargo-labs/cheesedb                          # the library
go install github.com/govinargo-labs/cheesedb/cmd/cheesedb@latest  # the command
Requires Go 1.26.5 or newer. Developed and tested on macOS; Linux runs the same tests in CI. Windows is not supported yet.
The peanut story, from the command line. A user is allergic to peanuts; a restaurant's web page says its satay sauce is peanut-free; the page turns out to be wrong.
cheesedb agent create story
cheesedb lot story user_message "I am allergic to peanuts"                           # lot 1
cheesedb lot story doctor_note "Allergy test result: peanut allergy confirmed"       # lot 2
cheesedb lot story web_page "Spice Garden menu: our satay sauce is peanut-free"      # lot 3
cheesedb remember story "The user is allergic to peanuts" 1 2                        # memory 4: from 1 OR 2
cheesedb remember story "Spice Garden's satay sauce has no peanuts" 3                # memory 5
cheesedb remember story "The satay at Spice Garden is safe for the user" 4,5         # memory 6: needs 4 AND 5
With an embedding model (setup), ask in your own words. Memories saved before the model was set up become searchable with cheesedb embed:
cheesedb embed story
cheesedb search story "can the user eat the satay at Spice Garden?"
# 6: The satay at Spice Garden is safe for the user (match 0.81)
# 5: Spice Garden's satay sauce has no peanuts (match 0.77)
# 4: The user is allergic to peanuts (match 0.57)
Without one, list what is alive: cheesedb active story.
Then the web page turns out to be wrong:
cheesedb recall story 3 fair erase        # recalled 3; memories removed: [5 6]
cheesedb search story "can the user eat the satay at Spice Garden?"
# 4: The user is allergic to peanuts (match 0.57)
cheesedb find story "peanut-free"         # not found anywhere (searched every file, byte by byte)
cheesedb recall story 1 fair erase        # memories removed: []: the doctor's note still backs the allergy
cheesedb verify story                     # OK. head fingerprint: ...
examples/plain-english runs this story step by step, with ask and a chat model, for a demo or a screen recording.
s, err := cheesedb.Open("/data/cheesedb")   // a folder you choose, created 0700
tok, err := s.CreateAgent("alice")        // returns Alice's token, once: keep it safe
alice, err := s.OpenAgent(tok)            // the only way to reach Alice's data
defer alice.Close()
a, _ := alice.AddLot("user_message", []byte("I live in Pune"))
b, _ := alice.AddLot("web_page", []byte("profile: lives in Pune"))
c, _ := alice.AddLot("weather_tool", []byte("Pune: rain"))
m1, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("user lives in Pune"), cheesedb.Leg{a}, cheesedb.Leg{b}) // learned from A, or from B
m2, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("Pune is rainy"), cheesedb.Leg{c})
m3, _ := alice.Remember([]byte("carry an umbrella"), cheesedb.Leg{m1, m2})            // needs M1 AND M2
removed, _ := alice.Recall(c, cheesedb.Fair, cheesedb.Untrusted) // the weather tool was wrong
// removed == [m2, m3]; m1 survives because it does not depend on C
cheesedb can find memories by meaning, so you and your AI can ask in your own words: "can the user eat the satay?" finds "the satay sauce has no peanuts". It needs an embedding model, which turns text into a list of numbers (a vector) so that texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. cheesedb stores the vectors, searches them, and removes them when their memory is recalled. The library never calls a model: the cheesedb command and its MCP server do, with the model you set up.
Set it up by adding an embedding model to ~/.cheesedb/llm.conf. Any OpenAI-compatible server works (Ollama, LM Studio, oMLX, vLLM, or a hosted API); a local one keeps your memories on your machine:
embed_base_url = http://localhost:11434/v1     # default: base_url
embed_model    = nomic-embed-text               # e.g. after: ollama pull nomic-embed-text
# embed_api_key = your-key                      (only if the server needs one)
If your chat server also serves the embedding model, embed_model alone is enough: the server and key are taken from base_url and api_key.
Use it:
cheesedb search alice "what should I eat?"    # the closest live memories, best first
cheesedb ask alice "what should I eat?"       # search, then the chat model answers from those memories only
cheesedb forget alice "the pizza place"       # shows the closest memory and what goes with it; erases after a yes
cheesedb embed alice                          # make memories saved before the model was set up searchable
cheesedb index alice                          # the agent's index and its model
Every memory saved with remember (in the command and in the MCP server) is made searchable at once, and MCP apps get a sixth tool, search. If the model is down, the memory is still saved and the answer says it is not searchable yet; cheesedb embed catches up. After changing the model, run cheesedb embed again: vectors of two models cannot be compared, so it rebuilds the index.
Without an embedding model, nothing changes: sources, memories, recall, erase, verify, reading by id, listing live memories and the five other MCP tools all work, and nothing is sent anywhere. If you already have a vector store, keep it, store only memory ids there, and check each result against cheesedb.
From Go, with vectors from any model:
alice.CreateIndex("default", 768, "nomic-embed-text") // dims and a label for the model
alice.Embed("default", m3, vec)                       // vec []float32 from your model
alice.EmbedBatch("default", items)                    // many at once, one disk sync per batch
hits, _ := alice.Search("default", queryVec, 5)       // []Hit{ID, Score}, best first
for _, h := range hits {
    it, _ := alice.Get(h.ID)                          // the text comes from the ledger
    fmt.Println(h.Score, string(it.Data))
}
ids, _ := alice.WouldRecall(m3, cheesedb.Fair)        // what a recall would remove, without removing it
- A recalled memory is never returned. Recall removes the vectors of everything it removes, at once. With Erase, the vectors are erased from disk together with the text, and both hash chains still verify (Verify, VerifyIndex). A vector can be turned back into an approximation of its text, so cheesedb treats it like the text.
- Exact search, small in RAM: the question is compared with every vector (cosine similarity), so there are no missed results and nothing to tune. In memory each vector takes one byte per value (about 0.8 KB at 768 values); the exact float32 values stay on disk, and the few rows that could still be in the top results are re-checked with them, so the answer is the same as a full float32 scan. The time grows with the number of memories; see How it scales.
- ask sends only what search found (10 memories by default) to the chat model, and tells it never to treat a missing memory as an answer, so it is told to say "I do not know" instead of guessing.
- forget finds memories, not sources. Sources are not in the search index; recall a source by its number. It shows everything that would go before it erases anything (WouldRecall).
- One index per model. Vectors from different models cannot be compared. From Go, to switch models, create a new index, embed into it, then DropIndex the old one.
- Without an index, nothing changes: same files, same head fingerprint, same speed. An index lives in its own folder with its own log (ARCHITECTURE.md section 9).
A Go program, offline with a stand-in embedder that matches shared words, or with a real model:
go run ./examples/vector-search
EMBED_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 EMBED_MODEL=nomic-embed-text go run ./examples/vector-search
cheesedb's own cost with a search index (768 values per memory), on an Apple M1 Max. No embedding model is included: with a local one, turning a question into a vector took 17 ms. Median of 3 runs; method and every number: BENCHMARKS.md.
The command and the MCP server open the store for every call, so each search reloads the index; they suit agents of up to about 100,000 memories. A Go program that keeps the store open loads it once. With real embeddings at 1M, search still ranked the right memories first among a million look-alikes, and none came back after their source was recalled.
The cheesedb command is a command-line tool with one command per feature, and a demo with a real LLM:
go install ./cmd/cheesedb     # puts cheesedb in ~/go/bin (add that folder to your PATH)
cheesedb help                 # every command
cheesedb agent create alice
cheesedb lot alice weather_tool "Pune: rain"
cheesedb demo                 # needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM (see cmd/cheesedb/llm.go)
It keeps its data in ~/.cheesedb (change it with CHEESEDB_DIR). The LLM commands read their server and model from ~/.cheesedb/llm.conf (search adds an embedding model there; see Ask in plain English):
base_url = http://localhost:8000/v1
model    = your-model-name
# api_key = your-key        (only if your server needs one)
The demo tells one story three ways. An agent learns from a user message, a web page and a weather tool. Then the weather tool turns out to be wrong. Here is a real run:
How to read it
- Three sources arrive. Each one is stored as a lot with a label: user_message, web_page, weather_tool.
- The model learns memories and says where each came from. The arrow on the right lists the sources: memory [6] came from [3], the weather tool. Memory [7] was built on [4] and [6].
- Ask a question. The model sees all 4 memories and answers from the weather forecast.
- The weather tool was wrong, so remove source [3] three ways:
  - A, a naive memory list. It deletes the source and nothing else. The model still sees the memories built from it, and gives the same answer.
  - B, cheesedb with Untrusted. One call removes [3] and everything learned from it, [6] and [7]. The model sees only 2 memories, so it no longer knows the forecast. The text is still in the files, and the demo finds the word "rain" in 3 places.
  - C, cheesedb with Erase. The model sees the same 2 memories, and the text is gone from the files. A search of every byte finds nothing.
- The table sums it up: does the model still use the bad data, and is the bad text still on disk?
cheesedb find runs the same byte-by-byte search, so you can check your own data.
cheesedb mcp <agent> serves one agent's memory to any app that speaks the Model Context Protocol (Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop and others), with no code. The app starts it and talks to it over standard input and output; nothing listens on a network port.
cheesedb agent create alice                      # once; the token is saved in ~/.cheesedb/tokens
claude mcp add cheesedb -- cheesedb mcp alice    # Claude Code
For apps with a settings file (Cursor, Claude Desktop), add the same command:
{ "mcpServers": { "cheesedb": { "command": "cheesedb", "args": ["mcp", "alice"] } } }
The model gets five tools, and a sixth, search, when an embedding model is set up (Ask in plain English):
A recall cannot be undone, so recall takes two calls. The first removes nothing: it lists what would be removed and gives a confirm code, and the model is told to show you the list and call again with the code only if you agree. The code fits only that exact list: if anything changes in between, the model gets a new preview instead. If your app supports MCP elicitation (forms a server can show you), the second call also asks you directly, in a form the model cannot fill in, and nothing is removed without your tick. In other apps the two calls are a speed bump, not a lock: a model that ignores its instructions can make both. There, set recall to need your approval in the app's tool permissions.
With an embedding model, the server also tells the model to search before it forgets a memory you describe in words. Search finds memories, not sources: to remove a source, the model recalls the id add_lot gave it.
The agent is fixed by the command line, and no tool takes an agent, so the model cannot switch to another agent through the tools. A tool that fails (an unknown id, a recalled parent) returns its reason to the model, which can correct its next call.
Things to know before you rely on it:
- The model declares the sources and legs itself. A recall is only as complete as the legs it wrote, and a prompt-injected model can declare them wrongly or recall things it should not (see Limits).
- A model that can also run shell commands as you can skip the tools and read every agent's files directly. Isolation holds only when the tools are the model's only way to the data. For real separation, the data would have to belong to another OS user, which is what the planned memory server is for.
- Each tool call opens the store and closes it again, so a second app window or the cheesedb command can use it in between. The cost is the replay time under Limits: small for a young agent, about 0.7 s per call at 1M memories. A search also reloads the index: 9 ms at 1,000 memories, 0.74 s at 100,000, 7.5 s at 1M (How it scales).
- Data lives in ~/.cheesedb, or in CHEESEDB_DIR if the app starts the command with that variable set, as for every cheesedb command.
- Lot: a source the agent learned from (a user message, a web page, a tool result). The caller labels it; cheesedb does not judge sources.
- Memory: something the agent knows.
- Leg: one way a memory was learned. A leg holds while ALL its parents are alive; a memory may have several legs.
- Fair recall: a memory survives while ANY of its legs holds.
- Strict recall: a memory dies if the recalled source is ANYWHERE in its history.
cheesedb enforces these itself; callers cannot get around them through the API:
- a memory always has at least one leg, and is never built on a recalled (dead) parent;
- recall is permanent;
- an agent's handle reaches only that agent's data (isolation by token);
- every write is on disk (fsync) before it is acknowledged, and a crash loses nothing that was acknowledged;
- damaged or edited records are detected (crc, content digest, hash chain);
- a search never returns a recalled lot or memory, and Erase removes their vectors from disk too.
Design: ARCHITECTURE.md. Security: THREAT_MODEL.md. Speed and size, including where cheesedb is slower than SQLite and PostgreSQL: BENCHMARKS.md.
Read these before relying on cheesedb.
Security
- Tamper-evident, not tamper-proof (v1). Anyone who can write the files can: 
  - change a record and rebuild every hash after it;
  - change or remove the newest records;
  - redact a record.
The files alone cannot reveal any of these. Verify() returns a head fingerprint: keep a copy somewhere else, and compare it later to detect them. v2 plans signed records and an external witness.
- Isolation stops mistakes and prompt injection, not the host program. A tool or agent holding Alice's handle cannot reach Bob. But the program that holds the store, or anyone with access to the folder as that OS user, can read every agent's files directly.
- Tokens are shown once. The store keeps only a hash of each token. A lost token cannot be recovered; the agent can only be deleted.
- Over MCP the model is not trusted, but it is powerful. It can add lots, declare legs, and recall (and by default erase) anything in its agent. An app that gives the model a shell lets it bypass the tools altogether. See Use from AI apps.
Data
- Legs are declared by the caller. Recall removes exactly what the declared legs say depends on a source. If a memory was really learned from a source but no leg says so, recalling that source will not remove it.
- Only Erase removes text from disk.
  - Recall(..., Erase) erases the text of the recalled source and of every dead memory below it before returning.
  - Recall(..., Untrusted) hides those memories from the agent, but their text stays in the files until Compact(), which runs only when you call it.
  - Memories still alive through another source keep their text.
- Deleting is not secure erasure. Earlier backups, snapshots and copies keep their data. SSDs and file systems (such as APFS) may keep old blocks after a file is removed.
- Agent names are compared byte by byte. Two names that look the same but are encoded differently in Unicode are two different agents.
Operations
- Damage near the end of an agent's log is cut off, not refused. A crash can leave a half-written batch (up to about 1 MiB) at the end of the active segment, so Open cuts any damage in that last region and reports it in Report.DroppedBytes. Real damage there, even one flipped byte, therefore drops every record after it. In a young agent whose log is under 1 MiB, that can be the whole log. Check Report() after opening. Sealed segments do not have this weakness: damage there is always ErrCorrupt. Batch commit markers could remove it later.
- Windows does not flush directories. Windows rejects Sync on a directory handle ("Access is denied"), so syncDir is a no-op there: a segment or agent folder created, a rename, or a seal file written just before a crash is not guaranteed on disk when the write returns. NTFS journals metadata, so the entry is usually recovered, but the guarantee is weaker than on macOS and Linux. Windows support remains on the roadmap; see issue #26.
- One open store per folder. cheesedb.Open locks the folder; a second process gets cheesedb.ErrLocked until the first calls Close. The lock works on macOS, Linux, the BSDs and Windows, on a local disk. It may not work on network drives (NFS, SMB), and other systems (for example Solaris, AIX) get no lock.
- Startup replays the whole log. It grows with history: about 0.7 s for an agent with 1M memories (BENCHMARKS.md).
- The whole memory graph is kept in RAM: about 205 bytes per memory. An agent's graph must fit in memory.
- About 200 durable writes per second per agent on the test machine, limited by fsync. Different agents write in parallel.
- A damaged agent key file stops the whole store from opening. It is reported rather than skipped, because skipping would hide that agent's data.
- Search is exact, and its index lives in RAM. The index format may still change. Every question is compared with every vector, so search slows as an agent grows; every vector is kept in RAM at one byte per value (about 0.8 KB at 768 values), and the first search after opening reads the whole index from disk. Each cheesedb command and each MCP tool call opens the store again, so at 1M memories every search pays that load (How it scales). No keyword search and no filters yet.
- A damaged index blocks Erase and Compact for that agent until it is dropped, because they could not erase its vectors. So does a dropped index whose folder could not be deleted. The agent itself still opens and works. If a crash interrupted an erase and an index is damaged at the next open, the erase stays pending, text included, until the index is dropped and Compact runs (Report().UnfinishedErase says so).
- The embedding server sees what is remembered and searched. The cheesedb command and MCP server send each new memory's text, and each search question, to the embedding server you set up. A local server keeps them on your machine; a hosted one keeps whatever its provider keeps, and an Erase cannot reach that copy.
- Older versions ignore indexes. If a version without indexes erases a memory, its vectors stay on disk until a current version next loads the index. Do not use an older version on a store with indexes when erasure matters.
Planned work, roughly in order. Plans can change, and nothing here is a promise of a date.
Toward v1.0 (a stable API and on-disk format)
- Windows support. The file lock already works; directory flushing and replacing an open file during Erase are the gaps.
- More fuzzing and crash tests. The record decoder already has a fuzz test. Still to do: feed damaged and truncated files to Open, and kill the process mid-write, to check recovery.
- Independent security review before anything is recommended for real data.
- Batch commit markers, so recovery can tell a half-written last batch from older damage exactly (see Limits).
Next
- Shared memory between agents. A shared space with named members and roles (read, write, admin), every record showing who wrote it, and a way to carry a recall of a shared memory into the private memories built on it. Design in progress.
- Automatic compaction, for example when dead text passes a size threshold. Today Compact() runs only when you call it.
- Encryption per agent. The record format already reserves a key id for it.
Memory server (v2)
- A server for several programs, over a Unix socket only, with per-agent tokens and access logging.
- Read tracking: what an agent read while answering becomes part of what its new memories depend on.
- Trust levels per source type, set by a rule table you configure.
- Signed records and signed head fingerprints, sent to an outside witness, so edits by someone with file access can be detected (see Limits).
- The MCP server moves onto the memory server, so several apps share one running process.
Search (v2.5)
- Faster search for large agents: keeping the index loaded between MCP calls, a lighter load, and an approximate index (IVF).
- Keyword search, and search that combines keywords with meaning.
- Sources in the search index, so forget can find a source by description too.
Scale (v3)
- Snapshots, so opening an agent loads a saved state and replays only newer records, instead of the whole log.
- Concurrent writers across agents, and log-shipping replication checked by the hash chain.
Under consideration (candidates we are weighing, not commitments; each needs a design first)
- Lossless compaction for long conversations. Store every message and tool result as a source, and make a conversation's summary a memory linked to them. A detail the summary dropped can then be pulled back exactly, and recalling a message also removes every summary built from it. Long agent sessions today lose earlier details when they are summarized to fit the context window.
- Superseding outdated facts. "I moved to Mumbai" retires "lives in Pune" and everything built on it, with a record of why, instead of both staying and contradicting each other.
- Blast radius and trace. For a source: every memory it shaped, before or after a recall. For a memory: the sources behind it. Also as MCP tools, so a model can find and recall a source it did not save in the same conversation.
- Source versions. When a document is updated, or access to it is revoked, the answers and summaries built from it become stale or are removed, instead of lingering in caches.
- Timestamps and model version on records, for traceability rules such as the EU AI Act's logging duty, while Erase still removes the content.
- A memory-mapped vector file, so the command and the MCP server search without reloading the whole index on every call.
- Session summaries for MCP apps that cannot hand cheesedb whole conversations.
"Lot" and "recall" are food-safety words. A cheese maker records which milk lots went into which wheels, so when one lot turns out to be contaminated, they recall exactly the cheese made from it. cheesedb does the same for what an agent remembers.

I do a web search of “w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com” and I see references to the Majestic Million, a name I haven’t heard in ages. Sure enough, that’s what siterate.org uses:
The Majestic Million ranks domains based on the number of different subnets linking to them.5 This domain is the fastest growing in the top 100.
Another, maybe unrelated anomaly I saw is ailawandorder.com (registered in 2023) at rank 80, whose “About Us” page says its CEO is serving as a Board Member at Majestic. This made me check rank 800 in case there was a pattern, and no, there isn’t, that’s nsw.gov.au.
Before I got rate limited from Majestic, I opened Site Explorer, and it told me w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com has 241,085,378 nofollow backlinks and 6 follow backlinks split across 5,163,708 referring domains. Checking Ahrefs, I see just 53 backlinks; they read like the ones I’ve been getting since The Article fell off.
All the backlinks on Majestic are “fresh”, which means in the last 120 days. In fact, the domain was bought (not by me 💔) for the first time (according to Certificate Transparency) on November 11, after most of the backlinks. I found an AI-generated PR from 2 weeks ago referencing the domain, and Tranco has data from October 5.
Majestic has indexed 1,267 pages on this domain and crawled 27. The site isn’t on the Wayback Machine so I can’t collect its pages.
In the Anchor Text table, the link count adds up to nine. There isn’t an “other” section. Are the remaining 240 million links images? No, they aren’t, it says the links are 100% TextLinks.
Then I downloaded Majestic Million myself and searched for the domain. There were six subdomains.
- 5721d0cd26c13f745e1b368a2b5dfb0c.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 157
- c0e3930fedc480e093a7bcad1a83c8a8.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 424
- 8628e302afeb346d191342ca114df068.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 554
- 2b1774347fbd085c628179dd339ddd26.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 822
- e62f444581ce540d3cf5ac627b37c501.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 1,111
- 56aa73e7edd6f4e1fd3975b8b03761c0.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 36,933
For comparison, jack.cab, which you’ve clearly heard of, is rank 804,163. What the fuck is going on?
By the way, w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com is at rank 38 on Tranco, which was designed to protect against this but still uses Majestic data.
Theories
I could probably figure out what’s happening here in 30 seconds by buying a Majestic subscription but I’m lazy.
- Copyright trap: maybe it’s fake, injected into the list by Majestic so they can discover who’s using their list. Could w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com and ailawandorder.com be in the top 100 for this reason? Probably not, because if they cared, they’d relicense the list away from CC-BY. Also, the domains are ranking higher in Majestic over time instead of staying static.
- Majestic got hacked, and the hackers for some reason decided to tamper with the DB like this. No. Are you stupid, are you dumb, are you Dario Amodei, are you all three‽
- Some loophole/gaming the rankings: Maybe “subnets” is counted in a stupid way for IPv6. Maybe the millions of domains are ip6.arpa. Majestic counts Class C subnets.
- A bunch of hacked websites linking to the domain: Seems unlikely, considering I’m unable to find a single backlink in the wild that wouldn’t be there for say, my website, and Ahrefs only has 53 backlinks for this domain. They could be cloaking.
Update (November 16): Answer!
Love the article! I work for Majestic
Great spot.
the answer:
Some internal experimentation. Choose a domain, make it esoteric, do some experiments. However, looks like we forgot to add a filter to avoid reporting it. We will sort that…
Moral of the story: don’t test in production.

Amazon's Discount Illusion: 1 in 3 "Deals" Offered No Savings– 1 in 10 Cost More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
13:39:07 UTC
22:39:07 KST

Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive
Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive
A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events. The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts, examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier.
The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales.
Groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page says, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.”
Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens, shared the following reaction:
“Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette.
“Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.”
Owens is the author of the recent book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet, which exposes how corporations are sophisticated pricing schemes to overcharge consumers.
- The report’s key findings include:
  - The price of nearly 1 in 3 products that Amazon described as “deals” was the same – or higher – during sale events than what customers could have purchased them for in the month leading up to the sale.
  - Some Amazon “deals” offered shoppers higher prices than they could have paid before the sale.
    - On Black Friday 2025, a pair of yellow Hunter Women’s Short Rain Boots “on sale” for $126.99 had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started, meaning customers looking for a deal could’ve paid 59% more if they waited for the sale.
    - On Cyber Monday 2025, a pair of men’s UGG Butte boots “on sale” for $179.98 had been $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event, meaning the “deal” cost 83% more than the recent low.
    - Among these “worse” deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid for the products in the weeks leading up to the sale.
- Since learning of our study, Amazon has removed the aforementioned deal pages our study drew from, but archived versions of these pages can be found at the following links: Black Friday 2024, Cyber Monday 2024, Black Friday 2025, Cyber Monday 2025.
- Amidst the ongoing affordability crisis, millions of Americans count on holiday sale events, like Black Friday, to deliver real savings. In 2025, a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions.
- Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts and require retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale.
ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND 
The new report builds on Groundwork’s work exposing corporate pricing abuses and delivering results for American consumers.
- In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to expose how Instacart was charging shoppers different prices for the exact same groceries at the same store and time.
- Following the publication of Groundwork’s Owens’ book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet, the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into major retailers’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, adding to growing scrutiny of corporate pricing practices and their impact on Americans’ wallets in response to Groundwork and Owens’ research.
- In October 2026, Groundwork exposed Walmart’s creepy patent filings and pricing playbook. The report digs into patent filings, privacy disclosures, and technology investments to reveal how the retailer is building the infrastructure that could allow it to deploy personalized pricing at scale.

Show HN: OpenTodo – a self-hosted, local-first task manager in one Go binary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
13:21:53 UTC
22:21:53 KST

Plan your day without renting your to-do list.
OpenTodo is a free, open-source to-do app you run on your own server or have hosted for you. It works on your phone and your computer, even offline, shares lists with your family or your team, and keeps your data with you.
Try the demo · Install · Docs · Website
New: OpenTodo for iPhone and iPad is in the App Store. It's the first release, a first step: it connects to your OpenTodo server and adds reminders on the phone, the share sheet, a Today widget and Face ID unlock. Expect some rough edges; tell us what to improve.
Ways to run it: PikaPods (hosted, no server needed) · Docker · Umbrel (coming soon) · Unraid · Home Assistant · Kubernetes (Helm) · Single binary · iPhone and iPad app (App Store) · Android app (APK from GitHub; Google Play and F-Droid coming soon) · all 20 platforms
Type a task the way you say it: Call Sarah next Wed 3pm #work p1 sets the date, time, project and priority. Dictate it, send a page from your phone's share menu or the browser extension (Chrome, Firefox), or forward an email. Anything without a home lands in the Inbox. Quick add · Voice · Capture
Today shows what is due and what is still open from earlier. Give tasks an estimate and drag them onto the Day or Week calendar to see whether the day fits. Today · Time blocking
Open one task in Focus and start a Pomodoro, Flowtime or countdown timer. The time is logged to the task. Focus
Share a project with your family or your team as viewer, editor or admin. Assign tasks, comment, and see what changed. Everyone can edit offline. Sharing
- Your data stays yours. Everything lives in one folder on your server. Export it at any time, import it anywhere, and schedule backups, encrypted if you like, to disk, S3 or WebDAV. Backups · Import and export
- Works offline on every device. Each phone and computer keeps a full copy, so the app works with no connection and syncs when it's back. Install the app
- Bring your tasks. Import from Todoist, TickTick, Things, Super Productivity, Microsoft To Do, Apple Reminders and more, with a preview and undo. Import
- Private by design. No telemetry, no analytics, no third-party scripts. Turn on end-to-end encryption and the server holds only ciphertext. Privacy · Encryption
- Bring your own AI, if you want it. Talk to an assistant in the app, or connect the one you already use. Off by default, and every change can be undone. AI
No subscription, no lock-in, no tracking.
✅ yes · ❌ no · ⚠️ partly, or not documented. Todoist and TickTick have a free plan with limits; Things is a one-time purchase per device type. Based on each product's public information as of November 2026. If an entry is wrong, open an issue with a source.
- No install: open the demo and press Try the demo. You get a private copy with sample data, deleted after a few hours.
- On your machine or server: docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v opentodo-data:/data ghcr.io/opentodoapp/opentodo:stable Open http://localhost:8080. The first visit creates your account. No configuration needed.
git clone https://github.com/OpenTodoApp/OpenTodo.git
cd OpenTodo
docker compose up -d
Data is kept in the opentodo-data volume. On a server reachable from the internet, finish setup right after starting it, or set OPENTODO_SETUP_CODE=required (the setup code). Behind a reverse proxy, set OPENTODO_BASE_URL=https://todo.example.com.
The image is published for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. :stable is the latest release, :1 follows every 1.x release, a minor tag such as :1.5 gets that line's fixes only, a full version such as :1.5.0 pins one release, and :latest follows the main branch. Upgrades from any release since 0.1.0 work directly, and nothing you rely on breaks within 1.x (stability). More in Running with Docker.
Download opentodo-<os>-<arch> for Linux, macOS or Windows from the latest release and run it. It serves on port 8080 and keeps its data in ./data. To build from source: make build && ./bin/opentodo (Go 1.26+ and Node 22+).
Managed hosting: PikaPods. These links support the project: OpenTodo receives a share when you host through them.
Nothing is required. Every setting is an optional environment variable with a safe default: see the configuration reference. To add people, keep sign-up closed and send invitation links (managing users).
The self-hosting handbook covers every platform, TLS, backups, upgrades and monitoring. The ot command-line client is in the CLI guide.
The app talks only to your own server: no analytics, crash reporters, update pings or third-party fonts. Two things are on by default and can be turned off: maps for task locations, fetched through your server with no account data, and web push to the service each phone's browser chose. Everything else the server contacts, such as webhooks, backup destinations, single sign-on, email or an AI provider, is something you set up. The audit log never records task content (what is logged).
Read the docs with screenshots and search at open-todo.app/docs, or in the app under Help. The same pages are in docs/.
- Start here: getting started · all user guides
- Self-hosting: handbook · configuration · backups
- Build on it: REST API · OpenAPI description · CLI · AI and agents · stability
- Project: changelog · roadmap · security
Every server describes its API at /api/v1/openapi.json (OpenAPI 3.1, generated from the code, stable through 1.x). Point a generator at it and you have a typed client:
curl -s https://todo.example.com/api/v1/openapi.json -o openapi.json
npx openapi-typescript openapi.json -o opentodo.d.ts
The same file is docs/openapi.json and an asset of every release. Sign in with an API token from Settings → Integrations → API tokens; the API guide has the details, and ot, the Obsidian plugin and the n8n nodes are clients built on it.
Under the hood
┌───────────────────────── device ─────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────── server ────────────┐
│ React PWA  ──►  IndexedDB (source of truth)              │      │ Go binary + SQLite             │
│                 │ every edit = field ops {ts, device}    │ sync │  ops log (append-only)         │
│                 └► outbox ──────────────────────────────►├─────►│  fields (last-writer-wins)     │
│                 ◄─ ops from other devices ◄──────────────┤◄─────┤  REST, CalDAV, email, import   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │  all write through ops         │
                                                                  └────────────────────────────────┘
- Every change is a small operation that sets one field of one entity, stamped with a hybrid logical clock and the device id.
- Devices apply changes locally first, then sync. The same per-field rule runs everywhere, so all devices agree no matter the order. Notes merge character by character.
- The REST API, CalDAV, email and imports write through the same log, so a task created with curl shows up on your phone right away.
- One Go binary with the web app inside and a single SQLite file. It idles at about 20 MB of memory and runs on a Raspberry Pi.
More in architecture and the sync protocol.
- Star and share. A star on GitHub helps other people find OpenTodo.
- Leave feedback in Discussions or on Discord.
- Report bugs in issues.
- Review a translation. The app speaks eight languages; tell us where a word feels wrong (translating).
- Test it on your devices and report back in the call for testers.
- Answer questions from other people in Discussions and on Discord.
- Sponsor: buy me a coffee or GitHub Sponsors.
To contribute code, read CONTRIBUTING.md: changes that alter behaviour start as an OpenSpec change. Security issues go to the address in SECURITY.md.
OpenTodo is free and always will be. If it helps you, you can buy a coffee or sponsor it; the support page says what it costs to run and where the money goes.
Thank you to everyone who keeps OpenTodo going. Supporters who want to be listed appear here.
AGPL-3.0-only. You can run, study, modify and share OpenTodo freely. If you offer a modified version as a network service, you must offer its source under the same license. That is what keeps a self-hosted project from being quietly turned back into a subscription.

After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.
Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.
ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.
Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.
ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.
But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.
The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.)
Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.
ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.
Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry.
Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.
The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.
My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.
“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.
Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.
“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”
Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.
In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.
Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.
ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”
ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.
But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.
Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.
That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.
Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.
“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”
Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.
Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.
The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said.
To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.
Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.
The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
12:52:05 UTC
21:52:05 KST

Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that’s designed to help users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they jump in and start listening to it. The new audio discovery feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story, in addition to recommended audiobook collections that are personalized to individual listening tastes.
Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
Audible’s new audio discovery feature will read you an AI overview of your next audiobook.
Audio discovery provides a soundbite synopsis, with the aim of preventing Audible users from having to research titles on other platforms. The feature plays users a snippet of the audiobook and a brief AI-generated overview including its themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. It can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews.
“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product and analytics officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.”
Audio discovery is rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions.
Audible is also using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes, in an effort to make titles that don’t appear on best-selling lists easier to discover. Like audio discovery, these personalized collections are rolling out to customers in the US, and also include commentary from Audible’s editors.
These are the latest AI-powered features that Audible is introducing in an effort to attract new users and fend off growing competition from rival platforms like Spotify. As part of this update, Audible is also expanding two beta features: Ask a Question, which allows users to ask AI about characters, plot points, references, and more; and Recaps, which provides spoiler-free audio summaries of what the user has already listened to. These are now available for a “select set” of additional English-language titles in the US, according to Audible, with a broader rollout planned to start in December.

Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.
Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.
Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.
That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.
At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.
Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.
The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”
Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.
Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.
“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.
Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.
Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.
Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

Zoox robotaxis are now on the Uber app in Las Vegas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Zoox robotaxis are officially available through the Uber app in Las Vegas, marking the Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company’s first partnership with a third-party ride-hailing platform.
The launch on Monday is a milestone for both companies. Uber gets to add another partner to its app as part of its broader strategy to become the primary purveyor of autonomous vehicle technology in North America, Europe, and the Middle East. Uber has partnered with more than 30 companies developing autonomous vehicle technology for sidewalk delivery robots, self-driving cars, robotaxis, and drones — though not all of those have turned into commercial deployments yet.
For Zoox, the partnership and launch gives it access to more potential customers who might otherwise not try its robotaxi, a needed boost as it trails market leaders Tesla and Waymo.
The partnership is expected to extend beyond Las Vegas. Zoox will begin initial robotaxi operations in Los Angeles this year (introducing the robotaxi and opening rides to Zoox employees, family, and friends), but commercial service will not begin until 2027. Rides will be available via the Uber app next year as well.
For now, all eyes are on Las Vegas, Zoox’s first commercial market and a city where Uber has ambitious robotaxi plans.
The two companies also announced a multi-year partnership with MGM Resorts International: they’re rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts properties in Las Vegas. Uber and Zoox said they’ll work with MGM Resorts to improve pickup and drop-off locations, along with signage to help riders navigate sprawling MGM properties and find the robotaxis.
Earlier this year, the Nevada Transportation Authority unanimously approved a permit that allowed Uber to deploy up to 1,000 robotaxis in Clark County — home to Las Vegas — through its partnerships with Hyundai subsidiary Motional and Zoox.
Zoox’s addition to the Uber app comes with some initial limitations. Customers won’t be able to select a Zoox robotaxi — at least initially. Instead, people who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save ride may be matched with one of Zoox’s custom-built robotaxis once they hail a ride. Customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi by opting for autonomous rides through “ride preferences” in the Uber app’s settings.
Uber plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
“Las Vegas will become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app,” he said on the call. “We will begin with limited fleets and expand supply over the coming months, with plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in our app.”
The plan to offer a dedicated autonomous option marks a shift in Uber’s approach to robotaxis, including its partnership with Waymo.
That exclusive partnership, which matches Waymo robotaxis with Uber riders in Austin and Atlanta, will end in January 2028. Waymo plans to offer its rides directly through its own smartphone app as it does in other cities. TechCrunch previously confirmed with Uber that it still plans to host Waymo robotaxis on its app for as long as the two companies agree.
And unlike its partnership with other AV developers, Uber told TechCrunch that it will not provide maintenance and other services for Zoox in the Las Vegas market.

The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
11:39:31 UTC
20:39:31 KST

The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life
Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.
Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.
So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.
I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”
And so it is.
So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.
Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…

Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.” […]

Jonas on November 2nd, 2011
Hi,
Your trcik worked for me but with something more. As anybody knows now, this problem is caused by residual charge which prevent the Thinkpad to boot (is it a BIOS bug?). The solution is to drain complety the electricity off the Thinkpad and to reboot it.
For me it happened that the button trick wouldn’t work alone. I have to connect my T60 (without the battery) to my unplugged maxi dock, and wait for the “eject” LED to lit. Then I let my Thinkpad as is, the dock’s LED consuming the residual electricity (I let it as is a few hours). When the LED turend OFF, I did the button trick to ensure that no electricity would stay and I replugged the battery. The Thinkpad rebooted, good as new!

RickyJo on March 26th, 2013
I think 2Smart is right. It’s not entirely uncommon for one to have to press the power button once or twice with no power attached to release the residual charge built up in capacitors. When the unit attempts to start it will use up the remaining power in the unsuccessful attempt. From there, you can sometimes start the machine. A common manifestation of this problem is fans spinning but no display. This can manifest after a power outage or other unexpected shut down.
It sounds to me like this particular system board has issues discharging properly.
Having worked phone support myself I know how these sort of myths can spawn and grow–people do what has worked for them without a full understanding of why–which is totally cool most of the time. In the end, it doesn’t matter; regardless of if people press and hold it a few moments or ten times it will still work the same.

WCR on September 10th, 2014
1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.
Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.
I hope this helps
Wine Computer Repair & Security

3 Solutions:
1 – The power button trick works, but not for every case, remove battery, remove power supply and PRESS 15 (or 20) times then keep pressing in the last one for 30 seconds.
2 – Remove Battery for at least 6 hours (could be less) and press the power button. (this one worked for me, but the issue happened again next morning)
3 – Download the Official Update for this BIOS from LENOVO’s website, run the upgrade tool, let it finish. After 2nd Solution This solve the Issue once and for all.
